While Adonijah feasted with his supporters at En-rogel, Nathan warned Bathsheba that David had sworn Solomon would reign after him, and Bathsheba reminded David of his oath before Nathan confirmed it. David swore again that Solomon would sit on his throne that very day, and ordered Zadok and Nathan to take Solomon to Gihon, anoint him, blow the trumpet, and proclaim, 'God save King Solomon.' The sound of the city rejoicing reached Adonijah's feast, and his guests scattered in fear. Adonijah fled to the horns of the altar, and Solomon spared him on condition of good behaviour. Before he died, David charged Solomon to walk in God's ways, and Solomon then dealt with the old scores: Adonijah was executed when he asked for Abishag as wife, a renewed claim on the throne; Abiathar was banished to Anathoth; Joab, who had fled to the altar, was executed for the murders of Abner and Amasa; and Shimei, who had cursed David, was confined to Jerusalem and later executed for leaving it. So the kingdom was established in Solomon's hand.
Discussion: Succession is where character shows: Adonijah crowned himself at a feast while David still lived, and Solomon's throne was secured by oath, anointing, and hard judgments on old crimes. David's charge to walk in God's ways sits beside his instructions to settle scores, and the two sit uneasily together. Reflect: 1) How do you tell ambition from legitimate succession? 2) What does David's failure ever to ask Adonijah 'Why?' suggest about parenting and leadership? 3) When does settling old scores become justice, and when revenge?
Significance: Solomon's succession turned a feast-day coup into a settled throne, through David's oath, Solomon's anointing at Gihon, and the removal of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei.
KeyPeople: King Solomon; Adonijah, Son of Haggith; Bathsheba; Nathan, Prophet; King David
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple

Retelling: Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh's daughter as wife, bringing her to the city of David until he had finished building his house, the house of the LORD, and Jerusalem's wall. Then Solomon went to Gibeon to sacrifice, for that was the great high place, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there. At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night and said, 'Ask what I shall give thee.' Solomon answered by remembering God's mercy to David his father, confessing that he was but a little child who did not know how to go out or come in, and asking for an understanding heart to judge God's great people and to discern between good and bad. The speech pleased the LORD, who said that because Solomon had asked for wisdom rather than long life, riches, or the lives of his enemies, he would give him a wise and understanding heart such as none before or after him would have, and would also give him riches and honour he had not asked for, so that no king would be like him all his days, with long life added if he walked in God's ways as David had. Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream, and he returned to Jerusalem and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the ark and made a feast for all his servants.
Discussion: Solomon's wisest moment was admitting he was a child who did not know how to lead. God rewarded the request for discernment with everything Solomon had not asked for. Reflect: 1) If God asked you tonight what you wanted, what would you actually answer? 2) How does admitting you do not know how to lead change the way you lead? 3) What gifts have come to you precisely because you asked for something else?
Significance: At Gibeon, Solomon's request for an understanding heart won him wisdom, riches, and honour, and set the terms for his whole reign.
RelatedEvents: Solomon's Wise Judgment

Story: The Queen of Sheba Visits Solomon
Retelling: When the queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions. She arrived at Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels bearing spices, very much gold, and precious stones, and she communed with Solomon about all that was in her heart. Solomon answered all her questions, and there was not anything hidden from the king which he told her not. When the queen saw all Solomon's wisdom, the house he had built, the meat of his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance of his ministers and their apparel, his cupbearers, and his ascent to the house of the LORD, there was no more spirit in her. She told the king that the report she had heard in her own land was true, and behold, the half had not been told her: his wisdom and prosperity exceeded the fame she had heard. Blessed be the LORD thy God, she said, who delighted in thee to set thee on the throne of Israel, because the LORD loved Israel for ever and made thee king to do judgment and justice. She gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, a great abundance of spices, and precious stones, and Solomon gave her all her desire, whatever she asked, besides what he gave out of his royal bounty. Then she returned to her own land with her servants.
Discussion: The queen of Sheba came to test Solomon and left blessing his God. Her visit shows wisdom as witness: a foreign ruler recognised the LORD through the order, justice, and splendour of Solomon's court. Reflect: 1) What would a visitor conclude about your God from the way your household or work is ordered? 2) How do hard questions strengthen faith rather than threaten it? 3) Why does the queen praise God, not Solomon, at the end of her visit?
Significance: The queen of Sheba's visit turned Solomon's wisdom into a witness, as a foreign ruler blessed the LORD who had set him on Israel's throne.
RelatedEvents: Building of Solomon's Temple

Retelling: King Solomon loved many strange women, together with Pharaoh's daughter: women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites, nations of which the LORD had said, 'Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods.' Solomon clung to these in love, and he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned away his heart. For when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. He went after Ashtoreth, goddess of the Zidonians, and Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites, and built a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, and for Molech, the abomination of Ammon, on the hill before Jerusalem, and did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods. The LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the LORD God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice, and who had commanded him concerning this very thing, that he should not go after other gods. The LORD said he would rend the kingdom from Solomon's son, leaving only one tribe for David's sake and for Jerusalem's sake, and he stirred up adversaries against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, Rezon of Damascus, and Jeroboam, Solomon's own servant, who had lifted up his hand against the king.
Discussion: Solomon's fall was gradual and relational: love for foreign wives became worship of foreign gods, and the wisest king in Israel built high places for Chemosh and Molech within sight of the temple. Reflect: 1) How do small compromises in relationships become large compromises in worship? 2) Why does the text stress that God had appeared to Solomon twice? 3) What adversaries have your own compromises stirred up?
Significance: Solomon's apostasy turned the builder of the temple into a builder of high places, and cost his son all but one tribe of the kingdom.
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides

Retelling: After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam built Shechem in Ephraim and lived there, and went out and built Penuel. Then he said in his heart, 'Now shall the kingdom return to the house of David: if this people go up to do sacrifice in the house of the LORD at Jerusalem, then shall the heart of this people turn again unto their lord, even unto Rehoboam king of Judah, and they shall kill me.' So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold, and said to the people, 'It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.' He set one calf in Bethel and the other in Dan, and the thing became a sin, for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan. Jeroboam made a house of high places and priests from the lowest of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi, and he ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day, like the feast in Judah, offering upon the altar at Bethel and burning incense.
Discussion: Jeroboam's calves were political religion: a new worship designed to keep a new kingdom from drifting back to Jerusalem. He kept the Exodus language, 'which brought thee up out of Egypt,' and pointed it at golden calves. Reflect: 1) How does fear for a position lead to reshaping worship? 2) When is convenience, 'it is too much for you to go up,' used to justify disobedience? 3) What modern calves carry God's own language while pointing away from him?
Significance: Jeroboam's golden calves at Bethel and Dan made political convenience into state idolatry and fixed the sin that would define the northern kingdom.
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides; The Man of God from Judah

Story: The Man of God from Judah
Retelling: By the word of the LORD, a man of God came from Judah to Bethel while Jeroboam stood by the altar to burn incense. He cried against the altar, 'O altar, altar, thus saith the LORD; Behold, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name; and upon thee shall he offer the priests of the high places that burn incense upon thee, and men's bones shall be burnt upon thee.' He gave a sign: the altar would be rent and its ashes poured out. When Jeroboam stretched out his hand and ordered the man seized, his hand dried up so that he could not pull it back, and the altar was rent as the man had said. Jeroboam begged the man to entreat the LORD, his hand was restored, and the king offered him a reward, but the man refused, for the LORD had commanded him to eat no bread, drink no water, and return by another way. On the road home, an old prophet of Bethel, who had heard what the man had done, rode after him, found him sitting under an oak, and lied to him, claiming an angel had told him to bring him back to eat and drink. The man of God believed him, returned, ate, and drank, and the word of the LORD came to him as he sat at table: because he had disobeyed the commandment of the LORD, his carcase would not come to the sepulchre of his fathers. On the way home a lion met him and slew him, but the lion did not eat the body or tear the ass, and the old prophet, finding them standing together, brought the man's body back and buried him in his own grave, saying, 'Alas, my brother.'
Discussion: The man of God obeyed God before a king and disobeyed him before a fellow prophet's lie, and the lion that killed but did not devour him became the sign that his death was judgment, not accident. Reflect: 1) Why is a lie from a religious voice harder to resist than a threat from a king? 2) How do you test a message that claims angelic authority against God's plain command? 3) What does the old prophet's grief suggest about the cost of misleading others?
Significance: The man of God from Judah condemned Jeroboam's altar, then died on the road home for disobeying the LORD's own command at another prophet's lying word.
RelatedEvents: Jeroboam's Golden Calves

Retelling: Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered all his host, thirty-two kings with him, with horses and chariots, and besieged Samaria, demanding Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children. Ahab first agreed, but when Ben-hadad demanded the right to search his house and take whatever pleased him, Ahab refused, and the elders of Israel backed him. A prophet told Ahab that the LORD would deliver the great Syrian multitude into his hand that day, so that he would know he was the LORD, and that the young men of the princes of the provinces would lead the attack. At noon, when Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk in the pavilions with the thirty-two kings, the young men went out, each slew his man, and the Syrians fled, with Ben-hadad escaping on a horse. The next year Ben-hadad returned, advised that Israel's gods were gods of the hills and that Syria would win on the plain, and the two armies camped opposite each other for seven days. On the seventh day Israel slew one hundred thousand Syrian footmen in one day, and the rest fled to Aphek, where a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of them. Ben-hadad hid in an inner chamber, and his servants, with sackcloth on their heads and ropes on their heads, came to Ahab begging for his life. Ahab called Ben-hadad his brother, made a covenant with him, and let him go, for which a prophet condemned him: because he had let go a man appointed to utter destruction, his life would go for that man's life.
Discussion: Twice God gave Ahab victories he had not earned, and twice the point was stated: that Ahab would know that he was the LORD. The second victory was squandered when Ahab treated God's appointed enemy as a brother and a business partner. Reflect: 1) How do you respond to victories you know you did not deserve? 2) When does mercy toward an enemy become disobedience to God? 3) What covenants have you made that traded away what God told you to hold?
Significance: Ahab's wars with Ben-hadad gave Israel two undeserved victories and one condemned peace, when Ahab spared the Syrian king God had appointed to destruction.
KeyPeople: King Ahab; Ben-hadad, King of Syria
RelatedEvents: Naboth's Vineyard; Micaiah and Ahab's Death at Ramoth-Gilead

Story: Micaiah and Ahab's Death at Ramoth-Gilead
Retelling: For three years there was no war between Syria and Israel, and then Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, came down to Ahab, king of Israel, who proposed they recover Ramoth-gilead from Syria together. Jehoshaphat agreed, but asked that they inquire at the word of the LORD first. Ahab gathered about four hundred prophets, who all said, 'Go up; for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king.' Jehoshaphat, unsatisfied, asked whether there was another prophet of the LORD, and Ahab answered that there was one, Micaiah son of Imlah, but that he hated him, for he never prophesied good about him, only evil. Micaiah was summoned, and at first he echoed the four hundred, but when Ahab adjured him to tell the truth, Micaiah said he saw all Israel scattered on the hills as sheep without a shepherd, and the LORD saying they had no master and should return in peace. He described a vision of the LORD on his throne, with the host of heaven around him, and a lying spirit sent to persuade Ahab's prophets, so that Ahab would go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead. Ahab struck him on the cheek through Zedekiah, and ordered Micaiah fed bread of affliction and water of affliction until he returned in peace. Micaiah answered, 'If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me.' Ahab disguised himself for battle while Jehoshaphat wore his robes, and the Syrian captains, ordered to fight only the king of Israel, chased Jehoshaphat until he cried out and they turned away. But a certain man drew a bow at a venture and smote Ahab between the joints of the harness, and though he was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians all day, he died at evening, and the blood ran out into the chariot. Dogs licked his blood at the pool of Samaria where harlots washed, as the word of the LORD by Elijah had said.
Discussion: Four hundred voices said what a king wanted to hear; one voice told him the truth and was imprisoned for it. Ahab's disguise and a random arrow together show that no precaution outruns God's word. Reflect: 1) How do you tell a true prophet from four hundred agreeable ones? 2) What do you do when the truth you hear is unwelcome? 3) Why did Ahab go to battle even after hearing Micaiah's warning?
Significance: Micaiah's true prophecy and Ahab's death at Ramoth-Gilead vindicated the lone prophet against four hundred court prophets and fulfilled Elijah's word against Ahab.
KeyPeople: King Ahab; Micaiah, Son of Imlah; King Jehoshaphat
RelatedEvents: Naboth's Vineyard; Jehoshaphat's Victory by Prayer and Praise

Retelling: After Ahab's death, Ahaziah, his son, reigned over Israel, and fell down through a lattice in his upper chamber at Samaria and was sick. He sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover from his disease. The angel of the LORD told Elijah the Tishbite to meet the messengers and ask them, 'Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baal-zebub?' Elijah declared that Ahaziah would not come down from his bed but would surely die. When the messengers reported this, Ahaziah sent a captain with fifty men to seize Elijah, who sat on a hill. The captain ordered, 'Thou man of God, the king hath said, Come down.' Elijah answered, 'If I be a man of God, then let fire come down from heaven, and consume thee and thy fifty.' Fire fell and consumed them. A second captain with fifty came with the same order and met the same fire. A third captain came, fell on his knees before Elijah, and begged him to spare his life and the lives of his fifty men, saying their predecessors had been consumed. The angel of the LORD told Elijah to go down with him and not be afraid, and Elijah went to the king and repeated the word: because Ahaziah had sent to inquire of Baal-zebub, as if there were no God in Israel, he would not recover but would die. So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD, and Jehoram reigned in his stead.
Discussion: Ahaziah's question revealed his theology: he looked for answers in Ekron because he acted as if there were no God in Israel. Elijah's fire was not a show of temper but a sign that the God of Israel still answered. Reflect: 1) Where do you look for answers when you are sick or afraid, and what does that reveal? 2) How does the third captain's humility change the outcome? 3) What does it mean to act as if there is a God in Israel?
Significance: Elijah's confrontation with Ahaziah's messengers showed that seeking Baal-zebub was itself the sin, and the king died by the word he refused to hear.
RelatedEvents: Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire

Story: Elisha Heals the Waters of Jericho
Retelling: After Elijah was taken up, the men of Jericho came to Elisha and said the situation of the city was pleasant, but the water was bad and the ground barren, so that it caused death and miscarriage. Elisha said, 'Bring me a new cruse, and put salt therein.' They brought it, and Elisha went to the spring of the waters, cast the salt in, and said, 'Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land.' So the waters were healed to this day, according to the saying that Elisha spoke. The spring at Jericho became a source of life for the city instead of a source of death.
Discussion: Elisha's first miracle after succeeding Elijah was not a spectacle but a healing of a city's water supply: ordinary life, crops, and children depended on it. A new cruse and a handful of salt carried God's word into a daily need. Reflect: 1) What 'bad water' in your community needs healing rather than attention? 2) How does God work through small, ordinary means? 3) What does it mean for a prophet's first act to be practical provision?
Significance: Elisha's healing of Jericho's waters opened his ministry with practical grace, turning a spring of death into a spring of life for the city.
RelatedEvents: Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire

Story: Elisha and the Youths at Bethel
Retelling: As Elisha went up from Jericho to Bethel, little children came out of the city and mocked him, saying, 'Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.' Elisha turned back, looked on them, and cursed them in the name of the LORD. Two she bears came out of the wood and tore forty-two of the children. Elisha went on from there to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria. The text gives no further explanation of the mockery, the curse, or the bears.
Discussion: This is the hardest of Elisha's miracles to read: a curse answered by bears against mocking youths at Bethel, the city of Jeroboam's calf. The mockery of 'go up' may have scorned Elijah's ascent and Elisha's succession, and Bethel was a centre of idolatry, but the passage itself explains nothing, and any retelling must say so. Reflect: 1) How do you read a passage whose moral logic the text does not explain? 2) What does contempt for God's messengers reveal about a city like Bethel? 3) Why is it important to admit what a passage does not say?
Significance: At Bethel, mockery of Elisha was answered by bears, in a brief and unexplained judgment at the heart of calf-worship. Doubt: the passage is two verses with no explanation of the mockery, the curse, or the bears' scale, so it is filed as borderline rather than as a fully narrated miracle.
RelatedEvents: Elisha Heals the Waters of Jericho

Retelling: After Ahab's death, Mesha, king of Moab, rebelled against Israel. Jehoram, king of Israel, went out with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and the king of Edom, marching seven days through the wilderness of Edom until there was no water for the host or their cattle. Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the LORD, and Elisha was found, who at first refused Jehoram, telling him to go to the prophets of his father and mother, but for Jehoshaphat's sake he agreed to inquire. Elisha called for a minstrel, and as the minstrel played, the hand of the LORD came upon him. He told them to make the valley full of ditches, for though they would see neither wind nor rain, the valley would be filled with water, and they would drink, with their cattle and beasts. He also promised that the LORD would deliver Moab into their hand, and they would smite every fenced city and choice city, fell every good tree, stop all wells, and mar every good piece of land with stones. In the morning, when the meat offering was offered, water came by the way of Edom, and the country was filled with water. The Moabites, rising early, saw the water red as blood in the sunrise and thought the kings had fought and slain one another, so they cried, 'Moab, to the spoil!' But Israel rose and smote them, pursuing them into their cities, and the campaign pressed on until Mesha, in desperation, offered his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall, and great indignation came upon Israel, so that they departed from him and returned to their own land.
Discussion: The Moabite campaign pairs a miracle of provision with a war that ends in horror: water without wind or rain saved an army, and Mesha's sacrifice of his son stopped it. Elisha's word was fulfilled, and still the campaign ended in retreat. Reflect: 1) How does God provide in a wilderness where you see neither wind nor rain? 2) What does it mean that a fulfilled prophecy can still end in an unsatisfying campaign? 3) How do you respond to evil, like child sacrifice, that human armies cannot answer?
Significance: Elisha's Moabite campaign brought water to a thirsty army and victory over Moab, ending in retreat after Mesha's desperate sacrifice on the wall.
KeyPeople: Elisha; King Jehoshaphat; Mesha, King of Moab
RelatedEvents: Elisha and the Widow's Oil

Retelling: When Elisha returned to Gilgal during a dearth in the land, the sons of the prophets were sitting before him, and he told his servant to set on the great pot and boil stew for them. One of them went into the field to gather herbs, found a wild vine, gathered wild gourds, filled his lap, and shred them into the pot, not knowing what they were. When the stew was poured out for the men to eat, they cried out, 'O thou man of God, there is death in the pot,' and they could not eat of it. Elisha said, 'Then bring meal,' and he cast the meal into the pot and said, 'Pour out for the people, that they may eat.' And there was no harm in the pot.
Discussion: A well-meaning gatherer nearly poisoned a whole company of prophets with wild gourds he did not recognise. Elisha's remedy was as ordinary as the danger: meal cast into the pot, and the meal was safe. Reflect: 1) What good intentions in your life have carried hidden harm? 2) How do you respond when a community meal, project, or plan turns out to be dangerous? 3) What ordinary remedies has God used in your own crises?
Significance: Elisha's purification of the poisoned stew at Gilgal turned a famine meal that carried death into safe food for the sons of the prophets.
RelatedEvents: Elisha Feeds One Hundred Men

Retelling: A man from Baal-shalisha brought Elisha, the man of God, bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley, and full ears of corn in his husk. Elisha said, 'Give unto the people, that they may eat.' His servant objected, 'What, should I set this before an hundred men?' Elisha answered, 'Give the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the LORD, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof.' So the servant set it before them, and they ate, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD.
Discussion: Twenty barley loaves fed one hundred men with food left over, because God's word, not the servant's arithmetic, set the portion. The servant's objection is the honest one, and the leftovers are the answer. Reflect: 1) What provision in front of you looks too small for the need? 2) How does firstfruits giving, the gift itself, become the means of feeding others? 3) Where have you seen leftovers after obedience, not before it?
Significance: Elisha's feeding of one hundred men with twenty barley loaves showed God's provision outrunning human arithmetic, with food left over.
RelatedEvents: Elisha Purifies the Poisoned Stew; Elisha and the Shunammite's Son

Story: The Siege of Samaria and the Four Lepers
Retelling: Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his whole host and besieged Samaria, and the famine inside became so severe that an ass's head sold for eighty pieces of silver and a measure of dove's dung for five, and women ate their own children. As the king of Israel passed on the wall, a woman cried to him for help over a bargain in which her son had been eaten and the other woman's son was hidden. The king tore his clothes, revealing sackcloth beneath, and swore to take Elisha's head that day, blaming the prophet for the siege. Elisha, sitting in his house with the elders, said the king's messenger was coming to take his head, and told them to shut the door against him. Then he prophesied that by the next day a measure of fine flour would sell for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel in the gate of Samaria. The king's officer scoffed, 'If the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?' Elisha answered that he would see it with his eyes but would not eat of it. That evening, four leprous men at the gate said to one another, 'Why sit we here until we die? If we go into the city, famine will kill us; if we sit here, we die; let us fall unto the host of the Syrians: if they save us alive, we shall live; if they kill us, we shall but die.' At twilight they went to the Syrian camp and found it empty: the LORD had made the Syrians hear the noise of chariots and horses and a great host, and they had fled, leaving tents, horses, asses, and all their provisions. The lepers ate, drank, and hid silver, gold, and clothing, then said, 'We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.' They reported to the gate, the king sent horsemen to verify, and the people plundered the Syrian camp, so that flour and barley sold exactly as Elisha had said. The scoffing officer, set in charge of the gate, was trampled by the crowd and died, seeing the plenty but not eating of it.
Discussion: The siege of Samaria pairs the worst of famine with the best of good news, and the messengers are four outcasts whom the city had left outside its gate. Their decision, 'we do not well' to keep good tidings to ourselves, is the story's challenge. Reflect: 1) What good news are you keeping to yourself while others starve? 2) How does God use outcasts as his messengers? 3) What is the difference between the officer's scoffing and the lepers' desperate faith?
Significance: The siege of Samaria ended in sudden plenty when four lepers found the Syrian camp abandoned and carried the good tidings back to a starving city.
RelatedEvents: Elisha at Dothan

Retelling: Elisha had warned the Shunammite woman, whose son he had raised, that the LORD had called for a famine of seven years, and told her to go and sojourn wherever she could. She went with her household and sojourned seven years in the land of the Philistines. When the seven years ended, she returned and cried to the king for her house and her land. At that very moment Gehazi, Elisha's servant, was telling the king about the great things Elisha had done, and had just reached the story of how Elisha restored a dead child to life, when the woman herself came in crying for her house and land. Gehazi said, 'My lord, O king, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life.' The king asked her, and she told him, and he appointed an officer to restore all that was hers, with all the fruits of the field since the day she left the land until now.
Discussion: The Shunammite's restoration turns on timing: she arrived at the king's court at the exact moment Gehazi was telling her own story. Seven years of exile ended in a single audience, with interest. Reflect: 1) What has a long exile cost you that restoration might repay? 2) How do you recognise God's timing in an ordinary coincidence? 3) What does full restoration, house, land, and seven years' produce, say about God's justice?
Significance: The Shunammite's land was restored in full, with seven years' produce, when she reached the king at the very moment Gehazi told her story.
KeyPeople: Elisha; The Shunammite Woman; Gehazi, Servant of Elisha
RelatedEvents: Elisha and the Shunammite's Son

Retelling: Elisha came to Damascus, and Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was sick. When the king heard the man of God had come, he sent Hazael with a present of forty camels' burden of all the good things of Damascus to ask whether he would recover. Elisha told Hazael to tell the king he would certainly recover, and then added that the LORD had shown him the king would surely die. Elisha stared at Hazael and wept, until Hazael asked why his lord wept. Elisha answered that he knew the evil Hazael would do to Israel: he would set their strongholds on fire, slay their young men with the sword, dash their children, and rip up their women with child. Hazael protested, 'But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?' Elisha answered, 'The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.' Hazael returned, told Ben-hadad he would recover, and the next day took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king's face so that he died, and Hazael reigned in his stead.
Discussion: Elisha wept while prophesying Hazael's rise, because he saw the suffering a new king would bring to Israel. Hazael's protest, 'is thy servant a dog,' became his own history within a day. Reflect: 1) How do you respond to knowledge of coming suffering that you cannot prevent? 2) What ambitions in you protest innocence while already moving toward power? 3) Why does Elisha weep instead of merely announcing?
Significance: Elisha's visit to Damascus announced Hazael's kingship over Syria with tears, for he foresaw the evil Hazael would do to Israel.
RelatedEvents: Jehu's Purge of Ahab's House

Retelling: When Elisha was fallen sick with the sickness of which he died, Joash, king of Israel, came down to him, wept over his face, and cried, 'O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.' Elisha told him to take bow and arrows, and when the king had taken them, Elisha put his hands on the king's hands and told him to open the east window and shoot. Elisha said, 'The arrow of the LORD's deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria: for thou shalt smite the Syrians in Aphek, till thou have consumed them.' Then he told Joash to take the arrows and smite upon the ground. Joash smote three times and stayed. Elisha was angry and said, 'Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice.' Joash did smite Syria three times and recovered the cities of Israel, as Elisha had said.
Discussion: Elisha's last prophecy was acted, not just spoken: a shot arrow, arrows struck on the ground, and a king whose half-hearted obedience limited his own victory. Three strikes meant three victories, not total deliverance. Reflect: 1) How does half-hearted obedience limit the victory God intended? 2) What arrows have you stopped striking too soon? 3) Why does a dying prophet's word still carry authority for a king?
Significance: Elisha's last prophecy to Joash gave Israel three victories over Syria, limited by the king's three half-hearted strikes on the ground.
RelatedEvents: A Dead Man Revived by Elisha's Bones

Story: A Dead Man Revived by Elisha's Bones
Retelling: Elisha died and was buried. The bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year, and as men were burying a man, they saw a band of raiders coming and cast the body hastily into Elisha's sepulchre. When the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood up on his feet. The text records nothing more about him: not his name, his family, or what he did after standing up.
Discussion: Elisha's last miracle happened after his death, without a word, a prayer, or a prophet present: contact with his bones revived a corpse. It is the book's final testimony that God's power in Elisha outlived Elisha himself. Reflect: 1) How does God's power continue through people after they are gone? 2) What legacy of faith are you leaving that might revive someone else? 3) Why does the text leave the revived man unnamed and his later life untold?
Significance: A dead man revived on touching Elisha's bones, the prophet's final miracle after his death. Doubt: the account is two verses with no name, word, or sequel for the revived man, so it is filed as borderline rather than as a fully narrated miracle.
RelatedEvents: Elisha's Last Prophecy to Joash

Retelling: Joash, who had been preserved from Athaliah as a child and crowned under Jehoiada the priest, set his heart on repairing the house of the LORD, which Athaliah's sons had broken up and whose dedicated things had been given to Baalim. At first the priests and Levites were slow to gather the money, for the people were taxed for the temple levy of Moses, and the collection lagged. So Joash ordered a chest to be made and set beside the altar on the right side, with a hole in its lid, and proclaimed throughout Judah and Jerusalem that the people should bring the levy to the LORD. All the princes and all the people rejoiced and brought their money until the chest was full, day after day, and the king and Jehoiada gave it to the workmen, who repaired the house of God and set it in its state. As long as Jehoiada lived, burnt offerings were offered continually in the house of the LORD, but after Jehoiada's death the princes of Judah came and persuaded Joash to abandon the temple, and he listened to them, served groves and idols, and even had Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, stoned in the temple court for protesting. So the reign that began with temple repair ended in temple apostasy.
Discussion: Joash's chest shows joyful giving repairing what a wicked queen had broken, and his later apostasy shows how quickly a king who followed a mentor can fall when the mentor dies. Reflect: 1) What in God's house, or in your own life, needs repair that everyone keeps postponing? 2) How do you keep faith your own when the person who taught it to you is gone? 3) What does Zechariah's stoning in the temple court say about a reform that did not reach the heart?
Significance: Joash's temple repair, funded by a chest at the altar, restored the house Athaliah had broken, but his reign ended in apostasy after Jehoiada's death.
KeyPeople: Joash, King of Judah; Jehoiada, High Priest
RelatedEvents: Joash Preserved and Athaliah Overthrown

Retelling: Abijah, king of Judah, stood on Mount Zemaraim and addressed Jeroboam and all Israel before battle, reminding them that God had given the kingdom to David and his sons for ever by a covenant of salt, and that Jeroboam, Solomon's servant, had rebelled, gathering vain men to himself when Rehoboam was young and tenderhearted. Abijah charged that Jeroboam had cast out the priests of the LORD and made priests of the lowest of the people, while Judah still had the sons of Aaron ministering, the Levites in their charges, and the daily burnt offerings, lamps, and shewbread in order. As Abijah spoke, Jeroboam set an ambush behind Judah, so that Judah was attacked before and behind. The men of Judah cried to the LORD, the priests sounded the trumpets, and as Judah shouted, God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. Israel fled, and five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell, while Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD God of their fathers. Jeroboam never recovered strength in Abijah's days, and Abijah grew mighty, taking fourteen wives and fathering twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
Discussion: Abijah's speech before battle makes the war a theological argument: legitimate priesthood and covenant against a rebel kingdom's invented worship. Judah, ambushed front and back, won by crying out and sounding trumpets, not by tactics. Reflect: 1) How do you tell a just cause from mere self-justification before a conflict? 2) What does reliance on God look like when you are ambushed from behind? 3) Why does the chronicler stress Judah's ordered worship before the battle?
Significance: Abijah's victory over Jeroboam vindicated Judah's covenant and priesthood against the northern kingdom's invented worship, after Judah was ambushed on two sides.
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides

Retelling: In the fifth year of Rehoboam, because Judah had forsaken the law of the LORD, Shishak, king of Egypt, came up against Jerusalem with twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and a people without number from Egypt, Libya, Sukkim, and Ethiopia. He took the fenced cities of Judah and came to Jerusalem. Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the princes, who had gathered at Jerusalem for fear of Shishak, and said, 'Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.' The princes and the king humbled themselves and said, 'The LORD is righteous.' When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves, he said they would not be destroyed, but would be given some deliverance, and Shishak would not pour out his wrath on Jerusalem, though they would become his servants, to know the difference between serving God and serving foreign kings. Shishak took the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house, including the shields of gold Solomon had made, and Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place, which the guard carried when the king went to the house of the LORD.
Discussion: Shishak's invasion is the first foreign humiliation of the divided kingdom, and it came with a lesson: Judah would learn what it meant to serve a foreign king after refusing to serve God. Humility did not recover the gold shields, but it saved the city. Reflect: 1) How does God use foreign pressure to teach what disobedience costs? 2) What brass shields, cheaper substitutes, have you accepted after losing the gold? 3) Why did humbling themselves save Jerusalem but not restore its treasures?
Significance: Shishak's invasion stripped Solomon's gold shields from Jerusalem, but Rehoboam's humility saved the city from destruction.
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides

Retelling: Asa, king of Judah, had done what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD, removing foreign altars, high places, and images, and commanding Judah to seek the LORD and keep his law. Then Zerah the Ethiopian came out against Judah with a host of a thousand thousand men and three hundred chariots, and reached Mareshah. Asa went out against him and set his army in the valley of Zephathah, with five hundred and eighty thousand men. Asa cried to the LORD, 'LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude. O LORD, thou art our God; let not man prevail against thee.' The LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah, and they fled, and Judah pursued them to Gerar, taking much spoil, and smote all the cities around Gerar, for the fear of the LORD came upon them, and they returned to Jerusalem with exceeding great spoil.
Discussion: Asa's prayer is one of the finest in Scripture: help is nothing to God, whether with many or with those who have no power. A million-man army fled before a king who rested on God rather than on numbers. Reflect: 1) What overwhelming force in your life makes Asa's prayer your own? 2) How does resting on God differ from passivity? 3) Why does Asa's reform, removing idols, come before his victory?
Significance: Asa's victory over Zerah's million-man army answered a prayer that God's help does not depend on numbers, and brought Judah great spoil.
RelatedEvents: Abijah's Victory over Jeroboam

Retelling: In the days of Ahaz, king of Judah, Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it. The Syrians and Israelites instead ravaged Judah: the Syrians carried away captives to Damascus, and Pekah slew one hundred and twenty thousand men of Judah in one day, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers, and carried away two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters as spoil to Samaria. But a prophet of the LORD, Oded, met the returning army at Samaria and warned them that their rage had reached up to heaven and that keeping their brothers as slaves would add guilt to their sin, so the captors, at the princes' urging, released the captives, clothed and fed them, and carried the feeble on asses back to Jericho. Ahaz, instead of trusting God, sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, with silver and gold from the house of the LORD and the king's house, saying, 'I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel.' Assyria came, took Damascus, slew Rezin, and carried its people captive, but also distressed Ahaz rather than strengthening him. Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser, saw an altar there, sent its pattern to Uriah the priest, and had a copy built in Jerusalem, replacing the LORD's altar and remodelling the temple courts after the Assyrian fashion.
Discussion: The Syro-Ephraimite war shows Judah attacked by its own brothers and rescued by a prophet's rebuke, while Ahaz answered by buying Assyria's help and copying a Damascus altar into the temple. Reflect: 1) How does fear drive you to copy the solutions of powerful neighbours? 2) What does Oded's intervention say about mercy toward captives who are your own kin? 3) When has a rescue you paid for become a new master?
Significance: Ahaz's Syro-Ephraimite war ended with Judah's captives freed by prophetic rebuke and its king enslaved to Assyria and its altar.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Samaria

Story: Amaziah's Wars with Edom and Israel
Retelling: Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, did what was right in the sight of the LORD, but not with a perfect heart. After securing his kingdom and executing his father's murderers, he mustered Judah and hired one hundred thousand mighty men of Israel for one hundred talents of silver to fight Edom. A man of God warned him not to take Israel's army, for the LORD was not with Israel, and Amaziah, though grumbling at the lost silver, dismissed them, and they returned home in fierce anger. Amaziah then led Judah to the Valley of Salt, slew ten thousand Edomites, and took ten thousand more alive, casting them from the top of a rock. But the dismissed Israelite soldiers, angry at their dismissal, raided Judah's cities on their way home, killing three thousand and taking much spoil. Flushed with his Edomite victory, Amaziah took the gods of Edom, set them up as his own gods, bowed before them, and burned incense to them, and the LORD's anger was kindled against him. Amaziah then challenged Jehoash, king of Israel, to face him in battle, and Jehoash answered with a parable of a thistle demanding a cedar's daughter, warning that a wild beast had trodden the thistle down. Amaziah would not hear, and at Beth-shemesh Israel smote Judah, Amaziah was captured, and Jehoash broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, took the temple and palace treasures and hostages, and returned to Samaria. Amaziah lived fifteen years after Jehoash's death, but a conspiracy was formed against him at Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish, where he was slain.
Discussion: Amaziah obeyed God about Edom's army and then worshipped Edom's gods: victory over an enemy became surrender to its idols, and pride after victory became a lost war with Israel. Reflect: 1) How does victory over one enemy become worship of that enemy's gods? 2) Why is it hard to accept a prophet's warning after a success? 3) What does Jehoash's thistle parable say about pride that challenges stronger powers?
Significance: Amaziah's wars with Edom and Israel turned a victory won by obedience into defeat, after he worshipped Edom's gods and challenged Israel in pride.
KeyPeople: Amaziah, King of Judah; Joash, King of Israel
RelatedEvents: Joash Repairs the Temple

Retelling: Uzziah, king of Judah, reigned fifty-two years, sought God in the days of Zechariah, and prospered, building towers, digging wells, and equipping a great army. But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction, and he went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense, a duty belonging only to the priests, the sons of Aaron. Azariah the priest followed him with eighty priests of the LORD, men of valour, and confronted him, saying, 'It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God.' Uzziah, holding a censer, became furious, and as he raged against the priests, leprosy rose up in his forehead before them in the house of the LORD beside the incense altar. The priests thrust him out, and he himself hastened to go out, because the LORD had smitten him. Uzziah was a leper to the day of his death, living in a separate house, cut off from the house of the LORD, while his son Jotham judged the people of the land. He was buried with his fathers in the field of burial for kings, for they said, 'He is a leper.'
Discussion: Uzziah's long, prosperous reign ended at the incense altar, where a king who had done everything right tried to do one priestly thing and was struck with leprosy in his forehead. Strength lifted his heart, and the temple he loved became the place of his judgment. Reflect: 1) How does long success prepare the ground for pride? 2) What boundaries has God set that even a good king must not cross? 3) How do you respond when faithful people confront you in the moment of your anger?
Significance: Uzziah's pride at the incense altar ended a fifty-two-year reign in leprosy, cutting the king off from the temple he had tried to serve as priest.
RelatedEvents: Amaziah's Wars with Edom and Israel

Story: Hezekiah Restores Worship and Keeps Passover
Retelling: In the first year of his reign, in the first month, Hezekiah opened the doors of the house of the LORD, which his father Ahaz had shut, and repaired them. He gathered the priests and Levites and told them to sanctify themselves and cleanse the house, for their fathers had trespassed, turned their faces from the LORD's habitation, shut the doors, put out the lamps, and ceased to burn incense or offer burnt offerings, so that God's wrath had fallen on Judah. The Levites cleansed the temple for eight days, carried the filth to the brook Kidron, and sanctified the house by the sixteenth day, and Hezekiah offered seven bullocks, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven he-goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. Then Hezekiah sent letters throughout Israel and Judah, from Beersheba to Dan, inviting all Israel to come to Jerusalem to keep the Passover to the LORD, for they had not kept it in great numbers as it was written. Some laughed the messengers to scorn, but some humbled themselves and came, and a very great congregation kept the Passover in the second month, since the priests had not sanctified themselves in time for the first. Many from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun ate the Passover without being cleansed, and Hezekiah prayed for them, 'The good LORD pardon every one that prepareth his heart to seek God, although he be not cleansed according to the purification of the sanctuary,' and the LORD hearkened and healed the people. They kept the feast seven days with gladness, and then kept another seven days, and the whole assembly of Judah, the priests, the Levites, and the strangers from Israel rejoiced, for since the days of Solomon there had not been such joy in Jerusalem. Afterward the people went out, broke the images and high places throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, and Hezekiah appointed the courses of priests and Levites and commanded the people's contributions, so that there were heaps of firstfruits and tithes.
Discussion: Hezekiah's reform began with cleaning a shut temple and ended with a Passover of unprecedented joy, in which the king prayed for unclean worshippers and God healed them. Order and mercy met: the temple was cleansed, and the feast was kept by people who were not yet clean. Reflect: 1) What shut doors in your life need opening before anything else can be repaired? 2) How does Hezekiah's prayer for the unclean shape the way you welcome imperfect worshippers? 3) Why does the chronicler say there had been no such joy since Solomon?
Significance: Hezekiah's restoration of worship and Passover cleansed Ahaz's shut temple and gathered a joyful, imperfect multitude that God pardoned and healed.
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Hezekiah's Illness and Recovery

Retelling: After Artaxerxes gave Ezra a letter authorising his return, Ezra gathered the heads of families at the river Ahava and found no Levites among them. He sent for ministers for the house of God from Casiphia, and by the good hand of God they brought Sherebiah and Hashabiah with their brethren, Levites who could serve. At Ahava, Ezra proclaimed a fast, that they might afflict themselves before God and seek of him a right way for themselves, their little ones, and all their substance. He was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect them, because he had told the king that God's hand was upon all who sought him for good. So they fasted and besought God, and he was intreated of them. Ezra then weighed out the silver, gold, and vessels for the house of God into the hands of twelve priests, charging them, 'Ye are holy unto the LORD; the vessels are holy also; and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering unto the LORD God of your fathers. Watch ye, and keep them, until ye weigh them before the chief of the priests and the Levites in the chambers of the house of the LORD at Jerusalem.' They departed from Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, and the hand of God was upon them, delivering them from the enemy and from ambush by the way. They came to Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, rested three days, and weighed the treasure in the house of God, where it was found complete, and offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel.
Discussion: Ezra's journey pairs fasting with responsibility: he refused a royal escort because he had boasted of God's protection, and then he weighed every talent of treasure into priests' hands and weighed it again in Jerusalem. Faith and accounting went together. Reflect: 1) When has your own testimony made you refuse an easy safeguard? 2) How does fasting before a journey change the journey itself? 3) What treasure has God entrusted to you that must arrive weighed and complete?
Significance: Ezra's journey to Jerusalem brought the exiles and the temple treasure safely home by fasting, prayer, and careful stewardship, without a royal escort.
RelatedEvents: Ezra Reads the Law; Ezra Confronts Intermarriage

Retelling: In the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, while Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, was in the citadel of Susa, his brother Hanani came from Judah with certain men, and Nehemiah asked them about the Jews who had escaped the captivity and about Jerusalem. They answered, 'The remnant that are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach: the wall of Jerusalem also is broken down, and the gates thereof are burned with fire.' When Nehemiah heard these words, he sat down, wept, mourned for days, fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven, saying, 'I beseech thee, O LORD God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments: let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant, which I pray before thee now, day and night, for the children of Israel thy servants, and confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against thee: both I and my father's house have sinned.' He confessed Israel's corruption, remembered God's promise that if they returned to him he would gather them from the uttermost part of heaven to the place he had chosen, and asked God to grant him mercy in the sight of the king, whose cupbearer he was.
Discussion: Nehemiah's prayer begins not with a plan but with weeping, fasting, and confession that includes himself: 'both I and my father's house have sinned.' The wall would be rebuilt by a man who first took his share of the blame. Reflect: 1) What bad news has moved you to weeping rather than to a plan? 2) How does confessing your own share of a community's sin change your prayers for it? 3) What does Nehemiah's use of God's own promise teach about praying Scripture back to God?
Significance: Nehemiah's prayer for Jerusalem turned bad news from Judah into confession, fasting, and a plea grounded in God's covenant promise of return.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Retelling: On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month, after the Feast of Tabernacles, the children of Israel assembled with fasting, sackcloth, and earth upon them, and separated themselves from all strangers. They stood and read in the book of the law of the LORD for a fourth part of the day, and for another fourth part they confessed and worshipped. The Levites stood on the stairs and cried with a loud voice to the LORD, and then led the people through the whole story of God's dealings: his choice of Abram, the Exodus, the giving of the law at Sinai, the manna and water in the wilderness, the conquest, and the long cycle in which Israel rebelled, God delivered them, and they rebelled again. The prayer confessed, 'Thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly,' and yet ended with God's great mercies. Then the people made a sure covenant and wrote it, sealing it with the names of Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites, and the princes. In the covenant they pledged not to give their daughters to the peoples of the land nor take their daughters for their sons, to keep the sabbath and the holy days without buying or selling on them, to observe the sabbatical year and remit debts, and to bring the firstfruits, tithes, and wood offerings to the house of God, promising, 'We will not forsake the house of our God.'
Discussion: Covenant renewal in Nehemiah is history retold as confession: a quarter of the day reading the law, a quarter confessing, and then a written, sealed promise. The people did not merely feel sorry; they signed specific commitments about marriage, sabbath, debt, and temple support. Reflect: 1) How does retelling God's story change the way you confess your own? 2) What specific, signed commitments would your repentance require? 3) Why does the covenant end with the house of God rather than with personal resolve?
Significance: Israel's covenant renewal turned a day of fasting and confession into a sealed, specific pledge to keep the sabbath, support the temple, and forsake foreign marriages.
RelatedEvents: Ezra Reads the Law

Retelling: At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, the Levites were sought out from all their places and brought to Jerusalem to keep the dedication with gladness, thanksgiving, singing, cymbals, psalteries, and harps. The priests and Levites purified themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall. Then Nehemiah brought the princes of Judah up on the wall and appointed two great companies of thanksgiving to walk in opposite directions around it: one company went to the right toward the dung gate with Ezra the scribe before them, and the other went to the left with Nehemiah following, each with singers, trumpets, and instruments, until the two companies met in the house of God. The priests sounded trumpets, the singers sang loud with Jezrahiah as their overseer, and the people offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy, and the wives and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off. On that day men were appointed over the chambers for the treasures, the offerings, the firstfruits, and the tithes, to gather into them the portions required by the law for the priests and Levites, for Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who ministered.
Discussion: The wall's dedication was a procession, not a ribbon-cutting: two choirs walking the whole circuit in opposite directions, meeting at the temple, with joy heard far outside the city. A defensive wall became an instrument of thanksgiving. Reflect: 1) How do you dedicate a completed work to God rather than merely admiring it? 2) What would it mean for the joy of your community to be heard afar off? 3) Why does the dedication end with provision for priests and Levites, not with celebration alone?
Significance: The dedication of Jerusalem's wall turned a defensive circuit into two choirs of thanksgiving meeting at the temple, with joy heard far beyond the city.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Retelling: After twelve years as governor, Nehemiah returned to the king of Babylon, and after certain days he obtained leave and came back to Jerusalem, where he found evils that had grown in his absence. Eliashib the priest had prepared a great chamber in the courts of the house of God for Tobiah the Ammonite, the very enemy who had opposed the wall, and the temple chambers that should have held offerings had been emptied for him. Nehemiah was grieved, cast out all Tobiah's household stuff, commanded the chambers to be cleansed, and brought back the vessels, offerings, and tithes, restoring the Levites who had fled to their fields for lack of support. He also found that the sabbath was being profaned: men were treading winepresses, loading asses, and bringing goods into Jerusalem on the sabbath, and men of Tyre sold fish and merchandise there on the holy day. Nehemiah contended with the nobles, shut the gates before the sabbath, posted servants at them, and warned the merchants who lodged outside the wall that he would lay hands on them if they came again. And he found Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, whose children could not even speak the Jews' language but spoke half in the speech of Ashdod. Nehemiah contended with them, cursed them, smote some, plucked off their hair, and made them swear they would not give their daughters to foreign sons nor take foreign daughters for their sons, reminding them that Solomon, beloved of God, had been caused to sin by foreign wives. He also cleansed the priesthood, for a son of Joiada had married the daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, and Nehemiah chased him away. He appointed treasurers over the treasuries and ended his book with the prayer, 'Remember me, O my God, for good.'
Discussion: Nehemiah's last chapter is reform by confrontation: a temple chamber emptied of an enemy's furniture, sabbath gates shut against merchants, and mixed marriages broken up with curses and pulled hair. The severity is inseparable from his love for a community slipping back into the sins that had caused the exile. Reflect: 1) What compromises creep back into a community when its reformer leaves? 2) How do you distinguish zealous reform from harshness? 3) Why does Nehemiah end not with a triumph but with a prayer to be remembered for good?
Significance: Nehemiah's final reforms cleansed the temple chamber, restored the sabbath, confronted intermarriage, and purged the priesthood, ending in a prayer to be remembered for good.
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Ezra Confronts Intermarriage

Story: Job's Losses in a Single Day
Retelling: Job was a blameless and upright man in the land of Uz, who feared God and turned away from evil, the greatest of all the men of the east. In the heavenly court the adversary asked whether Job feared God for nothing, pointing to the hedge God had put around him and his household, and the LORD allowed all Job had to be touched, only not Job himself. In a single day messengers came one after another: the Sabeans took his oxen and donkeys and killed his servants, the fire of God burned his sheep and servants, the Chaldeans took his camels and killed his servants, and a great wind struck the house where his sons and daughters were feasting, killing them all. Job tore his robe, shaved his head, fell to the ground and worshipped, saying, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
Discussion: Job lost everything without an explanation, and still worshipped. Reflect: 1) What would remain of your faith if your blessings were taken away? 2) How do you speak to God when loss comes all at once? 3) What does Job's worship in grief teach you about who God is, apart from what He gives?
Significance: Faith is not a bargain for blessing; Job's worship when he had nothing left shows trust in God Himself, not in His gifts. Doubt: Job is a poetic book and the historicity and genre of its prose frame are debated; only the prose frame is drafted here, not the poetic dialogues.
RelatedEvents: Job's Suffering and Restoration

Story: Job's Affliction and His Wife's Counsel
Retelling: The adversary came again before the LORD, and the LORD pointed to Job, who still held fast his integrity despite being moved against him without cause. The adversary answered, Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life — touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse Thee to Thy face. The LORD allowed Job's body to be touched, only his life spared, and Job was struck with sore boils from the sole of his foot to his crown, so that he sat among the ashes scraping himself with a potsherd. His wife said to him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die. Job answered, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this Job did not sin with his lips.
Discussion: Job's suffering moved from his possessions to his body, and from strangers' blows to his own wife's counsel. Reflect: 1) How do you respond when those closest to you urge you to give up? 2) Is your trust in God steady when the pain is in your own body, not just your circumstances? 3) What does it mean to receive both good and evil from God's hand without charging Him foolishly?
Significance: Faithfulness is tested most sharply when suffering turns personal and the counsel around you turns bitter; Job held his integrity without pretending his pain was small. Doubt: Job is a poetic book and the historicity and genre of its prose frame are debated; only the prose frame is drafted here, not the poetic dialogues.
RelatedEvents: Job's Suffering and Restoration; Job's Losses in a Single Day

Retelling: When Job's three friends heard of all the evil that had come upon him, they came, each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They had agreed together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him. When they lifted up their eyes from afar and did not recognise him, they wept, tore their robes, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven. Then they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.
Discussion: Before any of them offered an answer, Job's friends simply sat with him for a week in silence. Reflect: 1) When have words made someone's grief worse, and silence helped? 2) How do you sit with a suffering friend without rushing to explain their pain? 3) What does the size of Job's grief — greater than any speech — teach you about the limits of our answers?
Significance: Presence can be the first mercy to a sufferer; Job's friends were at their best before they began to argue, when they shared his grief in silence. Doubt: Job is a poetic book and the historicity and genre of its prose frame are debated; only the prose frame is drafted here, not the poetic dialogues.
RelatedEvents: Job's Suffering and Restoration

Retelling: After the long debate, the LORD spoke to Eliphaz the Temanite and said His wrath was kindled against him and his two friends, because they had not spoken of Him what was right, as His servant Job had. They were told to take seven bullocks and seven rams, go to Job, and offer a burnt offering for themselves, while Job prayed for them, and the LORD would accept him and not deal with them after their folly. They did so, and the LORD accepted Job. Then the LORD turned Job's captivity when he prayed for his friends, and gave him twice as much as he had before. His brothers, sisters, and former friends came and comforted him, each giving him a piece of money and an earring of gold. The LORD blessed Job's latter end more than his beginning: fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she asses, seven sons and three daughters — Jemima, Kezia, and Keren-happuch, the fairest in the land — and Job lived a hundred and forty years after this, saw his sons and his sons' sons to four generations, and died old and full of days.
Discussion: Job's ending is restoration, not an explanation — and it comes through praying for the friends who had wronged him. Reflect: 1) Why does God give Job's restoration only after Job prays for his friends? 2) How do you hold together God's gift of twice as much with the children who were never replaced? 3) What does it mean to trust God when the book ends without answering why you suffered?
Significance: Restoration is God's gift, not a reward Job earned or a bargain he struck, and it arrives alongside a silence about why he suffered that is never filled. Doubt: Job is a poetic book and the historicity and genre of its prose frame are debated; only the prose frame is drafted here, not the poetic dialogues.
RelatedEvents: Job's Suffering and Restoration

Retelling: When Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel marched against Jerusalem, the heart of Ahaz king of Judah and his people was moved, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind. The LORD sent Isaiah, with his son Shear-jashub, to meet Ahaz at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller's field, with this word: Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands. Ahaz was told to ask a sign of the LORD his God, in the depth or in the height above, but he refused, saying, I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD. Isaiah answered that the Lord Himself would give a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Before the child knew to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land of the two kings Ahaz dreaded would be forsaken — and Assyria, the power Ahaz trusted instead, would come upon Judah.
Discussion: Ahaz was offered any sign he wanted and refused it, preferring his own alliance to God's word. Reflect: 1) When has fear pushed you to trust a human alliance rather than God? 2) Why is refusing a sign sometimes a form of unbelief, not humility? 3) How does God's giving a sign anyway show grace to a king who would not ask?
Significance: God gives His sign even to an unwilling king, and the sign points beyond Ahaz's crisis to a child whose name — God with us — outlasts every empire. Doubt: this is a narrative scene wrapped around an oracle, so the sign itself dominates the episode.
KeyPeople: Isaiah; Ahaz, King of Judah; Shear-jashub
RelatedEvents: Isaiah's Vision and Call

Retelling: The LORD told Isaiah to take a great roll and write in it with a man's pen concerning Maher-shalal-hash-baz, and Isaiah took faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah. Then Isaiah went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. The LORD told him to call the child's name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, for before the child would have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria would be taken away before the king of Assyria. The child's name itself — speed to the spoil, haste to the prey — was the message: Assyria was coming, and the powers Judah feared would fall first.
Discussion: Isaiah's own child carried a sermon in his name. Reflect: 1) What does it cost a family when a parent's obedience becomes public? 2) Why does God sometimes write His warning in a life, not just in words? 3) How does this sign warn Judah that its feared enemies are not the real danger?
Significance: God's warnings are written into ordinary lives as well as spoken words; this child's name announced that Assyria would strip the very powers Judah feared. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
KeyPeople: Isaiah; Maher-shalal-hash-baz; Zechariah, Son of Jeberechiah
RelatedEvents: Isaiah's Vision and Call; The Sign to Ahaz

Retelling: In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him and he fought against Ashdod and took it, the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. Isaiah did so, walking naked and barefoot. The LORD said that as His servant Isaiah had walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia, so would the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. And the people of Judah, who had looked to Egypt and Ethiopia for help, would be afraid and ashamed of the very powers they had trusted.
Discussion: Isaiah preached for three years in the dress of a prisoner of war. Reflect: 1) Why would God make His prophet look like a captive to warn against trusting Egypt? 2) How do you react when God's warning embarrasses the respectable plans around you? 3) What alliances are you trusting that might be led away captive themselves?
Significance: Trust in foreign powers is exposed as shameful hope: the prophet wore the fate of Egypt so Judah could see where its trust was heading. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Isaiah's Vision and Call

Story: Hezekiah Shows His Treasures to Babylon
Retelling: After Hezekiah had been sick and recovered, Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to him, for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick. Hezekiah was glad of the envoys, and showed them all the house of his precious things — the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures. There was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah did not show them. Then Isaiah the prophet came and asked, What said these men? and whence came they unto thee? and, What have they seen in thine house? Hezekiah answered that they had seen all that was in his house. Isaiah said, Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon; nothing shall be left. And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. Hezekiah answered, Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken — for, he thought, there shall be peace and truth in my days.
Discussion: Hezekiah showed Babylon everything, and the prophet showed him what that openness would cost. Reflect: 1) When does showing off what God gave become an invitation to lose it? 2) Why did Hezekiah accept a word of judgment so calmly — humility, or relief that it would not fall in his own days? 3) What are you displaying to powers that may one day come to collect?
Significance: A king's pride in his treasures opened the door to exile: what Hezekiah displayed to Babylon, Babylon would one day carry away.
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah's Illness and Recovery

Retelling: The word came to Jeremiah: Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear My words. Jeremiah went down, and the potter was working a work on the wheels. The vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter, so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it. Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in Mine hand, O house of Israel. At what instant I speak concerning a nation, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it, if that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them — and likewise, a nation I promised to build, if it does evil, I will repent of the good.
Discussion: Jeremiah learned theology by watching a workman's hands. Reflect: 1) How does the potter's freedom comfort you, and how does it unsettle you? 2) What vessel is God remaking in your life right now, and are you resisting the wheel? 3) Why does God's warning always carry a way back — turn, and I will turn?
Significance: God is free as the potter over the clay, yet His judgments are never fixed against a people who turn; the same hand that mars can remake. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call

Story: Jeremiah Breaks the Flask at Topheth
Retelling: The LORD told Jeremiah to get a potter's earthen bottle, take some of the elders of the people and the elders of the priests, and go to the valley of the son of Hinnom, by the entry of the east gate, and proclaim there the words God would tell him. He proclaimed judgment on Jerusalem for forsaking God, burning incense to other gods, and filling the place with the blood of innocents — for building the high places of Baal to burn their sons in the fire, which God had not commanded, nor spoken, nor come into His mind. He declared that the place would no longer be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter, where the people would fall by the sword and their carcasses become meat for the fowls of heaven. Then, in the sight of the men who went with him, Jeremiah broke the bottle, saying, Even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again. He came back and stood in the court of the LORD's house and repeated the word to all the people.
Discussion: A smashed flask cannot be unbroken — and Jeremiah made Jerusalem watch it happen. Reflect: 1) Why does God sometimes give a warning that cannot be softened? 2) What in your life is being treated as unbreakable that God says will break? 3) How do you speak a hard word in the very place where it will be heard?
Significance: Some judgments, once the vessel is broken, cannot be mended on human terms; the flask at Topheth made Jerusalem's coming ruin visible before it arrived. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: When Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the LORD, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things, he struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD. On the next day Pashhur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah said to him, The LORD hath not called thy name Pashhur, but Magor-missabib — fear round about. For thus saith the LORD: Behold, I will make thee a terror to thyself, and to all thy friends, and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and thine eyes shall behold it. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall carry them captive into Babylon, and shall slay them with the sword. Pashhur himself, with all his house, would go into captivity to Babylon, die there, and be buried there, he and all his friends to whom he had prophesied lies.
Discussion: Jeremiah was beaten and locked in the stocks for preaching in the Temple — and answered with a new name for his persecutor. Reflect: 1) What happens when religious authority, not the king, is the one silencing God's word? 2) How do you keep speaking when the cost is public shame? 3) Why does Jeremiah rename Pashhur 'terror all around' — whose terror is it, in the end?
Significance: Speaking God's word in God's own house can bring beating and stocks from God's own officers; the prophet's answer names the coming terror for what it is.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call

Retelling: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah stood in the court of the LORD's house and warned all the cities of Judah that if they would not listen and walk in God's law, He would make Jerusalem a curse to all the nations of the earth, as He had made Shiloh. The priests, the prophets, and all the people seized him, saying, Thou shalt surely die, because thou hast prophesied that this house shall be like Shiloh and this city desolate.
