The princes of Judah heard, came up from the king's house, and sat in the entry of the new gate of the LORD's house. The priests and prophets pressed the charge, but Jeremiah answered, The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and this city all the words that ye have heard. Therefore now amend your ways and your doings, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, and the LORD will repent Him of the evil that He hath pronounced against you. As for me, behold, I am in your hand: do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you. But know ye for certain, that if ye put me to death, ye shall surely bring innocent blood upon yourselves, and upon this city, and upon the inhabitants thereof. The princes and all the people said, This man is not worthy to die, for he hath spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God. Elders reminded them that Micah had prophesied the same in Hezekiah's days and Hezekiah had not killed him, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan stood by Jeremiah so that he was not given into the hand of the people to put him to death.
Discussion: Jeremiah was tried for his life in the Temple court for preaching against the Temple. Reflect: 1) How do you defend a hard word without defending yourself? 2) Why did the princes, not the priests, acquit Jeremiah — and what does that say about who listens? 3) What does 'I am in your hand' teach about courage that leaves the outcome to God?
Significance: A prophet on trial for his life rests his defence on one fact — the LORD sent me — and leaves his fate in his judges' hands rather than softening the word.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call

Story: Jeremiah Buys the Field at Anathoth
Retelling: In the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, when the king of Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem, Jeremiah was shut up in the court of the prison in the king of Judah's house, because he had prophesied that the city would be given into the hand of the king of Babylon. The word of the LORD came to him: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth, for the right of redemption is thine to buy it. Hanamel came, just as the LORD had said, and Jeremiah knew it was the word of the LORD. He bought the field for seventeen shekels of silver, subscribed the evidence, sealed it, took witnesses, and gave the evidence of the purchase to Baruch the son of Neriah in the sight of Hanamel and of all the Jews who sat in the court of the prison. He charged Baruch to put both the sealed and the open evidence in an earthen vessel, that they might continue many days. Then Jeremiah prayed, and the LORD answered: Behold, I will bring upon this city all the evil I have pronounced, and I will gather them out of all countries and bring them again to this place — and fields shall be bought in this land again, for houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
Discussion: With the enemy at the walls, Jeremiah bought a field he could not use — the strangest investment in the Bible. Reflect: 1) What does it mean to invest in a future you will not live to enjoy? 2) How does a sealed deed in an earthen jar preach hope during a siege? 3) Where is God asking you to act as if His promise were already true?
Significance: Buying land in a besieged city is hope made legal: judgment is real, but God will bring His people back to fields they can own again.
KeyPeople: Jeremiah; Baruch; Zedekiah, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: In the days of Jehoiakim, the word came to Jeremiah: Go unto the house of the Rechabites, and speak unto them, and bring them into the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink. Jeremiah took the whole house of the Rechabites and set pots full of wine and cups before them, saying, Drink ye wine. But they said, We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab our father commanded us, saying, Ye shall drink no wine, neither ye, nor your sons for ever. Neither shall ye build house, nor sow seed, nor plant vineyard, nor have any, but all your days ye shall dwell in tents, that ye may live many days in the land where ye be strangers. And we have obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab our father in all that he hath charged us. Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: Go and tell the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will ye not receive instruction to hearken to My words? The sons of Jonadab have performed the commandment of their father which he commanded them, but I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking, and ye hearkened not unto Me. Therefore, because the Rechabites obeyed their father, Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before Me for ever.
Discussion: A nomad family's three-hundred-year-old vow shamed a whole nation. Reflect: 1) Why does obedience to a human father convict Judah more than any sermon? 2) What small, unfashionable obedience has your family or church kept that the world has forgotten? 3) How does God honour quiet faithfulness that never makes a headline?
Significance: Steadfast obedience to a father's command exposes a nation's disobedience to God — and God promises the faithful family a standing before Him for ever.
DateApprox: c. 600 BC (days of Jehoiakim; date debated)
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call

Retelling: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the word came to Jeremiah: Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah, even unto this day. Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD in the roll. Because Jeremiah was shut up and could not go into the house of the LORD, Baruch went on the fasting day and read the roll in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan. Micaiah the son of Gemariah heard the words and declared them to the princes in the scribe's chamber. The princes sent Jehudi to fetch the roll, and Jehudi read it in their ears; when they heard all the words they were afraid, and told Baruch to go and hide himself and Jeremiah, and laid the roll up in the chamber of Elishama the scribe. They told the king, who was sitting in the winterhouse with a fire burning on the hearth before him. As Jehudi read three or four leaves, the king cut the roll with a penknife and cast it into the fire, until all the roll was consumed — and yet the king and his servants were not afraid, nor rent their garments, though Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah made intercession that he would not burn the roll. The king commanded the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the LORD hid them. Then the word came to Jeremiah again: Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim hath burned — with this added: Jehoiakim shall have none to sit upon the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.
Discussion: A king burned God's word leaf by leaf — and God's word came back longer. Reflect: 1) Why did the princes tremble at the scroll while the king cut it up calmly? 2) What do you do with a word from God you do not want to hear — hide it, argue it, or burn it? 3) How does the rewritten scroll show that destroying the message never destroys the Sender?
Significance: Burning the scroll did not silence the word; it came back rewritten, with judgment added for the king who cut it up.
KeyPeople: Jeremiah; Baruch; Jehoiakim, King of Judah; Gemariah, Son of Shaphan; Jehudi
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned instead of Coniah, and neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land, listened to the words of the LORD spoken by Jeremiah. When Pharaoh's army came out of Egypt, the Chaldeans raised the siege of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah warned that Pharaoh's army would return to Egypt and the Chaldeans would come again and burn the city. As Jeremiah was going out of Jerusalem into the land of Benjamin, to separate himself there, Irijah the son of Shelemiah, captain of the ward at the gate of Benjamin, seized him, saying, Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans. Jeremiah said, It is false; I fall not away to the Chaldeans. But Irijah would not hear him, took him to the princes, who were angry with him, beat him, and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe, for they had made that the prison. Jeremiah remained there many days. Then Zedekiah sent and took him out, and asked him secretly in his house, Is there any word from the LORD? Jeremiah said, There is: for thou shalt be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. Jeremiah asked why he was imprisoned when the prophets who told Zedekiah the king of Babylon would not come had been proved false, and begged not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die there. Zedekiah commanded that Jeremiah be committed into the court of the prison, with a piece of bread daily out of the bakers' street, until all the bread in the city was spent.
Discussion: Jeremiah was arrested for desertion while telling the truth about the siege. Reflect: 1) How do you keep telling the truth when it gets you labelled a traitor? 2) Why did Zedekiah ask Jeremiah in secret what he would not hear in public? 3) What does Jeremiah's plea — do not send me back to die — teach about honest prayer under unjust imprisonment?
Significance: Truth-telling under siege looks like treason to frightened rulers; Jeremiah was beaten and jailed for a prophecy that was already coming true.
KeyPeople: Jeremiah; Irijah; Zedekiah, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Jeremiah in the Cistern

Retelling: Shephatiah, Gedaliah the son of Pashhur, Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashhur the son of Malchiah heard Jeremiah's words: He that remaineth in this city shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, but he that goeth forth to the Chaldeans shall live. They told Zedekiah that Jeremiah weakened the hands of the men of war and of all the people, and ought to be put to death. The king answered, Behold, he is in your hand, for the king is not he that can do any thing against you. So they took Jeremiah and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, which was in the court of the prison; they let him down with cords, and in the dungeon there was no water, but mire, and Jeremiah sank in the mire. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs in the king's house, heard of it, went to the king at the gate of Benjamin, and said, My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon, and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is, for there is no more bread in the city. The king commanded Ebed-melech to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah up out of the dungeon before he died. They took old cast clouts and old rotten rags, let them down by cords into the dungeon, and told Jeremiah to put them under his armholes, and they drew him up. Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison. Zedekiah then sent for him secretly at the third entry of the house of the LORD and asked him to hide nothing. Jeremiah warned him: if thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon's princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire, and thou shalt live, and thine house. Zedekiah, afraid of the Jews who had fallen to the Chaldeans, did not go — and Jeremiah told him to keep the matter secret, saying to the princes only that he had entreated the king not to send him back to Jonathan's house to die there.
Discussion: Jeremiah sank in the mud of a cistern for saying surrender was the way to live, and an Ethiopian courtier saved him with old rags and ropes. Reflect: 1) Why does the advice that saves lives sound like treason in a siege? 2) How does Ebed-melech, an outsider, shame the princes of Judah? 3) What do you do when the king asks for truth in secret but will not act on it in public?
Significance: The prophet who said surrender and live was left to die in the mud for it; his rescue came from an outsider's courage, not from the king who knew the truth.
KeyPeople: Jeremiah; Ebed-Melech; Zedekiah, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Jeremiah Arrested and Imprisoned

Retelling: After Jerusalem fell, the king of Babylon made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor over the poor of the land who were left. Jeremiah, released by Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard, chose to stay with Gedaliah at Mizpah. The captains of the forces in the fields, among them Johanan the son of Kareah, came to Gedaliah and warned him: Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? Gedaliah did not believe them. In the seventh month Ishmael came to Mizpah with ten men, ate bread with Gedaliah, and then rose up and struck Gedaliah with the sword, and killed him, with the Jews and the Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah. The next day, before anyone knew, eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria came with shaven beards, torn clothes, and cuttings, bringing offerings and incense to the house of the LORD; Ishmael went out weeping to meet them, lured them into the city, and slew them, casting their bodies into the pit that Asa the king had made — sparing only ten who said, Slay us not, for we have treasures in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey. Ishmael then took captive all the residue of the people at Mizpah, including the king's daughters, and departed to go over to the Ammonites. But Johanan and all the captains heard, fought Ishmael at the great waters of Gibeon, recovered the captives, and Ishmael escaped with eight men to the Ammonites.
Discussion: The remnant's one safe governor was murdered at his own table, and the fragile peace after the fall collapsed in a day. Reflect: 1) Why did Gedaliah refuse to believe the warning — trust, or naivety? 2) How does a single assassination unravel a whole community's future? 3) What do you do when the leaders left after disaster cannot hold the remnant together?
Significance: Gedaliah's murder ended the last ordered life in Judah after the fall and drove the frightened remnant toward the flight to Egypt they had been warned against.
KeyPeople: Gedaliah, Son of Ahikam; Ishmael, Son of Nethaniah; Johanan, Son of Kareah; Jeremiah
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; The Remnant Flees to Egypt

Retelling: After Gedaliah's murder, Johanan the son of Kareah and all the captains and all the people, from the least even unto the greatest, came to Jeremiah and said, Let our supplication be accepted before thee, and pray for us unto the LORD thy God, that He may show us the way wherein we may walk, and the thing that we may do. They promised, Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God. After ten days the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: If ye will still abide in this land, then will I build you, and not pull you down, and I will plant you, and not pluck you up; neither fear ye the king of Babylon. But if ye say, We will not dwell in this land, and go into Egypt, where ye shall see no war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor have hunger of bread, then the sword which ye fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine whereof ye were afraid shall follow close after you there, and there ye shall die. When Jeremiah had finished, Johanan and all the proud men said, Thou speakest falsely: the LORD our God hath not sent thee to say, Go not into Egypt to sojourn there — but Baruch the son of Neriah setteth thee on against us. So Johanan took all the remnant of Judah, men, women, children, and the king's daughters, with Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch, and they came into the land of Egypt, even to Tahpanhes. There the word came to Jeremiah: Take great stones in thine hand, and hide them in the clay in the brickkiln which is at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah, and say unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, My servant, and will set his throne upon these stones that I have hid, and he shall spread his royal pavilion over them.
Discussion: The remnant promised to obey whatever God said — then disobeyed the moment He said stay. Reflect: 1) Why do we ask God for guidance when we have already chosen the answer? 2) How does fear of Babylon in Judah become fear of Babylon in Egypt? 3) What does it mean that Jeremiah was carried to Egypt against his own prophecy, yet kept prophesying there?
Significance: A promised obedience that collapses at the first unwelcome word is no obedience at all; the flight to Egypt carried the very judgment the remnant fled Judah to escape.
KeyPeople: Jeremiah; Johanan, Son of Kareah; Baruch
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; The Murder of Gedaliah

Story: Jeremiah Forbidden to Marry or Mourn
Retelling: The word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah, saying, Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place. For thus saith the LORD concerning the sons and concerning the daughters that are born in this place, and concerning their mothers that bare them, and concerning their fathers that begat them in this land: They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented, neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth, and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine, and their carcasses shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth. Thou shalt not go into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them, for I have taken away My peace from this people, saith the LORD, even lovingkindness and mercies. Neither shalt thou go into the house of feasting, to sit with them to eat and to drink. For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will cause to cease out of this place in your eyes, and in your days, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride.
Discussion: Jeremiah's whole life — no wedding, no funeral, no feast — became the sermon. Reflect: 1) What does it cost to let your private life preach a public warning? 2) Why would God take away mourning itself as part of judgment? 3) How do you live faithfully in a community whose celebrations God says will cease?
Significance: When a people's peace is taken away, the prophet's celibacy, absence from funerals, and absence from feasts preach what words alone could not carry. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign in the form of a commanded way of life rather than a single enacted event.
DateApprox: Before the fall of Jerusalem (date debated)
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call

Retelling: The LORD said unto Jeremiah, Go and get thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, and put it not in water. Jeremiah got the girdle and put it on his loins. Then the word of the LORD came a second time: Take the girdle that thou hast got, which is upon thy loins, and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock. Jeremiah went and hid it by Euphrates. After many days the LORD said, Arise, go to Euphrates, and take the girdle from the place where thou hast hid it. Jeremiah went, dug, and took the girdle — and behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing. Then the word came: After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem. This evil people, which refuse to hear My words, which walk in the imagination of their heart, and walk after other gods, to serve them, and to worship them, shall even be as this girdle, which is good for nothing. For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto Me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith the LORD, that they might be unto Me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear.
Discussion: A new linen belt, buried by a river and dug up ruined, preached what pride does to a people. Reflect: 1) Why does God picture His people as a garment meant to cling close to Him? 2) What does it mean that Judah was ruined not by being far from God, but by refusing to cling? 3) How does a small, spoiled object preach louder than a long sermon?
Significance: A people made to cling to God like a belt to the waist, but proud and turned to other gods, ends up like a buried girdle — marred and good for nothing. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call

Story: Seraiah Casts the Book into the Euphrates
Retelling: The word which Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, when he went with Zedekiah the king of Judah into Babylon in the fourth year of his reign — Seraiah was a quiet prince. Jeremiah had written in a book all the evil that should come upon Babylon, even all these words that are written against Babylon. And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, When thou comest to Babylon, and shalt see, and shalt read all these words, then shalt thou say, O LORD, Thou hast spoken against this place, to cut it off, that none shall remain in it, neither man nor beast, but that it shall be desolate for ever. And it shall be, when thou hast made an end of reading this book, that thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of Euphrates, and shalt say, Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her, and they shall be weary.
Discussion: A book and a stone, thrown into a river, preached the fall of an empire. Reflect: 1) Why send Babylon's judgment by a quiet prince on a royal journey, rather than by an army? 2) How does a sinking stone preach what a thousand words cannot? 3) What does it mean that Babylon's fall was already written before Babylon itself had fallen?
Significance: Babylon, the power that carried Judah away, would itself sink like a stone-bound book in the Euphrates and not rise again. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Jeremiah's Call; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Story: Zedekiah's Broken Covenant over the Slaves
Retelling: The word came to Jeremiah from the LORD after king Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people at Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty unto them: that every man should let his manservant, and every man his maidservant, being a Hebrew or a Hebrewess, go free, that none should serve himself of them, to wit, of a Jew his brother. All the princes and all the people obeyed, and let every man his manservant and maidservant go free, and none served themselves of them any more. But afterward they turned, and caused the servants and the handmaids, whom they had let go free, to return, and brought them into subjection for servants and for handmaids. Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah: Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel: I made a covenant with your fathers in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondmen, saying, At the end of seven years let ye go every man his brother an Hebrew, which hath been sold unto thee. But your fathers hearkened not unto Me. Ye were now turned, and had done right in My sight, in proclaiming liberty every man to his neighbour, and ye had made a covenant before Me in the house which is called by My name. But ye turned and polluted My name, and caused every man his servant to return. Therefore thus saith the LORD: Ye have not hearkened unto Me, in proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother, and every man to his neighbour. Behold, I proclaim a liberty for you, saith the LORD, to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine, and I will make you to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth. And I will give the men that have transgressed My covenant into the hand of their enemies, and the city shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon's army, which shall burn it with fire.
Discussion: Judah freed its slaves under siege — then took them back — and God answered with a bitter wordplay. Reflect: 1) Why does freeing slaves under siege, then re-enslaving them, reveal more than the siege itself? 2) What does it mean that God answers a broken liberty with 'liberty' to sword, famine, and pestilence? 3) How do you keep a covenant made under pressure once the pressure lifts?
Significance: A liberty proclaimed and then revoked becomes its own judgment: God gives the covenant-breakers the 'liberty' they chose — to sword, pestilence, and famine.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Jeremiah's Call

Retelling: The hand of the LORD was upon Ezekiel, and He said, Arise, go forth into the plain, and I will there talk with thee. Ezekiel arose and went into the plain, and behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, as the glory which he saw by the river of Chebar, and he fell on his face. Then the Spirit entered into him and set him upon his feet, and spoke with him: Go, shut thyself within thine house. And thou, O son of man, behold, they shall put bands upon thee, and shall bind thee with them, and thou shalt not go out among them. And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover, for they are a rebellious house. But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD: He that heareth, let him hear; and he that forbeareth, let him forbear.
Discussion: Ezekiel's voice was taken away except when God opened it. Reflect: 1) What does it mean for a prophet to speak only when God opens his mouth? 2) How does silence itself preach to a rebellious house? 3) When has God shut your mouth so that only His word, not yours, would come out?
Significance: A prophet who cannot speak unless God opens his mouth embodies the message: Israel will hear only what God gives, and nothing of the prophet's own. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Call and the Scroll

Retelling: The LORD told Ezekiel, Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem. And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about. Moreover take thou unto thee an iron pan, and set it for a wall of iron between thee and the city, and set thy face against it, and it shall be besieged, and thou shalt lay siege against it. This shall be a sign to the house of Israel.
Discussion: Ezekiel built a toy siege in exile while the real city still stood. Reflect: 1) Why make a model of a siege that has not happened yet? 2) What does the iron pan between prophet and city say about how cut off Jerusalem already was? 3) How do you warn people who believe the worst cannot happen to them?
Significance: A clay tile with a toy siege preached what words had not: Jerusalem's siege was already drawn, and the iron wall between God and His city was already set. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Siege Signs; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: The LORD told Ezekiel, Lie thou also upon thy left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel upon it: according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon it thou shalt bear their iniquity. For I have laid upon thee the years of their iniquity, according to the number of the days, three hundred and ninety days: so shalt thou bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. And when thou hast accomplished them, lie again on thy right side, and thou shalt bear the iniquity of the house of Judah forty days: I have appointed thee each day for a year. Therefore thou shalt set thy face toward the siege of Jerusalem, and thine arm shall be uncovered, and thou shalt prophesy against it. And behold, I will lay bands upon thee, and thou shalt not turn thee from one side to another, till thou hast ended the days of thy siege.
Discussion: Ezekiel lay bound on one side for over a year, carrying in his body the years of Israel's sin. Reflect: 1) What does it mean for a prophet to bear a people's sin in his own body? 2) Why a day for a year — what does slow, counted time teach about judgment? 3) How do you stay faithful to an obedience that takes months and earns only stares?
Significance: A prophet lying bound for 390 days and then 40 more made Israel's long years of iniquity visible in a single suffering body. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Siege Signs

Retelling: The LORD told Ezekiel, Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof, according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon thy side, three hundred and ninety days shalt thou eat thereof. And thy meat which thou shalt eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day: from time to time shalt thou eat it. Thou shalt drink also water by measure, the sixth part of an hin: from time to time shalt thou drink. And thou shalt eat it as barley cakes, and thou shalt bake it with dung that cometh out of man, in their sight. Even thus, said the LORD, shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the Gentiles, whither I will drive them. Ezekiel answered, Ah Lord GOD! behold, my soul hath not been polluted: for from my youth up even till now have I not eaten of that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces; neither came there abominable flesh into my mouth. Then the LORD said, Lo, I have given thee cow's dung for man's dung, and thou shalt prepare thy bread therewith. And He said, Son of man, behold, I will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem: and they shall eat bread by weight, and with care, and they shall drink water by measure, and with astonishment, that they may want bread and water, and be astonied one with another, and consume away for their iniquity.
Discussion: Ezekiel ate weighed, rationed, defiled bread for over a year, tasting Jerusalem's siege before it happened. Reflect: 1) Why does God make His prophet taste the famine he preaches? 2) What does Ezekiel's protest — and God's concession to cow's dung — show about God's care even in judgment? 3) How do you preach a hard word without losing compassion for those who will suffer it?
Significance: Weighed bread and measured water, baked over dung, let the exiles taste in advance the defilement and hunger of the siege to come. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Siege Signs

Retelling: The LORD told Ezekiel, Thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair. Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them. Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts. Then take of them again, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; for thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel. For thus saith the Lord GOD: This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her. And she hath changed My judgments into wickedness more than the nations. Therefore a third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee: and a third part shall fall by the sword round about thee; and I will scatter a third part into all the winds, and I will draw out a sword after them.
Discussion: Ezekiel shaved his head and divided the hair into thirds — burned, sword-struck, scattered. Reflect: 1) Why divide one man's hair to preach one city's fate? 2) What does the few hairs kept in the prophet's skirt say about the remnant? 3) How does a city set 'in the midst of the nations' fall further than the nations around it?
Significance: One head of hair, weighed and divided three ways, told Jerusalem its whole future: famine, sword, and scattering, with only a few kept. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Siege Signs; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: The word of the LORD came to Ezekiel: Son of man, thou dwellest in the midst of a rebellious house, which have eyes to see, and see not; they have ears to hear, and hear not: for they are a rebellious house. Therefore, thou son of man, prepare thee stuff for removing, and remove by day in their sight; and thou shalt remove from thy place to another place in their sight: it may be they will consider, though they be a rebellious house. Then shalt thou bring forth thy stuff by day in their sight, as stuff for removing: and thou shalt go forth at even in their sight, as they that go forth into captivity. Dig thou through the wall in their sight, and carry out thereby. In their sight shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulders, and carry it forth in the twilight: thou shalt cover thy face, that thou see not the ground: for I have set thee for a sign unto the house of Israel. Ezekiel did so as he was commanded: he brought forth his stuff by day, as stuff for captivity, and in the evening he dug through the wall with his hand, and brought it forth in the twilight, and bore it upon his shoulder in their sight. In the morning the word came: Son of man, hath not the house of Israel, the rebellious house, said unto thee, What doest thou? Say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD: This burden concerneth the prince in Jerusalem, and all the house of Israel that are among them. I am your sign: like as I have done, so shall it be done unto them: they shall remove and go into captivity. And the prince that is among them shall bear upon his shoulder in the twilight, and shall go forth: they shall dig through the wall to carry out thereby: he shall cover his face, that he see not the ground with his eyes. My net also will I spread upon him, and he shall be taken in My snare: and I will bring him to Babylon to the land of the Chaldeans; yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there.
Discussion: Ezekiel packed his bags in daylight, dug through a wall at dusk, and slipped out with his face covered — acting out the king's own escape. Reflect: 1) Why act out an escape that has not happened, in front of people who refuse to see? 2) What does the covered face say about a king who will be taken to Babylon yet never see it? 3) How do you warn people who have eyes but will not see?
Significance: A staged midnight escape preached Zedekiah's fate in advance: he would flee by night, face covered, and be carried to Babylon without ever seeing it. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Call and the Scroll; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: The word of the LORD came to Ezekiel: Son of man, eat thy bread with quaking, and drink thy water with trembling and with carefulness. And say unto the people of the land, Thus saith the Lord GOD of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and of the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread with carefulness, and drink their water with astonishment, that her land may be desolate from all that is therein, because of the violence of all them that dwell therein. And the cities that are inhabited shall be laid waste, and the land shall be desolate; and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Discussion: Ezekiel ate and drank as a man under siege — trembling, careful, astonished — though no army was at his door. Reflect: 1) Why does God make an exile in Babylon eat like a man in besieged Jerusalem? 2) What does eating 'with carefulness' teach about taking daily bread for granted? 3) How does a prophet's trembling meal preach that judgment is not far away, but already at the table?
Significance: A trembling meal in Babylon preached a desolate land in Judah: the siege would reach every table, and the people would know the LORD in their want. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Siege Signs

Retelling: The word of the LORD came to Ezekiel: Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down. Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not thy lips, and eat not the bread of men. So Ezekiel spoke unto the people in the morning, and at even his wife died, and in the morning he did as he was commanded. The people said unto him, Wilt thou not tell us what these things are to us, that thou doest so? Ezekiel answered, The word of the LORD came unto me, saying, Speak unto the house of Israel: Thus saith the Lord GOD: Behold, I will profane My sanctuary, the excellency of your strength, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pitieth; and your sons and your daughters whom ye have left shall fall by the sword. And ye shall do as I have done: ye shall not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men. And your tires shall be upon your heads, and your shoes upon your feet: ye shall not mourn nor weep; but ye shall pine away for your iniquities, and mourn one toward another. Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign: according to all that he hath done shall ye do: and when this cometh, ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD. And thou, son of man, in the day when I take from them their strength, the joy of their glory, the desire of their eyes, and that whereupon they set their minds, their sons and their daughters — in that day he that escapeth shall come unto thee, to cause thee to hear it with thine ears. In that day shall thy mouth be opened to him which is escaped, and thou shalt speak, and be no more dumb: and thou shalt be a sign unto them; and they shall know that I am the LORD.
Discussion: Ezekiel lost his wife and was forbidden to mourn her — so that his grief would preach Jerusalem's grief. Reflect: 1) What does it cost a prophet when his own sorrow becomes the sermon? 2) Why would God forbid mourning for the very loss He inflicted? 3) How do you grieve faithfully when God says the normal comforts are not yours to take?
Significance: A prophet forbidden to weep for his wife became the sign of a people who would lose their sanctuary and their children and have no mourning left to mourn with. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Ezekiel's Siege Signs; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Retelling: The word of the LORD came to Ezekiel: Moreover, thou son of man, take thee one stick, and write upon it, For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions: then take another stick, and write upon it, For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions: and join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand. And when the children of thy people shall speak unto thee, saying, Wilt thou not show us what thou meanest by these? Say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD: Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in Mine hand. And the sticks whereon thou writest shall be in thine hand before their eyes. And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD: Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land. And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all. Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions: but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be My people, and I will be their God. And David My servant shall be king over them; and they shall all have one shepherd: they shall also walk in My judgments, and observe My statutes, and do them. And they shall dwell in the land that I have given unto Jacob My servant, wherein your fathers have dwelt; and they shall dwell therein, even they, and their children, and their children's children for ever: and My servant David shall be their prince for ever. Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them: and I will place them, and multiply them, and will set My sanctuary in the midst of them for evermore.
Discussion: Two sticks in one hand preached one nation under one king again. Reflect: 1) Why does God preach reunion with two pieces of wood, after centuries of division? 2) What does it mean that the reunited people get one shepherd — David — rather than two kings? 3) How does a covenant of peace, with God's sanctuary in the midst, answer the valley of dry bones that came just before?
Significance: Two sticks joined in the prophet's hand promised what division had made unthinkable: one nation, one king, one shepherd, and God's sanctuary among them for ever. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: The Valley of Dry Bones; Ezekiel's Call and the Scroll

Story: Hosea Marries Gomer and Names the Children
Retelling: The word of the LORD that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel. The LORD said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD. So Hosea took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son. And the LORD said, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel. And it shall come to pass at that day, that I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel. She conceived again and bore a daughter, and God said, Call her name Lo-ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away. But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the LORD their God. Then she weaned Lo-ruhamah and conceived and bore a son, and God said, Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not My people, and I will not be your God. Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not My people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.
Discussion: Hosea's children were given names no child should carry — and each name was a sermon. Reflect: 1) What does it mean for a family to carry God's judgment in their children's names? 2) How do Jezreel, No-mercy, and Not-my-people preach Israel's story in three words? 3) Why does the chapter end with 'sons of the living God' after 'not my people'?
Significance: A prophet's marriage and his children's names made Israel's unfaithfulness personal: judgment named out loud, yet ending in a promise that 'not my people' would become sons of the living God. Doubt: this is a lived parable — a marriage used as a prophetic sign — so whether it is read as straightforward biography or prophetic sign-act is debated.
RelatedEvents: Hosea's Marriage

Retelling: The LORD said unto Hosea, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine. So Hosea bought her to him for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley. And he said unto her, Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man: so will I also be for thee. For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim. Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the LORD their God, and David their king; and shall fear the LORD and His goodness in the latter days.
Discussion: Hosea paid silver and barley to buy back a wife who had left him — the price of God's love made visible. Reflect: 1) What does it cost to love someone who has chosen someone else? 2) Why does Hosea's purchase come with 'many days' of waiting, not instant restoration? 3) How does this bought-back wife picture what God has done for you?
Significance: Love that buys back the unfaithful at a price, then waits through many days without king or sacrifice, pictures God's costly pursuit of Israel to the end. Doubt: this is a lived parable — a marriage used as a prophetic sign — so whether it is read as straightforward biography or prophetic sign-act is debated.
RelatedEvents: Hosea's Marriage

Story: The Locust Plague in Joel's Day
Retelling: The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel. Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land. Hath this been in your days, or even in the days of your fathers? Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation. That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten. Awake, ye drunkards, and weep, and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine, for it is cut off from your mouth. For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion. He hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree: he hath made it clean bare, and cast it away; the branches thereof are made white. Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth. The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests, the LORD's ministers, mourn. The field is wasted, the land mourneth; for the corn is wasted, the new wine is dried up, the oil languisheth. The husbandmen are ashamed, the vine dressers howl for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field is perished. The vine is dried up, the fig tree languisheth, the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men. The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down, for the corn is withered. How do the beasts groan! The herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate. O LORD, to Thee will I cry: for the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and the flame hath burned all the trees of the field. The beasts of the field cry also unto Thee, for the rivers of waters are dried up, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness. And Joel called the people to sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the LORD their God, and cry unto the LORD, for the day of the LORD is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come.
Discussion: Wave after wave of locusts stripped the land bare, and even the Temple offerings stopped. Reflect: 1) Why does Joel tell parents to pass this disaster down to their children's children? 2) What does it mean when a natural disaster cuts off worship itself? 3) How does a call to fast and assemble turn a plague into a summons to return to God?
Significance: A land stripped by successive swarms, with field, flock, and Temple offering all cut off, becomes Joel's summons: the day of the LORD is at hand, so cry to the LORD. Doubt: the locusts are described as a devastating invasion, and whether the passage pictures a literal plague, an invading army, or both is debated.

Retelling: The word of the LORD came unto Zechariah, saying, Take of them of the captivity, even of Heldai, of Tobijah, and of Jedaiah, which are come from Babylon, and come thou the same day, and go into the house of Josiah the son of Zephaniah. Then take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them upon the head of Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and speak unto him, saying, Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, saying, Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH; and he shall grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD. Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both. And the crowns shall be to Helem, and to Tobijah, and to Jedaiah, and to Hen the son of Zephaniah, for a memorial in the temple of the LORD. And they that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the LORD, and ye shall know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you.
Discussion: A crown was set on a priest's head — king and priest in one man. Reflect: 1) Why crown a high priest, when kings and priests were kept apart? 2) Who is the Branch who builds the Temple and bears the glory? 3) What does it mean that people 'far off' will come and build, and the crowns stay as a memorial?
Significance: Crowns of silver and gold on Joshua's head pictured a coming Branch who would be both priest and king, building the LORD's Temple with a counsel of peace. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
KeyPeople: Zechariah the Prophet; Joshua, Son of Jehozadak
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple

Retelling: Zechariah fed the flock of the slaughter, whose possessors slew them and held themselves not guilty, and they that sold them said, Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich, and their own shepherds pitied them not. He took unto him two staves, the one he called Beauty, and the other he called Bands, and fed the flock. Three shepherds also he cut off in one month, and his soul loathed them, and their soul also abhorred him. Then said he, I will not feed you: that that dieth, let it die; and that that is to be cut off, let it be cut off; and let the rest eat every one the flesh of another. And he took his staff, even Beauty, and cut it asunder, that he might break his covenant which he had made with all the people. And it was broken in that day, and so the poor of the flock that waited upon him knew that it was the word of the LORD. And he said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for his price thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto him, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And Zechariah took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD. Then he cut asunder his other staff, even Bands, that he might break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. And the LORD said, Take unto thee yet the instruments of a foolish shepherd. For, lo, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, which shall not visit those that be cut off, neither shall seek the young one, nor heal that that is broken, nor feed that that standeth still: but he shall eat the flesh of the fat, and tear their claws in pieces. Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened.
Discussion: Zechariah broke two staffs and was paid thirty pieces of silver — the price of a shepherd, thrown to the potter. Reflect: 1) What do Beauty and Bands stand for, and what breaks when both are cut? 2) Why is thirty pieces of silver a 'goodly price' said with bitter irony? 3) How does the worthless shepherd at the end warn every leader who feeds himself instead of the flock?
Significance: A shepherd's broken staffs, a contemptible wage cast to the potter, and a worthless shepherd under woe together picture a flock abandoned by its leaders and a covenant broken. Doubt: this is a prophetic sign-act, a staged picture or lived sign, rather than an ordinary historical episode.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple

Retelling: In the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, wine was before him, and Nehemiah took up the wine and gave it unto the king. Now Nehemiah had not been beforetime sad in the king's presence. The king said, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? This is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then Nehemiah was very sore afraid, and said unto the king, Let the king live for ever: why should not my countenance be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' sepulchres, lieth waste, and the gates thereof are consumed with fire? Then the king said, For what dost thou make request? So Nehemiah prayed to the God of heaven, and said unto the king, If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers' sepulchres, that I may build it. And the king said, with the queen also sitting by him, For how long shall thy journey be, and when wilt thou return? So it pleased the king to send him, and Nehemiah set him a time. Moreover he asked for letters unto the governors beyond the river, that they might convey him over till he came into Judah, and a letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king's forest, that he might give him timber to make beams for the gates of the palace which appertained to the house, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that he should enter into. And the king granted him, according to the good hand of his God upon him. When Nehemiah came to the governors beyond the river and gave them the king's letters, Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, and it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel.
Discussion: A cupbearer's sad face became a request to rebuild a ruined city — prayed in a breath, answered by a king. Reflect: 1) Why did Nehemiah pray before answering a king who could kill him for sadness? 2) What does it mean to ask for letters and timber, not just permission — practical faith? 3) How do you know when sorrow of heart is a call to act, not just to feel?
Significance: One prayed sentence before a king turned a cupbearer's grief into royal letters and timber: God opens the way for the rebuilding before a single stone is laid.
KeyPeople: Nehemiah; Artaxerxes; Sanballat; Tobiah the Ammonite
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Story: Nehemiah Inspects the Broken Wall by Night
Retelling: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem, and was there three days. Then he arose in the night, he and some few men with him, and told no man what his God had put in his heart to do at Jerusalem. There was no beast with him, save the beast that he rode upon. He went out by night by the gate of the valley, even before the dragon well, and to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and the gates thereof were consumed with fire. Then he went on to the gate of the fountain, and to the king's pool, but there was no place for the beast that was under him to pass. Then he went up in the night by the brook, and viewed the wall, and turned back, and entered by the gate of the valley, and so returned. The rulers knew not whither he went, or what he did, neither had he as yet told it to the Jews, nor to the priests, nor to the nobles, nor to the rulers, nor to the rest that did the work. Then said he unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach. Then he told them of the hand of his God which was good upon him, and also the king's words that he had spoken unto him. And they said, Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work. But when Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they laughed them to scorn, and despised them, and said, What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king? Then Nehemiah answered them, The God of heaven, He will prosper us; therefore we His servants will arise and build: but ye have no portion, nor right, nor memorial, in Jerusalem.
Discussion: Nehemiah rode the ruins by night before he told anyone what he planned. Reflect: 1) Why inspect alone at night before announcing anything? 2) How does seeing the brokenness firsthand change a leader's call from slogan to plan? 3) What do you do when the first response to 'let us rise up and build' is laughter and scorn?
Significance: A secret night ride over broken walls turned private grief into a public call — and the people's answer, 'let us rise up and build,' began the work.
KeyPeople: Nehemiah; Sanballat; Tobiah the Ammonite; Geshem
RelatedEvents: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Nehemiah's Request to the King

Retelling: When Joseph learned that Mary, to whom he was betrothed, was with child, he planned to divorce her quietly rather than expose her to shame. But an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and told him not to fear taking Mary as his wife, because the child conceived in her was from the Holy Spirit. The angel said the son would be named Jesus, because he would save his people from their sins, and that this fulfilled the prophet's word that a virgin would bear a son called Immanuel, God with us. Joseph woke, obeyed, took Mary as his wife, and when the child was born, named him Jesus.
Discussion: Joseph's obedience came before he understood everything: he trusted God's word in a dream over the shame and confusion around him. Reflect: 1) Where does obedience require trusting God before you see the outcome? 2) How does Joseph's quiet protection of Mary shape the way you treat people under suspicion? 3) What does the name Jesus, saviour from sins, mean for your own need?
Significance: God announced the incarnation to Joseph as well as to Mary, and Joseph's obedience gave Jesus a lawful home in David's line. The Saviour's mission was named before he was born: he would save his people from their sins.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Story: The Shepherds Visit the Newborn Jesus
Retelling: On the night Jesus was born, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks near Bethlehem when an angel of the Lord appeared, the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified. The angel told them not to fear: he brought good news of great joy for all people, that in David's city a Saviour had been born, Christ the Lord, and the sign would be a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger. Suddenly a multitude of angels praised God, saying glory to God in the highest and peace to those on whom his favour rests. The shepherds hurried to Bethlehem, found Mary, Joseph, and the baby in the manger exactly as told, spread the word about what they had heard, and returned glorifying and praising God.
Discussion: The first evangelists were night-shift shepherds, not priests or kings: God announced his Son to ordinary workers and they told everyone. Reflect: 1) Who in your life would least expect to hear good news from you? 2) How does the shepherds' hurry challenge slow, cautious faith? 3) What does it mean that this joy is for all people?
Significance: The gospel was first preached by angels to shepherds and then by shepherds to their neighbours, showing from the first night that Christ came for the lowly as well as for all people.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Retelling: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem, wise men from the east arrived in Jerusalem asking where the king of the Jews had been born, because they had seen his star and come to worship him. King Herod was troubled, gathered the chief priests and scribes, and learned from them that the Messiah was to be born in Bethlehem, as the prophet Micah had written. Herod sent the wise men to Bethlehem, asking them to report back so that he too might worship, though he meant to kill the child. The star went ahead of them until it stopped over the house, and entering, they saw the child with Mary his mother, fell down and worshipped him, and opened their treasures, offering gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home by another way.
Discussion: The wise men followed a star across borders to worship a child in a house, while the king in Jerusalem plotted murder: the same news divides hearts. Reflect: 1) What has God used to draw you toward Jesus? 2) How do you tell true worship from Herod's false worship? 3) What costly gift does worship ask of you?
Significance: Gentile seekers recognised and worshipped Israel's newborn king before his own ruler did, and their gifts honoured him as king, priest, and sacrifice to come.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Herod the Great
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Flight into Egypt

Retelling: After the wise men left, an angel warned Joseph in a dream to take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, because Herod was about to search for the child to kill him. Joseph rose by night and escaped with them to Egypt, where they stayed until Herod's death, fulfilling the word, Out of Egypt I called my son. When Herod realised he had been outwitted, he ordered the killing of all boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity aged two and under, matching the time he had learned from the wise men. After Herod died, an angel told Joseph in another dream to return, but hearing that Archelaus reigned in Judea, Joseph was warned again and withdrew to Galilee, settling in Nazareth, fulfilling that Jesus would be called a Nazarene.
Discussion: Joseph obeyed three dreams in a row, each one uprooting his family, and God preserved the child through a refugee's flight. Reflect: 1) How do you obey when God's guidance disrupts your plans? 2) Where do you see God protecting his purposes through ordinary, frightened people? 3) What does Jesus' own experience as a refugee child mean for how you see displaced people?
Significance: The infant Messiah was hunted, hidden, and brought home again, so that even his childhood retraced Israel's story: called out of Egypt and raised in obscurity in Nazareth.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Herod the Great
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Massacre of the Innocents

Retelling: When Herod saw that the wise men had outwitted him, he flew into a rage and gave orders to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under, in accordance with the time he had learned from the wise men. The slaughter fulfilled Jeremiah's lament: a voice heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more. Herod's cruelty could not reach the child he hunted, who was already safe in Egypt, but Bethlehem's families bore the cost of his fear.
Discussion: This is the darkest page of the nativity, and Scripture does not soften it: the Saviour's birth provoked murder, and innocent families grieved. Reflect: 1) How do you hold God's protection of Jesus alongside the grief of Bethlehem's mothers? 2) Where does power still answer fear with violence against the defenceless? 3) What comfort does Rachel's uncomforted weeping, held inside God's story, offer mourners?
Significance: Herod's massacre shows the world's violent resistance to the newborn king from the very beginning, and it anchors the Christmas story in real grief rather than sentiment.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Herod the Great
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Flight into Egypt

Story: The Presentation of Jesus in the Temple
Retelling: When the time came for their purification under the Law of Moses, Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, offering the sacrifice of a pair of doves or two young pigeons, the offering of the poor. In the temple was Simeon, a righteous and devout man waiting for the consolation of Israel, to whom the Holy Spirit had promised he would not die before seeing the Lord's Messiah. Guided by the Spirit, Simeon took the child in his arms, praised God, and said he could now depart in peace, for his eyes had seen God's salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. He blessed them and told Mary that this child was destined for the falling and rising of many in Israel and for a sign spoken against, and that a sword would pierce her own soul. The prophetess Anna, who had worshipped in the temple for decades, also came up, gave thanks to God, and spoke about the child to all who were waiting for Jerusalem's redemption.
Discussion: Simeon and Anna had waited a lifetime, and they recognised the Saviour as a baby in arms: long faithfulness sharpens sight. Reflect: 1) What are you waiting for God to show you? 2) How does Simeon's warning to Mary prepare you for a Saviour who divides responses? 3) What does Anna's lifelong worship say about faithfulness without a platform?
Significance: At his presentation Jesus was publicly recognised as God's salvation for Israel and the Gentiles, and Mary was warned that his mission would pierce her own heart.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary; Simeon; Anna the Prophetess
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Story: The Boy Jesus in the Temple
Retelling: Every year Jesus' parents went to Jerusalem for Passover, and when he was twelve they took him with them. After the feast, as they travelled home, Mary and Joseph realised Jesus was not among the caravan, and after searching a day they returned anxiously to Jerusalem. After three days they found him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions, and everyone who heard him was amazed at his understanding and answers. His mother asked why he had treated them so, saying she and his father had been anxiously searching, and Jesus answered, Didn't you know I had to be in my Father's house? They did not understand what he meant. He returned with them to Nazareth and was obedient to them, and he grew in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men.
Discussion: At twelve, Jesus already knew whose Son he was, yet he went home and lived obediently in obscurity for years: identity did not skip ordinary faithfulness. Reflect: 1) How does Jesus' question about his Father's house shape your own sense of belonging to God? 2) What does his return to Nazareth teach about honouring parents while following God? 3) Where is God growing you quietly, without an audience?
Significance: The only recorded episode from Jesus' childhood shows him already conscious of his Father's business, yet choosing years of obedient obscurity before his public ministry.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; Joseph, Husband of Mary
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Story: The Disciples Pluck Grain on the Sabbath
Retelling: One Sabbath, as Jesus and his disciples walked through grainfields, the hungry disciples began to pick heads of grain and eat them. The Pharisees objected that this was unlawful on the Sabbath. Jesus answered from Scripture: David, when hungry, entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread, which only priests might eat, and the priests themselves work in the temple on the Sabbath yet are innocent. He added that something greater than the temple was here, that God desires mercy, not sacrifice, and concluded that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
Discussion: The Sabbath was made for human flourishing, not as a trap for the hungry: Jesus reads the Law through mercy. Reflect: 1) Where do religious rules in your life hinder mercy instead of serving it? 2) How does Jesus' appeal to David challenge proof-texting without context? 3) What does it mean to live under the Lord of the Sabbath rather than under Sabbath anxiety?
Significance: Jesus claimed authority over the Sabbath itself, grounding that claim in Scripture and in God's desire for mercy, and so set the pattern for his Sabbath controversies.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; James, Son of Zebedee; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Man with a Withered Hand

Retelling: After spending the night in prayer on a mountainside, Jesus called to himself those he wanted, and appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him and to be sent out to preach and to have authority to drive out demons. They were Simon, whom he named Peter, James son of Zebedee and his brother John, Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who would betray him. The appointment followed a night of prayer and preceded their public mission.
Discussion: Jesus chose ordinary, clashing men after a night of prayer, and named them to be with him before sending them anywhere: presence precedes mission. Reflect: 1) What does it mean that discipleship starts with being with Jesus, not doing for him? 2) How does the mix of tax collector, zealot, and betrayer in one group challenge your idea of a worthy team? 3) Why does Luke stress the night of prayer before the choice?
Significance: The Twelve were appointed as the authorised core of Jesus' mission, chosen in prayer and charged to preach and to confront evil, and their number recalled the twelve tribes of Israel.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; Andrew; James, Son of Zebedee; John the Apostle; Philip; Bartholomew; Matthew; Thomas; James, Son of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot; Judas Iscariot
RelatedEvents: Jesus Sends Out the Twelve

Story: John the Baptist Asks from Prison
Retelling: From prison, John the Baptist heard about the deeds of the Messiah and sent his disciples to ask Jesus, Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else? Jesus replied by pointing to what was happening: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, those with leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is proclaimed to the poor. He closed with a blessing on anyone who does not stumble on account of him. John, who had announced the coming one, now asked from a cell whether he had been right, and Jesus answered with evidence rather than rebuke.
Discussion: Even the forerunner asked his question from prison, and Jesus answered with deeds, not scolding: doubt brought honestly to Jesus is met with evidence. Reflect: 1) What do you do with faith when circumstances contradict what you expected? 2) How does Jesus' list of healings and good news for the poor define his Messiahship? 3) Where might you be stumbling over Jesus because he does not match your expectations?
Significance: John's question and Jesus' answer together define the Messiah by his works: healing, raising, and good news for the poor, in fulfilment of Isaiah's hope.
RelatedEvents: The Death of John the Baptist; The Raising of the Widow's Son at Nain

Retelling: While Jesus was speaking to the crowds, his mother and brothers arrived and, unable to reach him through the crowd, sent word asking to speak with him. Someone told him, Your mother and brothers are outside, wanting to speak to you. Jesus replied, Who is my mother, and who are my brothers? Then, pointing to his disciples, he said, Here are my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother. He did not reject his family, but he redefined belonging around doing the Father's will.
Discussion: Jesus widened the family circle without breaking it: belonging to him is marked by doing the Father's will, not by blood alone. Reflect: 1) How does this redefinition comfort those whose families do not share their faith? 2) Where might family loyalty compete with obedience to God in your life? 3) What does it mean practically to treat fellow disciples as brother and sister?
Significance: Jesus taught that the truest kinship is obedience to the Father, making the community of disciples a family bound by God's will.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary, Mother of Jesus; James, Brother of Jesus
RelatedEvents: Jesus Rejected at Nazareth

Retelling: As Jesus and his disciples travelled, they came to a village where a woman named Martha opened her home to him. Her sister Mary sat at the Lord's feet listening to what he said, while Martha was distracted by all the preparations. She came to Jesus and asked, Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself? Tell her to help me! Jesus answered, Martha, Martha, you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed, or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her. Service was not condemned, but listening to Jesus was named the one necessary thing.
Discussion: Martha's serving was good and needed, yet it became anxious distraction, while Mary's listening was called better: service must not crowd out the Lord himself. Reflect: 1) Where has good work made you worried and upset rather than attentive? 2) What would choosing the better part look like in your busiest week? 3) How do you honour both serving and sitting at Jesus' feet without pitting sisters against each other?
Significance: Jesus honoured hospitality while insisting that listening to his word is the one necessary thing, and that it cannot be taken from the one who chooses it.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Martha; Mary of Bethany; Lazarus
RelatedEvents: Raising of Lazarus

Retelling: People brought little children to Jesus so that he might place his hands on them and pray for them, but the disciples rebuked those who brought them. When Jesus saw this he was indignant and said, Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. He added that whoever will not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it. Then he took the children in his arms, placed his hands on them, and blessed them.
Discussion: The disciples saw children as interruptions; Jesus saw them as the pattern of kingdom entrance: small, dependent, and welcomed by touch. Reflect: 1) Who do you treat as an interruption to real ministry? 2) What does receiving the kingdom like a child mean for an adult used to earning? 3) How does Jesus' embrace of children shape a church's welcome?
Significance: Jesus welcomed children as full members of the kingdom's welcome, making childlike dependence, not achievement, the way into God's reign.
RelatedEvents: The Rich Young Ruler

Retelling: At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples who people said the Son of Man was. They reported the guesses: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. Then he asked the sharper question, But what about you? Who do you say I am? Simon Peter answered, You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Jesus blessed him, saying flesh and blood had not revealed this but his Father in heaven, and declared that on this rock he would build his church, and the gates of Hades would not overcome it, giving Peter the keys of the kingdom. Then he ordered the disciples not to tell anyone that he was the Messiah.
Discussion: Peter's confession came not from crowd opinion but from the Father's revelation, and it became the foundation-stone of the church's identity. Reflect: 1) Whose opinion of Jesus most shapes yours: the crowd's or the Father's? 2) What does it mean to confess Jesus as Messiah and Son of the living God today? 3) Why would Jesus order silence about a true confession at that moment?
Significance: The disciples' confession that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of the living God, marks the turning point of the Gospels, and on it Jesus promised to build his church.
RelatedEvents: Transfiguration

Retelling: On the evening before Passover, Jesus, knowing the Father had put all things under his power and that he had come from God and was returning to God, rose from the meal, took off his outer clothing, wrapped a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin, and began to wash his disciples' feet, drying them with the towel. When he came to Simon Peter, Peter protested, Lord, are you going to wash my feet? Jesus answered that unless he washed him, Peter would have no part with him, and Peter then asked for his hands and head as well. After washing them all, Jesus put on his clothes and asked whether they understood: he, their Lord and Teacher, had washed their feet, and they ought to wash one another's feet, for he had set them an example to do as he had done.
Discussion: The Lord of all took the slave's task on the night of betrayal: greatness in his kingdom is measured by washing feet. Reflect: 1) Where does pride keep you from accepting Jesus' cleansing service? 2) What foot-washing task, literal or figurative, is yours toward someone who may betray you? 3) How does this scene reframe leadership in your home, church, or work?
Significance: On his last evening Jesus enacted servanthood as the shape of discipleship, cleansing his followers and commanding them to serve one another as he had served them.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper

Retelling: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests and asked, What are you willing to give me if I deliver him over to you? They counted out thirty pieces of silver for him, and from that time Judas watched for an opportunity to hand Jesus over when no crowd was present. Luke records that Satan entered Judas, and that he conferred with the chief priests and the officers of the temple guard about how he might betray Jesus. The bargain was struck before the Passover meal, and the betrayal price was fixed in advance of the arrest.
Discussion: Judas sold his Master for the price of a slave's compensation, and the chief priests bought a quiet arrest: betrayal often starts as a bargain, not a blow. Reflect: 1) What small bargains have you made that traded loyalty for gain or safety? 2) How does the chief priests' willingness to pay for secrecy expose fear of the crowds? 3) Where do you need to name a compromise before it becomes a betrayal?
