Significance: The betrayal was arranged in advance for thirty pieces of silver, showing that Jesus' arrest was not an accident of the crowd but a purchased, deliberate act.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper

Story: The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane
Retelling: While Jesus was still speaking in Gethsemane, Judas arrived with a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders. Judas had arranged a sign: the one he kissed would be Jesus. Going at once to Jesus, he greeted him, Rabbi, and kissed him, and Jesus answered, Do what you came for, friend. The men seized Jesus and arrested him. One of those with Jesus drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest's servant, but Jesus told him to put his sword back, for all who draw the sword will die by the sword, and healed the servant's ear. Jesus asked the crowd why they had come with swords and clubs as against a robber, when he had sat teaching daily in the temple, and said this had taken place so the Scriptures would be fulfilled. Then all the disciples deserted him and fled.
Discussion: The arrest combined a friend's kiss, a sword, and a surrender: Jesus stopped his own defence and went willingly, so that Scripture would be fulfilled. Reflect: 1) How does Jesus' refusal of the sword challenge the instinct to defend God's cause by force? 2) What does it mean that the disciples' flight is recorded without softening? 3) Where do you recognise a kiss of false friendship in your own story?
Significance: Jesus was arrested at night by a kiss of betrayal, yet he remained in command of the scene, forbidding violence and submitting to the Scriptures' fulfilment.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Judas Iscariot; Simon Peter; Malchus
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Crucifixion; Jesus Heals Malchus' Ear

Retelling: Those who had arrested Jesus took him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled, and Peter followed at a distance. The chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin sought false evidence against Jesus to put him to death, but found none that agreed, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two claimed he had said he could destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. The high priest demanded, Are you the Messiah, the Son of God? Jesus answered, You have said so, and added that from now on they would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. The high priest tore his clothes, declared blasphemy, and the council condemned him as worthy of death, while the guards mocked, blindfolded, and struck him.
Discussion: Jesus' own answer condemned him in their court: he would not deny being the Messiah and Son of God, even to save his life. Reflect: 1) What does Jesus' refusal to trim his claim under threat say about truth under pressure? 2) How do false witnesses and a rushed night trial warn you about justice done in anger? 3) Where are you tempted to soften who Jesus is to stay safe?
Significance: Before Israel's council Jesus openly claimed to be the Messiah and Son of God enthroned at God's right hand, and that confession became the charge on which he was condemned.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Peter Denies Jesus

Retelling: While Jesus was on trial inside, Peter sat outside in the courtyard warming himself by a fire. A servant girl said he had been with Jesus of Galilee, and Peter denied it before them all. A second time, as he went out to the gateway, another person recognised him and Peter denied it with an oath. A little later the bystanders said his accent gave him away, and Peter began to call down curses and swear, I don't know the man! Immediately a rooster crowed, and Peter remembered Jesus' words, Before the rooster crows, you will disown me three times. Luke adds that the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter. Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Discussion: Peter's denials escalated from evasion to curses in one courtyard, yet the rooster and the Lord's look broke him into tears: failure named honestly is the doorway to restoration. Reflect: 1) Where does fear make you deny what you know is true? 2) How does the Lord's look, rather than a lecture, bring Peter to tears? 3) What does Peter's bitter weeping, without yet a resolution, teach about repentance?
Significance: The boldest disciple denied his Lord three times in a single night, exactly as Jesus had foretold, and his tears mark the beginning, not the end, of his story.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Crucifixion; Jesus Before the Sanhedrin

Retelling: When Judas, who had betrayed Jesus, saw that Jesus was condemned, he was seized with remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, I have sinned, for I have betrayed innocent blood. They answered, What is that to us? That's your responsibility. Judas threw the money into the temple and left, and went away and hanged himself. The chief priests, unwilling to put blood money into the treasury, used it to buy the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners, which is why it is called the Field of Blood. Matthew notes this fulfilled what was spoken by the prophets about thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field.
Discussion: Judas confessed his sin truly, but he took his confession to men who would not carry it, and despair, not repentance, ended his story: remorse without return to Jesus is not repentance. Reflect: 1) What is the difference between Judas' remorse and Peter's tears? 2) Where do you take guilt when the people you confess to shrug it off? 3) How does the Field of Blood warn against pricing loyalty?
Significance: Judas' remorse, rejected by the priests he served, ended in suicide, and the blood money bought a burial field, fulfilling prophecy and standing as the dark counterpart to Peter's restoration.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Judas Agrees to Betray Jesus

Retelling: At daybreak the Jewish leaders bound Jesus and handed him to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, charging him with subverting the nation, opposing taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be Messiah, a king. Pilate asked, Are you the king of the Jews? Jesus answered, You have said so, and otherwise remained silent before the accusations, to Pilate's amazement. Pilate found no basis for a charge, and learning Jesus was a Galilean, sent him to Herod, who returned him. Pilate, warned by his wife's dream and convinced of Jesus' innocence, tried to release him under the Passover custom, but the chief priests stirred the crowd to demand Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, instead. Pilate asked what he should do with Jesus, the crowd shouted, Crucify him! Pilate washed his hands, declared himself innocent of this man's blood, and handed Jesus over to be flogged and crucified.
Discussion: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent and still handed him over to keep the crowd quiet: a verdict can be true and still be betrayed. Reflect: 1) Where does pressure from a crowd or a career tempt you to wash your hands of a true verdict? 2) How does Jesus' near-silence before Pilate speak louder than defence? 3) What does Barabbas' release say about substitution at the heart of the cross?
Significance: The Roman governor three times found no guilt in Jesus yet sentenced him to death under crowd pressure, and the guilty Barabbas walked free in his place.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Jesus Before Herod

Retelling: When Pilate learned that Jesus was under Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod Antipas, who happened to be in Jerusalem at the time. Herod was greatly pleased, because for a long time he had wanted to see Jesus, having heard about him, and he hoped to see him perform a sign. He plied Jesus with many questions, but Jesus gave him no answer, while the chief priests and scribes stood by vehemently accusing him. Herod and his soldiers ridiculed and mocked Jesus, dressing him in an elegant robe, and then sent him back to Pilate. That day Herod and Pilate, who had been enemies, became friends.
Discussion: Herod wanted a performance, not a king, and Jesus answered curiosity with silence: the gospel is not entertainment for the powerful. Reflect: 1) What is the difference between wanting to see Jesus and wanting to be entertained by him? 2) How does Jesus' silence before Herod challenge the urge to justify yourself to every accuser? 3) What does the new friendship of Herod and Pilate say about opposition uniting against Jesus?
Significance: Herod, who had killed John the Baptist, met Jesus only as a curiosity, mocked him, and returned him to Pilate, and the two rulers became friends over the prisoner neither would acquit.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Before Pilate; The Crucifixion

Story: Simon of Cyrene Carries Jesus' Cross
Retelling: As the soldiers led Jesus out to be crucified, they seized a man named Simon from Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and put the cross on him to carry behind Jesus. Mark names him as the father of Alexander and Rufus. A large number of people followed, including women who mourned and wailed for him, and Jesus turned to them and said, Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; weep for yourselves and for your children, warning of days when people would say blessed are the childless, and would call on the mountains to fall on them. If people do these things when the tree is green, he asked, what will happen when it is dry? Simon, a passer-by pressed into service, walked the road to Calvary carrying the cross behind Jesus.
Discussion: Simon did not volunteer; he was seized and made to carry a condemned man's cross, and following Jesus behind him became the literal picture of discipleship. Reflect: 1) What cross have you been pressed to carry that you did not choose? 2) How does Jesus' warning to the weeping women reframe pity into repentance? 3) Where does following behind Jesus, rather than ahead of him, change your direction?
Significance: A bystander from Cyrene was compelled to carry Jesus' cross, and on the way Jesus warned Jerusalem's mourners that judgment, not mere pity, was what the city needed.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

Retelling: Two criminals were crucified with Jesus, one on either side. One of them hurled insults at him: Aren't you the Messiah? Save yourself and us! But the other rebuked him, saying, Don't you fear God, since you are under the same sentence? We are punished justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong. Then he said, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Jesus answered him, Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.
Discussion: A dying criminal with no time for good works, baptism, or a better life was promised paradise on the strength of one plea: remember me. Reflect: 1) What does this promise say about salvation by grace rather than by record? 2) How does the second thief's confession, justly punished, innocent Jesus, model honest repentance? 3) What does today mean for someone who fears it is too late?
Significance: Beside the cross, a condemned criminal confessed Jesus' innocence and kingship and received the promise of paradise that very day, showing that grace reaches even the final hour.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

Retelling: As evening approached on Preparation Day, Joseph of Arimathea, a rich and respected member of the council who had not consented to Jesus' condemnation and was himself waiting for the kingdom of God, went boldly to Pilate and asked for Jesus' body. Pilate, surprised he was already dead, confirmed it with the centurion and gave the body to Joseph. With Nicodemus, who brought about a hundred pounds weight of myrrh and aloes, Joseph took the body, wrapped it in clean linen cloths with the spices, and laid it in his own new tomb cut out of rock, in a garden near where Jesus was crucified. He rolled a great stone across the entrance and went away, while Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sat opposite the tomb. The next day the chief priests asked Pilate to secure the tomb, and they sealed the stone and posted a guard.
Discussion: Joseph and Nicodemus, quiet sympathisers until now, stepped into the open at the costliest moment: the burial made Jesus' death public, honourable, and verifiable. Reflect: 1) What does Joseph's boldness at evening say about courage that arrives late but still counts? 2) Why does the sealed, guarded tomb matter for the resurrection claim? 3) How do the women sitting opposite the tomb model faithful presence when nothing can be done?
Significance: Jesus was truly buried by named, honourable witnesses in a new rock tomb, sealed and guarded, so that the empty tomb three days later could not be explained as confusion about where he lay.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Joseph of Arimathea; Nicodemus; Mary Magdalene; Mary, Mother of James and Joses
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Story: The Guards Report the Empty Tomb
Retelling: While the women were on their way from the tomb, some of the guards went into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened. The chief priests met with the elders, devised a plan, and gave the soldiers a large sum of money, telling them to say, His disciples came during the night and stole him away while we were asleep. If this report reached the governor, they promised, they would satisfy him and keep the soldiers out of trouble. So the soldiers took the money and did as they were instructed, and Matthew notes that this story has been widely circulated among the Jews to this very day.
Discussion: The first official response to the resurrection was a bribe: a story bought to explain away an empty tomb, admitting the tomb was empty while denying the risen Lord. Reflect: 1) Why does the bribed story itself confirm the tomb was empty? 2) How do money and fear still shape explanations of Jesus today? 3) What does it cost to tell the truth when an easier story is on offer?
Significance: The guards' own report, bought and retold, unintentionally testifies that the tomb was empty on the third morning, while the priests chose a purchased lie over the risen Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene

Retelling: Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and found the stone removed, and after Peter and John had come and gone, she stood outside weeping. As she wept she looked into the tomb and saw two angels in white, who asked why she was crying, and she answered, They have taken my Lord away, and I don't know where they have put him. Turning around, she saw Jesus standing there but did not recognise him, supposing him to be the gardener, until he said her name, Mary. She turned and cried out, Rabboni! Jesus told her not to hold on to him, for he had not yet ascended to the Father, but to go to his brothers and say he was ascending to his Father and their Father, to his God and their God. Mary went and announced to the disciples, I have seen the Lord! Matthew records that as she and the other Mary left the tomb, Jesus met them and they clasped his feet and worshipped him.
Discussion: The risen Lord first revealed himself to a weeping woman outside the tomb, and she became the first witness of the resurrection to the apostles. Reflect: 1) Why does Jesus reveal himself by speaking Mary's name? 2) How does Mary's journey from weeping to announcing model witness? 3) What does it mean that the first resurrection preacher was a woman whose testimony the world discounted?
Significance: Mary Magdalene, first at the tomb and first to see the risen Lord, carried the first resurrection announcement to the disciples: I have seen the Lord.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Mary Magdalene; Mary, Mother of James and Joses; Simon Peter; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Guards Report the Empty Tomb

Retelling: On the first day of the week, two disciples were walking to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking about all that had happened. Jesus himself came up and walked along with them, but they were kept from recognising him. He asked what they were discussing, and Cleopas answered, Are you the only one visiting Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there? They told him about Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet powerful in word and deed, whom they had hoped was the one to redeem Israel, but who had been crucified, and how some women had astounded them that morning with a vision of angels saying he was alive. Then Jesus explained, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, what was said in all the Scriptures concerning himself, though their hearts burned without yet recognising him. At Emmaus they urged the stranger to stay, and as he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, their eyes were opened and they recognised him, and he disappeared from their sight. At once they returned to Jerusalem to tell the Eleven that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon.
Discussion: The risen Jesus walked seven miles unrecognised, opening the Scriptures before opening their eyes: understanding comes through the word before the breaking of bread. Reflect: 1) Where have you walked with Jesus unrecognised in disappointment? 2) How does Jesus' reading of Moses and the Prophets reshape what the Messiah had to suffer? 3) What makes hearts burn, and what sends witnesses hurrying back the same hour?
Significance: On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus taught two disappointed disciples from the whole of Scripture and was recognised in the breaking of bread, turning their flight from Jerusalem into an urgent return with the news.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene

Story: Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening
Retelling: On Easter evening, while the disciples were together behind locked doors for fear, Jesus himself stood among them and said, Peace be with you. They were startled and frightened, thinking they saw a ghost, so he showed them his hands and his side, and invited them to touch him, saying a ghost does not have flesh and bones as he had. Still disbelieving for joy, they watched as he ate a piece of broiled fish before them. Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, that the Messiah would suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins would be preached in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. He told them to stay in the city until clothed with power from on high, and he breathed on them, saying, Receive the Holy Spirit.
Discussion: The risen Jesus did not appear as a ghost or a vision but as flesh that could be touched and fed, and he turned frightened fugitives into witnesses to all nations. Reflect: 1) Why does Jesus prove his resurrection with hands, side, and fish rather than argument alone? 2) How does Peace be with you answer locked doors and fear? 3) What does it mean to wait for power before going out as witnesses?
Significance: On Easter evening the risen Christ stood bodily among his frightened disciples, proved his resurrection, opened the Scriptures, and commissioned them as witnesses to all nations.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; John the Apostle; Thomas
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Great Commission; Jesus Appears to Thomas

Retelling: Thomas, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus first appeared to them, and when they told him, We have seen the Lord! he said, Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. A week later the disciples were again together, and Thomas was with them. Though the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them, said Peace be with you, and turned to Thomas: Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe. Thomas answered him, My Lord and my God! Jesus said, Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.
Discussion: Thomas asked for the evidence the others had already received, and Jesus gave it without scolding, then blessed those who would believe without touching: doubt honestly brought to Jesus ends in worship. Reflect: 1) What evidence are you honestly asking Jesus for? 2) How does Thomas' confession, My Lord and my God, go beyond the other disciples' report? 3) What blessing belongs to believers who have not seen?
Significance: Thomas, who demanded to touch the wounds, became the first to confess the risen Jesus as My Lord and my God, and Jesus blessed all who believe without seeing.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Jesus Appears to the Disciples on Easter Evening

Story: Jesus Appears to Seven Disciples by the Sea of Galilee
Retelling: Afterwards Jesus appeared again to his disciples by the Sea of Galilee, where Simon Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, James and John, and two others were together. Peter said, I'm going out to fish, and the others went with him, but that night they caught nothing. At dawn Jesus stood on the shore, though they did not recognise him, and called out to cast the net on the right side of the boat. When they did, they could not haul in the net for the great number of fish, one hundred and fifty-three, yet the net was not torn, and John said to Peter, It is the Lord! Peter jumped into the water and swam to shore, where Jesus had a charcoal fire with fish and bread ready, and invited them, Come and have breakfast. After breakfast Jesus asked Peter three times, Simon son of John, do you love me? and each time restored him with the charge to feed his lambs and sheep, foretelling that Peter would one day be led where he did not want to go. Jesus then told Peter to follow him.
Discussion: Three denials by a charcoal fire were answered by three questions beside another charcoal fire, and a failed night's fishing by a net-breaking catch: restoration, not replacement, is how Jesus reinstates his own. Reflect: 1) How does Jesus' threefold question heal Peter's threefold denial? 2) What does breakfast on the beach say about the risen Lord's care for ordinary work? 3) What does Follow me mean for you after failure?
Significance: By the Sea of Galilee the risen Jesus gave a miraculous catch, shared breakfast, and restored Peter with threefold love and commission, closing the Gospel with Follow me.
KeyPeople: Jesus; Simon Peter; Thomas; James, Son of Zebedee; John the Apostle
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; Peter Denies Jesus

Story: Jesus Heals a Demoniac in the Capernaum Synagogue
Retelling: On the Sabbath in Capernaum, Jesus entered the synagogue and taught with authority, unlike the scribes, and the people were amazed. A man possessed by an impure spirit cried out, What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God! Jesus rebuked him, Be quiet! and Come out of him! The impure spirit shook the man violently and came out with a shriek, without injuring him. The people were astonished and asked what this new teaching with authority was, that even impure spirits obeyed him, and news about Jesus spread throughout Galilee.
Discussion: The first miracle Mark records is not a healing of the body but a confrontation in worship: authority over evil, exercised by a word, in the synagogue itself. Reflect: 1) How does the demon's accurate confession challenge faith that knows the right words without obeying? 2) What does Jesus' silence command say about testimony from evil? 3) Where do you need Jesus' authoritative word rather than more discussion?
Significance: In the Capernaum synagogue Jesus' authoritative teaching was confirmed by an authoritative word that drove out an impure spirit, and his fame spread through Galilee.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples

Retelling: When Jesus entered Simon Peter's house in Capernaum, he found Peter's mother-in-law lying in bed with a fever. Mark and Luke record that they told Jesus about her at once. Jesus went to her, took her by the hand and helped her up, and rebuked the fever, and the fever left her. Immediately she got up and began to wait on them, serving the household and its guests. The healing took place on the same Sabbath as the synagogue exorcism, at the start of Jesus' Galilean ministry, in an ordinary home.
Discussion: The first healing in Peter's own house was quiet, domestic, and instantly fruitful: she was raised up, and she served. Reflect: 1) How does this small household miracle dignify care given at home? 2) What does her immediate service say about gratitude that turns at once to serving others? 3) Where is Jesus present in your own house's fevers and sickrooms?
Significance: Jesus healed Peter's mother-in-law of a fever with a touch and a word, and her restored strength turned at once to serving him and his disciples.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of the First Disciples; Jesus Heals a Demoniac in the Capernaum Synagogue

Story: Jesus Heals a Man with a Withered Hand
Retelling: On another Sabbath Jesus entered the synagogue, where a man with a shrivelled hand was present, and the Pharisees watched to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath so they could accuse him. Jesus asked them whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill, and told the man to stand up in front of everyone. Then he said to the man, Stretch out your hand. The man stretched it out, and his hand was completely restored, as sound as the other. The Pharisees went out and plotted with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus, while the healed man stood whole among them.
Discussion: Healing on the Sabbath forced the question into the open: is the Sabbath for doing good or for watching a man suffer? Jesus answered by healing in full view. Reflect: 1) Where do you watch suffering while debating rules? 2) How does Stretch out your hand call for trust before the healing is seen? 3) What does the plot to kill Jesus after a healing reveal about hardened hearts?
Significance: On the Sabbath Jesus restored a shrivelled hand in full view of his critics, teaching that doing good is lawful on the Sabbath, and the healing hardened his opponents toward murder.
RelatedEvents: The Disciples Pluck Grain on the Sabbath

Retelling: As Jesus went on from healing Jairus' daughter, two blind men followed him, calling out, Have mercy on us, Son of David! When he had gone indoors, the blind men came to him, and Jesus asked, Do you believe that I am able to do this? They answered, Yes, Lord. Then he touched their eyes and said, According to your faith let it be done to you, and their sight was restored. Jesus warned them sternly not to tell anyone, but they went out and spread the news about him all over that region. This healing is distinct from the later healing of Bartimaeus and his companion at Jericho: it takes place in Galilee, in a house, and follows the raising of Jairus' daughter.
Discussion: Two blind men saw what sighted critics missed, calling Jesus Son of David, and Jesus tied the healing to their faith in his power. Reflect: 1) What does their persistent following, crying for mercy, teach about prayer? 2) How does Do you believe I am able to do this make faith personal? 3) Why would Jesus warn them to silence, and why could they not keep it?
Significance: In Galilee Jesus restored sight to two blind men who confessed him as Son of David, a healing distinct from the later Jericho healing of Bartimaeus.
RelatedEvents: The Healing of Bartimaeus

Retelling: While the two blind men were going out, a man who was demon-possessed and could not talk was brought to Jesus. When the demon was driven out, the man who had been mute spoke, and the crowd was amazed, saying, Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel! But the Pharisees said, It is by the prince of demons that he drives out demons. The healing belongs to the early Galilean ministry, after the raising of Jairus' daughter, and it is narrated separately from the later healing of a blind and mute demoniac: here the man's affliction is muteness alone, and the charge it provokes is recorded in brief.
Discussion: A voice restored became a voice of amazement for the crowd and of accusation for the Pharisees: the same miracle divides its witnesses. Reflect: 1) What silenced voice in your life or community needs Jesus' freeing word? 2) How does amazement differ from the Pharisees' explanation? 3) Where do you explain away God's work rather than wonder at it?
Significance: Jesus freed a demon-possessed man who could not speak, and the crowd marvelled at what had never been seen in Israel, while the Pharisees attributed the work to the prince of demons.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Blind and Mute Demoniac

Story: Jesus Heals a Blind and Mute Demoniac
Retelling: Then they brought Jesus a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute, and Jesus healed him, so that he could both talk and see. All the people were astonished and said, Could this be the Son of David? But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this fellow drives out demons. This is a separate narration from the earlier healing of a mute demoniac: here the man is both blind and mute, the healing restores both sight and speech, and the crowd's astonishment turns explicitly to the question of whether Jesus is the Son of David, provoking the full Beelzebul controversy that follows.
Discussion: Sight and speech restored together made the crowd ask the right question, Could this be the Son of David? while the Pharisees answered it with the worst explanation. Reflect: 1) How does restored sight and speech picture what Jesus does for the spiritually blind and mute? 2) What makes the crowd's question better than the Pharisees' answer? 3) Where are you tempted to attribute God's work to an evil source?
Significance: Jesus healed a demon-possessed man who was both blind and mute, restoring sight and speech together, and the crowd wondered whether he was the Son of David.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Mute Demoniac

Story: Jesus Heals a Woman Bent Double
Retelling: One Sabbath Jesus was teaching in a synagogue when a woman appeared who had been crippled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not straighten up at all. When Jesus saw her, he called her forward and said, Woman, you are set free from your infirmity. Then he put his hands on her, and immediately she straightened up and praised God. The synagogue leader, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, told the crowd to come for healing on other days, but Jesus answered that even on the Sabbath people untie their ox or donkey to water it, and asked whether this daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan for eighteen years, should not be set free on the Sabbath day. His opponents were humiliated, and the people delighted at his wonderful deeds.
Discussion: Eighteen years bent double ended with a word, a touch, and straightened praise on the Sabbath: liberation, not rule-keeping, is the Sabbath's joy. Reflect: 1) What long bent-over burden have you carried that Jesus calls you forward to free? 2) How does daughter of Abraham dignify a woman the synagogue had overlooked? 3) Where does indignation at God's timing mask a refusal to rejoice?
Significance: On the Sabbath Jesus freed a woman bent double for eighteen years, calling her a daughter of Abraham and defending Sabbath liberation against the synagogue leader's indignation.
RelatedEvents: The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda

Story: Jesus Heals a Man with Dropsy
Retelling: One Sabbath Jesus went to eat in the house of a prominent Pharisee, where he was being carefully watched, and in front of him was a man suffering from abnormal swelling of the body, called dropsy. Jesus asked the Pharisees and experts in the Law, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not? They remained silent, so he took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. Then he asked them, If one of you has an ass or an ox fallen into a pit on the Sabbath day, will you not immediately pull it out? They had nothing to say. The healing took place before the meal and the parable of the wedding feast that followed it.
Discussion: Jesus asked the question before he healed, and silence answered him: no one could defend leaving a suffering man unhealed on the Sabbath. Reflect: 1) Where does careful watching replace compassion in your gatherings? 2) How does Jesus' well-side argument expose inconsistent mercy? 3) What suffering person is in front of you while you debate the rules?
Significance: At a Pharisee's Sabbath meal Jesus healed a man with dropsy after his critics fell silent, showing that mercy to the suffering cannot wait for a more convenient day.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Heals a Woman Bent Double

Story: Jesus Heals a Deaf and Mute Man in the Decapolis
Retelling: After leaving Tyre and Sidon, Jesus went through the Decapolis to the Sea of Galilee, where some people brought to him a man who was deaf and could hardly talk, and begged Jesus to place his hand on him. Jesus took him aside, away from the crowd, put his fingers into the man's ears, spat and touched his tongue, looked up to heaven and with a deep sigh said to him, Ephphatha! which means, Be opened! At this the man's ears were opened, his tongue was loosened, and he began to speak plainly. Jesus commanded them not to tell anyone, but the more he did so, the more they kept talking about it, and people were overwhelmed with amazement, saying, He has done everything well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.
Discussion: Jesus took the man aside and healed him privately, with touch, sigh, and a word: Be opened. Reflect: 1) What does Jesus' private, tactile care say about dignity for those who cannot hear or speak? 2) How does Ephphatha speak to closed ears and tied tongues in your own life? 3) Why does amazement overflow even a command to silence?
Significance: In the Decapolis Jesus opened the ears and loosened the tongue of a deaf and mute man with the word Ephphatha, and the Gentile crowds declared he had done everything well.
RelatedEvents: The Canaanite Woman's Daughter

Story: Jesus Heals a Blind Man at Bethsaida
Retelling: When Jesus and his disciples came to Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him. Jesus took the blind man by the hand and led him outside the village, spat on his eyes and put his hands on him, and asked, Do you see anything? The man looked up and said, I see people; they look like trees walking around. Once more Jesus put his hands on his eyes, and then his eyes were opened, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly. Jesus sent him home, telling him not to go into the village. This two-stage healing is unique in the Gospels, and it stands in Mark's narrative between the feeding of the four thousand and Peter's confession.
Discussion: Sight came in stages: first trees walking, then everything clearly, and Jesus led the man outside the village to heal him personally. Reflect: 1) Where is your sight still partial, like trees walking? 2) What does Jesus' willingness to touch a second time say about gradual healing? 3) How does being led by the hand picture guidance when you cannot see the way?
Significance: At Bethsaida Jesus healed a blind man in two stages, first partial sight and then clear sight, after leading him by the hand outside the village.
RelatedEvents: The Feeding of the Four Thousand

Story: The Coin in the Fish's Mouth
Retelling: After Jesus and his disciples arrived in Capernaum, the collectors of the temple tax came to Peter and asked, Doesn't your teacher pay the temple tax? Peter answered, Yes, he does, and when he entered the house Jesus spoke first, asking from whom the kings of the earth collect duty and taxes, from their own children or from others? Peter answered, From others, and Jesus said, Then the children are exempt. But so that we may not cause offence, he told Peter to go to the lake, throw out a line, and take the first fish he caught; opening its mouth, he would find a four-drachma coin, enough for the tax for both of them. Peter did so, and paid the tax for Jesus and himself.
Discussion: The Son, exempt as a child of the King, still paid the tax to avoid needless offence, and provided it by a miracle: freedom exercised as consideration for others. Reflect: 1) Where does insisting on your rights cause offence that love would avoid? 2) How does a coin in a fish's mouth show God's provision in ordinary work? 3) What does it mean that Jesus paid a temple tax for the temple of his own Father?
Significance: Jesus, though exempt as the King's Son, miraculously provided the temple tax for himself and Peter from a fish's mouth, so as not to give offence.
RelatedEvents: Transfiguration

Retelling: During the arrest in Gethsemane, Simon Peter drew a sword and struck the high priest's servant, cutting off his right ear. John names the servant as Malchus. Jesus commanded Peter to put his sword away, saying, Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me? and adding that all who draw the sword will die by the sword. Luke alone records the healing itself: Jesus touched the man's ear and healed him, even as the crowd seized him. The last miracle before the cross was therefore a healing of an enemy's wound, inflicted by his own disciple in his defence.
Discussion: Jesus healed the ear his own disciple had cut off, in the middle of his arrest: his last miracle before the cross was mercy to an enemy. Reflect: 1) How does healing Malchus confront the instinct to wound for Jesus' sake? 2) What does it mean that Jesus stopped his own rescue to heal his captor's servant? 3) Where are you called to repair damage done in misguided defence of God?
Significance: As he was arrested, Jesus healed the ear of Malchus, the high priest's servant, whom Peter had wounded with a sword, forbidding violence in his defence.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane

Retelling: Jesus told another parable: The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and mixed into three measures of meal until the whole was leavened. The leaven is tiny beside the flour, hidden once mixed, and yet it transforms the whole batch from within, quietly and completely. Luke records the same parable beside the mustard seed, pairing small beginnings with inward, pervasive growth. Nothing in the story explains itself further; the point lies in the hidden, thorough work of the kingdom.
Discussion: The kingdom does not arrive by spectacle but works like yeast: hidden, small, and thorough. Reflect: 1) Where is God's kingdom working hiddenly in your life, like yeast in dough? 2) How does this parable correct the expectation that God's work must be visible to be real? 3) What small, faithful mixture, prayer, word, or kindness, might God be using to leaven a whole household?
Significance: The kingdom of heaven works like leaven hidden in a large measure of flour: small, unseen, and transforming everything it touches.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Mustard Seed

Story: The Parable of the Growing Seed
Retelling: Jesus said, This is what the kingdom of God is like: a man scatters seed on the ground, and night and day, whether he sleeps or gets up, the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. All by itself the soil produces grain, first the stalk, then the head, then the full kernel in the head, and as soon as the grain is ripe, he puts the sickle to it, because the harvest has come. The farmer's part is to scatter and to harvest; the growth itself belongs to the earth and to God, and it proceeds whether the farmer watches or sleeps.
Discussion: The kingdom grows while the farmer sleeps: sowing and harvest are ours, but growth is God's secret work. Reflect: 1) Where are you anxiously watching for growth only God can give? 2) How does this parable free you from measuring every seed's progress? 3) What does readiness for harvest look like when the growth has been God's?
Significance: The kingdom grows like seed scattered on the ground: the farmer sows and reaps, but the sprouting, stalk, head, and full kernel come by God's own power, day and night.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Sower

Retelling: Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is like a net let down into the lake, which caught all kinds of fish. When it was full, the fishermen pulled it up on the shore, sat down, and collected the good fish in baskets, but threw the bad away. So it will be at the end of the age, Jesus said: the angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous, throwing the wicked into the blazing furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The net gathers indiscriminately now; the sorting belongs to the end, and to the angels, not to the fishermen.
Discussion: The net catches everything for now, and the sorting waits for the end: the church gathers widely and judges narrowly, if at all. Reflect: 1) How does this parable restrain premature sorting of people into good and bad fish? 2) What does the final separation say about taking judgment seriously without seizing it? 3) How do you live as one caught in the net, awaiting the shore?
Significance: The kingdom gathers all kinds like a dragnet, and only at the end of the age will the angels separate the wicked from the righteous.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Wheat and the Weeds

Story: The Parable of the Friend at Midnight
Retelling: Jesus said, Suppose you have a friend, and you go to him at midnight and say, Friend, lend me three loaves of bread; a friend of mine on a journey has come to me, and I have no food to offer him. And suppose the one inside answers, Don't bother me. The door is already locked, and my children and I are in bed. I can't get up and give you anything. I tell you, Jesus said, even though he will not get up and give you the bread because of friendship, yet because of your shameless audacity he will surely get up and give you as much as you need. The parable follows the Lord's Prayer and precedes the teaching to ask, seek, and knock.
Discussion: Midnight boldness is commended, not condemned: prayer may be shamelessly persistent, because the need is real and the neighbour's door is not God's door. Reflect: 1) Where has politeness kept you from asking God boldly at midnight? 2) How does this parable differ from the persistent widow's plea to an unjust judge? 3) What need of a travelling friend, someone else's need, drives your boldest prayer?
Significance: A friend at midnight receives bread not by friendship alone but by shameless persistence, teaching disciples to pray boldly and without giving up.
RelatedEvents: The Persistent Widow

Story: The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree
Retelling: Jesus told this parable: a man had a fig tree growing in his vineyard, and when he came looking for fruit on it he found none, so he said to the keeper of the vineyard, For three years now I've been coming to look for fruit on this fig tree and haven't found any. Cut it down! Why should it use up the soil? The keeper answered, Sir, leave it alone for one more year, and I'll dig around it and fertilise it. If it bears fruit next year, fine! If not, then cut it down. The parable is distinct from the later cursing of the fig tree: here the tree is given one more year of patient cultivation, not withered at once.
Discussion: Judgment is delayed by a gardener's plea for one more year of digging and fertilising: patience has a purpose, and the purpose is fruit. Reflect: 1) How does the keeper's intercession shape your prayers for fruitless people, including yourself? 2) What does one more year of cultivation look like practically? 3) Where does patience end and the axe fall, and who decides?
Significance: A fruitless fig tree is granted one more year of digging and fertilising before the axe, picturing God's patience that seeks fruit rather than immediate judgment.
RelatedEvents: The Cursing of the Fig Tree

Story: The Parable of the Watchful Servants
Retelling: Jesus said, Be dressed ready for service and keep your lamps burning, like servants waiting for their master to return from a wedding banquet, so that when he comes and knocks they can immediately open the door. It will be good for those servants whose master finds them watching when he comes; truly, he will dress himself to serve, have them recline at table, and come and wait on them. But if a servant says to himself, My master is taking a long time in coming, and begins to beat the other servants and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master will come on a day he does not expect and cut him to pieces, assigning him a place with the unbelievers. Matthew's parallel tells the same story as the faithful and wise servant put in charge of the household, who gives food at the proper time, contrasted with the wicked servant who abuses his charge. The one who knew the master's will and did not prepare will be beaten with many blows; the one who did not know, with few.
Discussion: Readiness is not anxiety but faithful work with lamps burning: the master rewards watchful servants by serving them himself. Reflect: 1) What does dressed ready and lamps burning look like in your daily work? 2) How does delay tempt servants to abuse rather than serve? 3) What charge has your Master left you that faithfulness means carrying out on time?
Significance: Disciples must live as servants with lamps burning for their master's return, faithful in their charge, because he will come at an hour they do not expect.
RelatedEvents: The Wise and Foolish Virgins; The Parable of the Talents

Story: The Parable of the New Wine and New Cloth
Retelling: When John's disciples asked why Jesus' disciples did not fast, Jesus answered with two pictures. No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, he said, for the patch will pull away from the garment, making the tear worse. And no one pours new wine into old wineskins; if they do, the skins will burst, the wine will run out, and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins, and both are preserved. Luke adds the saying that no one after drinking old wine wants the new, for they say, The old is better. The pictures defend the newness of Jesus' ministry: it cannot simply patch or contain the old order.
Discussion: New wine bursts old skins: Jesus' coming cannot be fitted as a patch onto old forms without tearing both. Reflect: 1) Where are you trying to patch Jesus onto an unchanged life? 2) How does new wine challenge both novelty for its own sake and clinging to the old because it tastes better? 3) What new wineskin, practice, community, or habit, does the new wine of the gospel require?
Significance: Jesus' new ministry is like unshrunk cloth and new wine: it cannot be patched onto old garments or poured into old wineskins without ruining both.
RelatedEvents: The Calling of Matthew

Retelling: After telling the parables of the kingdom, Jesus asked his disciples whether they had understood all these things, and they answered, Yes. He said to them, Therefore every teacher of the law who has become a disciple in the kingdom of heaven is like the owner of a house who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old. The trained scribe, made a disciple, does not discard the old treasure of Scripture, nor cling to it alone, but brings out both old and new for the household. The parable closes the chapter of kingdom parables, turning the hearer into a steward of treasures.
Discussion: A disciple-scribe brings out old and new together: the kingdom does not cancel the old treasure, and the old treasure is not enough without the new. Reflect: 1) What old treasure from Scripture are you neglecting, and what new treasure are you resisting? 2) How does this parable shape teaching that serves a household rather than showing off? 3) What does it mean to be a steward, not an owner, of these treasures?
Significance: Every teacher of the law become a disciple of the kingdom is like a householder bringing new treasures out of the storeroom along with the old.
RelatedEvents: The Parable of the Sower

Story: The Parable of the Two Debtors
Retelling: While Jesus reclined at a Pharisee's table and a sinful woman anointed his feet, he told his host Simon this parable: Two people owed money to a certain moneylender. One owed him five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. Neither of them had the money to pay him back, so he forgave the debts of both. Now which of them will love him more? Simon replied, I suppose the one who had the bigger debt forgiven. You have judged correctly, Jesus said, and he turned the parable on Simon: the woman's many sins were forgiven, as her great love showed, while Simon, who had shown little love, presumed a smaller debt. The parable is told inside the anointing episode, but it is a complete parable of its own, with its own question and answer.
Discussion: Forgiven much, love much: the size of love reveals the size of debt we admit, and the Pharisee's small love betrayed a small sense of debt. Reflect: 1) Do you see yourself as the fifty-denarii debtor or the five-hundred debtor, and what does that do to your love? 2) How does the woman's love prove forgiveness rather than earn it? 3) Where does respectable religion hide an unpaid debt?
Significance: Two debtors, one forgiven five hundred and one fifty, show that the one forgiven more loves more, exposing Simon's cold welcome beside the sinful woman's lavish love.
RelatedEvents: The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus

Story: Counting the Cost: The Tower Builder and the King Going to War
Retelling: As large crowds travelled with Jesus, he turned and said that no one could be his disciple without hating, by comparison, father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even their own life, and carrying their cross. Then he gave two pictures of counting the cost. Suppose one of you wants to build a tower: won't you first sit down and estimate the cost, to see whether you have enough to complete it? Otherwise, after laying the foundation and failing to finish, everyone will ridicule you, saying, This person began to build and wasn't able to finish. Or suppose a king about to go to war against another king: won't he first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand men to oppose the one coming with twenty thousand? If not, he will send a delegation while the other is still a long way off and ask for terms of peace. In the same way, Jesus concluded, those who do not give up everything they have cannot be his disciples.
Discussion: Discipleship is begun with eyes open, like a builder estimating or a king counting troops: following Jesus costs everything, and he says so before you start. Reflect: 1) What have you not yet counted in the cost of following Jesus? 2) How does the tower's unfinished foundation warn against enthusiastic beginnings? 3) What does giving up everything mean concretely for your possessions, family, and plans?
Significance: Before following him, disciples must count the cost like a tower builder estimating his funds and a king counting his troops, for no one who will not give up everything can be his disciple.
RelatedEvents: The Rich Young Ruler

Retelling: Jesus asked, To what can I compare this generation? They are like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others: We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn. For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He has a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, Here is a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. But wisdom is proved right by her deeds. The generation refused both John and Jesus, faulting the ascetic and faulting the feaster, and the brief marketplace picture exposes a refusal that no approach could satisfy. Doubt: this is a short simile rather than a story-parable with characters and plot, so its standing as a parable is debatable.
Discussion: A generation that would neither dance nor mourn faulted John for fasting and Jesus for feasting: refusal can disguise itself as criticism of style. Reflect: 1) Where do you fault God's messengers for opposite reasons and miss the message? 2) How does wisdom proved right by her deeds answer the marketplace critics? 3) What would dancing or mourning appropriately look like in response to Jesus?
Significance: This generation is like children in the marketplace who would neither dance to the pipe nor mourn to the dirge, rejecting both John's austerity and Jesus' feasting. Doubt: this is a short simile rather than a story-parable with characters and plot, so its standing as a parable is debatable.
RelatedEvents: The Death of John the Baptist

Retelling: Jesus said, Suppose one of you has a servant ploughing or looking after the sheep. Will he say to the servant when he comes in from the field, Come along now and sit down to eat? Won't he rather say, Prepare my supper, get yourself ready and wait on me while I eat and drink; after that you may eat and drink? Will he thank the servant because he did what he was told to do? So you also, Jesus concluded, when you have done everything you were told to do, should say, We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty. The picture is brief and deliberately unsentimental: obedience is duty, not merit, and it earns no extra praise. Doubt: this is a short illustrative saying about duty rather than a story-parable with a developed plot, so its standing as a parable is debatable.
Discussion: Obedience is duty, not merit: even complete obedience leaves the servant unworthy of extra praise, because the work was owed. Reflect: 1) Where do you expect thanks for doing what you were told to do? 2) How does unworthy servant correct both pride in service and resentment at serving? 3) What would serving without keeping score change in your work for God?
Significance: Even servants who have done everything commanded should say only, We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty, for obedience earns no surplus merit. Doubt: this is a short illustrative saying about duty rather than a story-parable with a developed plot, so its standing as a parable is debatable.
RelatedEvents: The Unforgiving Servant

Story: The Lesson of the Fig Tree
Retelling: As part of his teaching about the coming of the Son of Man, Jesus said, Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: as soon as its twigs get tender and its leaves come out, you know that summer is near. Even so, when you see all these things, you know that it is near, right at the door. Truly I tell you, he said, this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things have happened. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away. Luke adds that he told them this parable about the fig tree and all the trees: when they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves that summer is near. The lesson is a sign-reading illustration inside the Olivet teaching, distinct from the cursing of the fig tree, which was an acted event. Doubt: this is an illustrative saying within a discourse rather than a standalone story-parable, so its standing as a separate parable row is debatable.
Discussion: Leaves on the fig tree mean summer is near, and the signs Jesus named mean his coming is near: discernment reads the season instead of predicting the day. Reflect: 1) How does the fig tree teach readiness without date-setting? 2) What signs in your own life show a season changing? 3) What does it mean to trust words that will never pass away when heaven and earth will?
Significance: Learn from the fig tree: when its twigs get tender and leaves come out, summer is near, and so the signs Jesus named show his coming is near, right at the door. Doubt: this is an illustrative saying within a discourse rather than a standalone story-parable, so its standing as a separate parable row is debatable.
RelatedEvents: The Wise and Foolish Virgins; The Parable of the Talents

Retelling: After the lame man was healed, the people ran together to Peter and John in Solomon's porch. Peter told them not to marvel as though the healing had come by their own power or holiness: it was faith in the name of Jesus, whom they had delivered up and denied before Pilate, that had made the man strong. He said they had acted in ignorance, as their rulers had, but God had fulfilled what the prophets had foretold, that Christ should suffer. He called them to repent and be converted, that their sins might be blotted out and times of refreshing might come from the Lord. He reminded them that Moses had promised a prophet like himself, that all the prophets from Samuel onward had foretold these days, and that they were children of the covenant God made with Abraham, in whom all kindreds of the earth would be blessed. God had raised up Jesus and sent him first to them, to bless them by turning each one away from his iniquities.
Discussion: Peter turns a miracle into a message: the healing points to Jesus, and the crowd's guilt is met not with despair but with a call to repent. Notice how he is both blunt about what they did and gentle about ignorance and the way back. Reflect: 1) When God works through you, how do you keep the attention on Jesus rather than yourself? 2) What does repentance look like as a turning, not just a feeling? 3) How does the promise to Abraham shape who the gospel is for?
Significance: The first sermon after Pentecost's sequel shows the apostolic pattern: a sign, a plain account of Jesus, a call to repentance, and a promise of refreshing for all who turn.
Themes: Repentance; Witness; Jesus' Name; Covenant Promise
RelatedEvents: Peter Heals the Lame Man; Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin

Story: Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin
Retelling: While Peter and John were still speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple, and the Sadducees came upon them, grieved that they taught the people and preached through Jesus the resurrection from the dead. They laid hands on them and held them until the next day. The next day the rulers, elders, scribes, Annas, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and others of the high priest's kindred gathered in Jerusalem and asked, By what power, or by what name, have ye done this? Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, answered that if they were examined for the good deed done to the impotent man, by what means he was made whole, then let it be known that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stood before them whole. Jesus was the stone set at nought by the builders which had become the head of the corner, and there was salvation in no other name under heaven given among men. When the council saw the boldness of Peter and John, perceived they were unlearned and ignorant men, and took knowledge that they had been with Jesus, and saw the healed man standing with them, they could say nothing against it. They commanded them to go aside, conferred, and threatened them that they speak no more in the name of Jesus. Peter and John answered, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye: for we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard. The council further threatened them and let them go, finding no way to punish them because all men glorified God for what was done, for the man was above forty years old on whom this miracle of healing was shewed.
Discussion: This is the church's first trial, and its defence is a person, not an argument: a healed man standing there and a name that saves. Peter obeys God rather than men, but he does so without abuse or evasion. Reflect: 1) What evidence of Jesus do people see standing beside your words? 2) When human authority forbids speaking of Christ, where is the line between boldness and recklessness? 3) How does Peter's answer keep both respect and refusal together?
Significance: The gospel's first clash with authority establishes the principle the church has lived by ever since: when commanded to be silent about Jesus, believers must speak, because they cannot but speak what they have seen and heard.
RelatedEvents: Peter Preaches at Solomon's Porch; The Believers Pray for Boldness; The Apostles Before the Council

Retelling: Being let go, Peter and John went to their own company and reported all that the chief priests and elders had said to them. When the company heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord and prayed, Lord, thou art God, which hast made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all that in them is. They recalled the words of David: Why did the heathen rage, and the people imagine vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord, and against his Christ. For truly, they said, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, had gathered against God's holy child Jesus, whom God had anointed, to do whatever God's hand and counsel had determined before to be done. And now, Lord, they prayed, behold their threatenings, and grant unto thy servants that with all boldness they may speak thy word, by stretching forth thine hand to heal, and that signs and wonders may be done by the name of thy holy child Jesus. When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together, and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
Discussion: The church's first response to a threat is not a strategy meeting but a prayer that names God's sovereignty first and asks for boldness, not safety. They do not pray for the threats to vanish; they pray to speak through them. Reflect: 1) What do you ask God for first when opposition comes? 2) How does remembering that God determined the outcome change your fear? 3) What would boldness, rather than safety, look like in your situation?
Significance: Persecution drives the young church to prayer, and prayer to boldness: the shaken room and the fresh filling show that courage is a gift God gives his people when they ask, not a temperament some possess.
Themes: Prayer; Boldness; God's Sovereignty; Holy Spirit
RelatedEvents: Peter and John Before the Sanhedrin; The Apostles Before the Council

Retelling: As the number of disciples multiplied, a murmuring arose from the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration. The twelve called the multitude of the disciples together and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables. They told the disciples to look out among them seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom they might appoint over this business, while the apostles gave themselves continually to prayer and to the ministry of the word. The saying pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, who, when they had prayed, laid their hands on them. And the word of God increased, and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly, and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.
Discussion: A practical complaint about food becomes a lesson in church order: the apostles neither dismiss the widows nor abandon the word, but share the work with proven, Spirit-filled servants. Stephen and Philip, chosen to serve tables, soon preach, heal, and die for the faith. Reflect: 1) How does your church handle a just complaint without pitting mercy against ministry? 2) What does it mean to be full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom in ordinary service? 3) Why does shared service lead to the word increasing?
Significance: The first organised diaconate shows that caring for the overlooked is not a distraction from the gospel but part of its fruit, and that faithful service in small things is the ground from which wider ministry grows.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Philip Preaches in Samaria

Retelling: Saul was consenting to Stephen's death. At that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem, and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men carried Stephen to his burial and made great lamentation over him. As for Saul, he made havoc of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women and committing them to prison. But they that were scattered abroad went everywhere preaching the word.
Discussion: Persecution does what comfort could not: it moves the gospel out of Jerusalem into Judaea and Samaria, exactly the widening circle Jesus had named. Saul's havoc and the scattered believers' preaching stand side by side in the same verses. Reflect: 1) How has hardship ever carried the gospel further than comfort did? 2) What does it mean that ordinary scattered believers, not only apostles, preached the word? 3) How do you honour both grief for Stephen and hope in the scattering?
Significance: The scattering turns Stephen's martyrdom into mission: the church leaves Jerusalem not by a plan but by persecution, and the word spreads through unnamed believers who preach wherever they land.
RelatedEvents: Martyrdom of Stephen; Philip Preaches in Samaria

Story: Saul Received in Jerusalem and Sent to Tarsus
Retelling: When Saul was come to Jerusalem, he assayed to join himself to the disciples, but they were all afraid of him and believed not that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared unto them how he had seen the Lord in the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how he had preached boldly at Damascus in the name of Jesus. And he was with them coming in and going out at Jerusalem, and he spake boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and disputed against the Grecians. But they went about to slay him, which when the brethren knew, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him forth to Tarsus. Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified, and walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied.
Discussion: Conversion does not instantly win trust: the disciples' fear is understandable, and Barnabas's vouching is what opens the door. Saul preaches boldly, is threatened, and is quietly sent away, and the churches find rest. Reflect: 1) Who has vouched for you when your past made people afraid? 2) How do you earn trust after a changed life rather than demanding it? 3) When is withdrawing to safety wisdom rather than retreat?
Significance: Barnabas's mediation turns a feared persecutor into a received brother, and Saul's brief, dangerous Jerusalem ministry ends in a season of rest and growth for the churches before his wider work begins.
RelatedEvents: The Conversion of Paul; The Church at Antioch

Retelling: As Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda. There he found a certain man named Aeneas, which had kept his bed eight years, and was sick of the palsy. Peter said unto him, Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately. And all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord.
Discussion: Aeneas is healed in a single sentence, and the healing's whole purpose is the turning of two towns to the Lord. Peter claims no power of his own: Jesus Christ makes whole. Reflect: 1) Why does Luke record this brief healing between Saul's conversion and Tabitha's raising? 2) What does it mean for a healing to point beyond itself to turning to the Lord? 3) How do you speak of Christ's power without claiming it as your own?
Significance: Aeneas's eight-year paralysis ends in a moment, and the quiet miracle at Lydda prepares the way for Tabitha's raising and for Peter's journey to the Gentile mission, showing Christ's healing power at work through his apostle beyond Jerusalem.
RelatedEvents: Peter Raises Tabitha; Peter and Cornelius

Retelling: They which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only. But some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord. Then tidings of these things came unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem, and they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch. When he came and had seen the grace of God, he was glad, and exhorted them all that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord, for he was a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith, and much people was added unto the Lord. Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
Discussion: Antioch is where the gospel crosses to Gentiles without a council first, and where Jerusalem's response is not suspicion but Barnabas's gladness. A whole year of teaching follows, and a new name is born. Reflect: 1) How do you respond when God works beyond the lines you expected? 2) What does a year of steady teaching do that a moment of excitement cannot? 3) What does it mean to be called a Christian before the world gives you any other name?
Significance: Antioch becomes the missionary church: the first place where Gentiles are reached in numbers, where Barnabas and Saul teach together for a year, and where the disciples first bear the name Christian.
Themes: Mission; Gentile Inclusion; Teaching; Church Growth
RelatedEvents: Barnabas and Saul Sent Out from Antioch; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Story: Relief Sent to Judea in the Famine
Retelling: In those days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch. And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world, which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar. Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea. Which also they did, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
Discussion: A prophecy of famine becomes a collection, not a panic: Gentile believers at Antioch send help to Jewish believers in Judaea, each according to ability, carried by trusted hands. Generosity here is fellowship made practical. Reflect: 1) How does your church turn warnings about need into concrete help? 2) What does giving according to ability, rather than equally, require of each giver? 3) Why does it matter that Barnabas and Saul, not strangers, carried the gift?
Significance: The first recorded relief gift binds the young Gentile church to the Jewish mother church in practical love, and it gives Barnabas and Saul their first joint mission before they are sent out as missionaries.
RelatedEvents: The Church at Antioch; Barnabas and Saul Sent Out from Antioch

Story: Barnabas and Saul Sent Out from Antioch
Retelling: Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers: Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Discussion: The missionary journeys begin not with a strategy but with worship and fasting, and the church sends its two best teachers rather than keeping them. The call is heard together and confirmed by laying on hands. Reflect: 1) How does your church discern a call: by vote, by voice, or by worship and fasting together? 2) What does it cost a church to send its best people away? 3) How do you tell a genuine call from a good idea?
Significance: Antioch's sending is the hinge of Acts: from here the gospel moves deliberately to the Gentile world, and the church learns that mission begins in worship and is confirmed by the whole body, not by individuals alone.
KeyPeople: Barnabas; Paul; Simeon Niger; Lucius of Cyrene; Manaen
RelatedEvents: The Church at Antioch; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Retelling: Barnabas and Saul, sent forth by the Holy Ghost, departed unto Seleucia, and from thence sailed to Cyprus. When they were at Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews, and they had also John to their minister. When they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus, which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, who called for Barnabas and Saul and desired to hear the word of God. But Elymas the sorcerer, for so is his name by interpretation, withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith. Then Saul, who also is called Paul, filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him and said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness, and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand. Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord.
Discussion: The first missionary encounter is a contest over one man's hearing: a sorcerer tries to turn the deputy from the faith, and Paul names the opposition plainly and answers it with a sign. Sergius Paulus believes not because of the marvel alone but because he is astonished at the doctrine of the Lord. Reflect: 1) How do you tell opposition that is spiritual from opposition that is merely human? 2) Why does Luke pair the blinding with the deputy's belief in the teaching? 3) When is plain speech about evil necessary, and when is it merely harsh?
Significance: On Cyprus the gospel wins its first Gentile ruler, and Paul steps forward as the mission's spokesman: the word, defended and demonstrated, overcomes a court sorcerer's opposition and opens the Gentile world.
KeyPeople: Paul; Barnabas; John Mark; Elymas; Sergius Paulus
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Preaches at Pisidian Antioch

Retelling: Paul and his company loosed from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia, where John departing from them returned to Jerusalem. They came to Antioch in Pisidia, and went into the synagogue on the sabbath day and sat down. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent unto them, saying, Ye men and brethren, if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on. Paul stood up and preached the history of Israel, from the choosing of the fathers through Egypt, the wilderness, the judges, Samuel, Saul, and David, and declared that of David's seed God had raised unto Israel a Saviour, Jesus. He told of John's baptism, of Jesus' condemnation in Jerusalem, his burial, and his resurrection, witnessed by those who came up with him from Galilee, and of the promises fulfilled in the Psalms. Through this man, he said, is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins, and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. When the Jews were gone out of the synagogue, the Gentiles besought that these words might be preached to them the next sabbath. The next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God. When the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy, and spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming. Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you, but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles. For so hath the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth. When the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region. But the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women, and the chief men of the city, and raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them out of their coasts. But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came unto Iconium. And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost.
Discussion: Paul's first recorded sermon is a history lesson with a verdict: everything Israel's story promised has come in Jesus, and forgiveness and justification are offered through him, not through the law. The same sermon divides its hearers: Gentiles rejoice, and the Jewish leaders expel the preachers. Reflect: 1) How does Paul use Israel's history rather than bypassing it? 2) What does justification by faith mean in contrast to justification by the law? 3) Why does a joyful church remain after its teachers are expelled?
Significance: Pisidian Antioch sets the pattern for the Gentile mission: the gospel offered first to Jews, then turned to the Gentiles when rejected, received with gladness, and followed by persecution that cannot stop the word.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul and Barnabas at Iconium

Retelling: At Iconium Paul and Barnabas went both together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spake that a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles, and made their minds evil affected against the brethren. Long time therefore abode they speaking boldly in the Lord, which gave testimony unto the word of his grace, and granted signs and wonders to be done by their hands. But the multitude of the city was divided, and part held with the Jews, and part with the apostles. And when there was an assault made both of the Gentiles, and also of the Jews with their rulers, to use them despitefully, and to stone them, they were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about, and there they preached the gospel.
Discussion: Iconium shows a divided city: many believe, opponents stir others, and the apostles stay a long time speaking boldly with signs following, until a planned stoning forces flight. Boldness and retreat are both faithfulness here. Reflect: 1) How long do you stay when a place is divided over the gospel? 2) What role do signs play: proof, or testimony to the word of grace? 3) When does leaving become obedience rather than failure?
Significance: Iconium's long, contested ministry proves the gospel can take root in a divided city, and that flight from a planned stoning is not defeat but the mission moving on to Lystra and Derbe.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Stoned at Lystra

Retelling: At Lystra there sat a certain man, impotent in his feet, being a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked. The same heard Paul speak, who stedfastly beholding him, and perceiving that he had faith to be healed, said with a loud voice, Stand upright on thy feet. And he leaped and walked.
