When the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men. And they called Barnabas, Jupiter, and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker. Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people. Which when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of, they rent their clothes, and ran in among the people, crying out, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein, who in times past suffered all nations to walk in their own ways, and nevertheless left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness. And with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them. And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead. Howbeit, as the disciples stood round about him, he rose up, and came into the city, and the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe.
Discussion: Lystra turns in a single day from worship to murder: the crowd first makes the apostles gods, then stones Paul at the persuasion of opponents. Paul's refusal of worship is as important as the healing, for he points from the miracle to the living God who gives rain and fruitful seasons. Reflect: 1) How do you refuse praise that belongs to God without despising the people who offer it? 2) Why does the same crowd swing from honour to violence? 3) What does Paul's return into the city, the day after being stoned, say about courage?
Significance: At Lystra the mission meets raw paganism and raw violence together: the apostles reject divine honours, preach the Creator to people without the Scriptures, and Paul survives a stoning and walks back into the city that cast him out.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Return Journey and the Appointment of Elders

Story: The Return Journey and the Appointment of Elders
Retelling: After preaching the gospel at Derbe and teaching many, Paul and Barnabas returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and to Antioch, confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God. And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed. And after they had passed throughout Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia. And when they had preached the word in Perga, they went down into Attalia, and thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled. And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles. And there they abode long time with the disciples.
Discussion: The mission does not end with converts but with churches: the apostles retrace their steps through the very cities that stoned and expelled them, strengthen the disciples, and appoint elders with prayer and fasting. Then they report back to the church that sent them. Reflect: 1) Why return to dangerous places instead of moving on to new ground? 2) What does appointing elders, rather than leaving converts to themselves, protect? 3) How does a mission report honour both God and the sending church?
Significance: The return journey completes the first mission: new churches are not left alone but confirmed, taught that tribulation is the road to the kingdom, given elders, commended to the Lord, and reported to Antioch as the door of faith opened to the Gentiles.
Themes: Church Planting; Leadership; Endurance; Mission Report
Place: Derbe; Lystra; Iconium; Pisidian Antioch; Perga; Attalia; Antioch
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Jerusalem Council

Retelling: Some days after the Jerusalem Council, Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do. And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work. And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus, and Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God. And he went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.
Discussion: Two faithful men, who had risked their lives together, disagree so sharply over Mark that they part, and the mission doubles rather than dies: Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus, and Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia. Luke does not hide the contention or resolve it with blame. Reflect: 1) How do you disagree with a fellow worker without breaking fellowship? 2) What does it mean that God works through a painful parting? 3) How did Barnabas's second chance to Mark later bear fruit?
Significance: The parting of Paul and Barnabas shows that even apostles disagree sharply, that a disagreement over a person can be honest on both sides, and that the mission goes forward through two teams instead of one.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Jerusalem Council; Paul Takes Timothy

Retelling: Paul came to Derbe and Lystra, and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus, the son of a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed, but his father was a Greek, which was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium. Him would Paul have to go forth with him, and took and circumcised him because of the Jews which were in those quarters, for they knew all that his father was a Greek. And as they went through the cities, they delivered them the decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at Jerusalem. And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily.
Discussion: Timothy joins the mission because the brethren report well of him, and Paul circumcises him not as a condition of salvation, which the Jerusalem Council had just settled, but so that no needless barrier stands before Jewish hearers. Principle and prudence walk together. Reflect: 1) What does a good report from your own church community say about readiness for ministry? 2) How do you tell the difference between a gospel essential and a removable barrier? 3) Why does delivering the Council's decrees strengthen rather than burden the churches?
Significance: Timothy's joining brings Paul his lifelong fellow worker, and the episode shows the Council's decision lived out: freedom in Christ, with a willing concession for the sake of the hearers, while the churches grow daily.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Macedonian Call

Retelling: Paul and his company went throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia. After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit suffered them not. And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas. And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: there stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us. And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.
Discussion: This is a vision, not a historical road map: Paul sees a Macedonian man in the night calling for help, and the company reads closed doors together with the vision as God's call. Note the change to we: Luke himself joins the party at Troas. Reflect: 1) How do you read closed doors alongside open ones? 2) What does it mean to decide a call together, not alone? 3) How does a cry for help from strangers become a mission?
Significance: The Macedonian call carries the gospel from Asia into Europe: closed doors in Asia and Bithynia, a night vision at Troas, and an immediate crossing that changes the map of the mission.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Lydia's Conversion at Philippi

Retelling: Loosing from Troas, Paul's company came with a straight course to Samothracia, and the next day to Neapolis, and from thence to Philippi, which is the chief city of that part of Macedonia, and a colony. And on the sabbath we went out of the city by a river side, where prayer was wont to be made, and we sat down, and spake unto the women which resorted thither. And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us, whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul. And when she was baptized, and her household, she besought us, saying, If ye have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and abide there. And she constrained us.
Discussion: Europe's first convert is a businesswoman at a riverside prayer meeting, and Luke gives the credit to God: the Lord opened her heart to attend to Paul's words. Her conversion at once becomes hospitality, a house opened to the missionaries. Reflect: 1) What does it mean that God opens a heart, and preaching still matters? 2) How does Lydia's household baptism show the gospel reaching a whole house? 3) What does her constrained hospitality teach about welcome after conversion?
Significance: Lydia's conversion plants the Philippian church in a merchant's household: the gospel's European beginning is a woman's open heart, a baptism, and a home offered to the mission.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison

Story: Paul Frees the Enslaved Girl at Philippi
Retelling: As Paul's company went to prayer, they were met by a damsel possessed with a spirit of divination, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying. The same followed Paul and the missionaries, and cried, saying, These men are the servants of the most high God, which shew unto us the way of salvation. And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour.
Discussion: The girl's words were true, but Paul refuses a testimony from a spirit of divination and frees her in the name of Jesus Christ, ending her masters' profit from her. Deliverance here is both spiritual and economic: a person stops being a source of gain. Reflect: 1) Why would Paul silence a true statement from a wrong source? 2) How does freeing one exploited person threaten an entire business? 3) What does grief, rather than anger, tell you about Paul's motive?
Significance: The girl's deliverance shows the gospel confronting exploitation directly: a spirit is cast out, a trafficked gift ends, and the mission's next step is prison, because freedom has a price for those who profited from bondage.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison

Story: Paul and Silas in the Philippian Prison
Retelling: When her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone, they caught Paul and Silas, and drew them into the marketplace unto the rulers, and brought them to the magistrates, saying, These men, being Jews, do exceedingly trouble our city, and teach customs which are not lawful for us to receive, neither to observe, being Romans. And the multitude rose up together against them, and the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them. And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely, who, having received such a charge, thrust them into the inner prison, and made their feet fast in the stocks. And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God, and the prisoners heard them. And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken, and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed. And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled. But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here. Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas, and brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved? And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. And they spake unto him the word of the Lord, and to all that were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes, and was baptized, he and all his, straightway. And when he had brought them into his house, he set meat before them, and rejoiced, believing in God with all his house. And when it was day, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go. And the keeper of the prison told this saying to Paul, The magistrates have sent to let you go: now therefore depart, and go in peace. But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison, and now do they thrust us out privily? Nay verily, but let them come themselves and fetch us out. And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates, and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans. And they came and besought them, and brought them out, and desired them to depart out of the city. And they went out of the prison, and entered into the house of Lydia, and when they had seen the brethren, they comforted them, and departed.
Discussion: Midnight praise in stocks, an earthquake that opens every door, and a jailer who asks the question of the whole book: what must I do to be saved? Paul's refusal to slip away quietly protects the new church, because a public wrong is answered publicly. Reflect: 1) What does singing at midnight do that arguing cannot? 2) Why does the jailer's conversion begin with his own despair, not with a sermon? 3) When is insisting on your rights an act of love for others, not pride?
Significance: The Philippian prison turns suffering into song, an earthquake into an open door, and a jailer's despair into a household's baptism, and it leaves the young church with a public vindication rather than a secret escape.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul at Thessalonica

Retelling: Paul and Silas passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures, opening and alleging that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead, and that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ. And some of them believed, and consorted with Paul and Silas, and of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women not a few. But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people. And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also, whom Jason hath received, and these all do contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus. And they troubled the people and the rulers of the city, when they heard these things. And when they had taken security of Jason, and of the other, they let them go. And the brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night unto Berea.
Discussion: Three sabbaths of reasoning from the Scriptures build a church of Jews, Greeks, and chief women, and the charge against it is political: another king, one Jesus. Jason's house becomes the first casualty, and security is taken for his good behaviour. Reflect: 1) What does it mean to prove from the Scriptures that Christ must suffer and rise? 2) Why does the gospel sound political even when it is preached in a synagogue? 3) How do you honour hosts like Jason who bear the cost of your ministry?
Significance: Thessalonica shows the gospel's power to turn a city upside down in three weeks, and its cost: the preachers leave by night, and the new believers, led by Jason, carry the charge of another King.
Themes: Preaching; Resurrection; Persecution; Kingship of Jesus
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul at Berea

Retelling: The brethren immediately sent away Paul and Silas by night unto Berea, who coming thither went into the synagogue of the Jews. These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. Therefore many of them believed, also of honourable women which were Greeks, and of men, not a few. But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was preached of Paul at Berea, they came thither also, and stirred up the people. And then immediately the brethren sent away Paul to go as it were to the sea, but Silas and Timotheus abode there still. And they that conducted Paul brought him unto Athens, and receiving a commandment unto Silas and Timotheus for to come to him with all speed, they departed.
Discussion: The Bereans are Luke's model hearers: they receive the word eagerly and check it daily against the Scriptures, and their nobility is shown by study, not by suspicion. Even so, opposition follows Paul from Thessalonica, and he leaves alone for Athens. Reflect: 1) What does readiness of mind plus daily searching look like in your own hearing of preaching? 2) How do you test a message without hardening against it? 3) Why does Luke praise the Bereans rather than the crowds who believed at once?
Significance: Berea gives the church its pattern for discernment: welcome the word, then search the Scriptures daily to see whether these things are so, and believe on evidence rather than on excitement.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul at Athens

Retelling: While Paul waited at Athens, his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry. Therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met with him. Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoicks, encountered him, and some said, What will this babbler say? Others, He seemeth to be a setter forth of strange gods, because he preached unto them Jesus, and the resurrection. And they took him, and brought him unto Areopagus, saying, May we know what this new doctrine, whereof thou speakest, is? For thou bringest certain strange things to our ears: we would know therefore what these things mean. For all the Athenians and strangers which were there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell, or to hear some new thing. Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands, neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things, and hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation, that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us. For in him we live, and move, and have our being, as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device. And the times of this ignorance God winked at, but now commandeth all men every where to repent, because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained, whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead. And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter. So Paul departed from among them. Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed, among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
Discussion: Paul preaches to philosophers without quoting the Scriptures they do not accept: he starts from their altar to an unknown god, proclaims the Creator who needs nothing, and ends with resurrection and judgment. Some mock, some defer, and a few believe. Reflect: 1) How do you find a starting point in someone else's world without surrendering your message? 2) Why does the resurrection divide the audience when creation does not? 3) What counts as success when only a few believe?
Significance: The Areopagus speech is the gospel's classic encounter with philosophy: creation, providence, repentance, and resurrection proclaimed to a city of idols and ideas, with mockery, curiosity, and a small harvest side by side.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul at Corinth

Retelling: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth, and found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome, and came unto them. And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought, for by their occupation they were tentmakers. And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks. And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ. And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles. And he departed thence, and entered into a certain man's house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue. And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house, and many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized. Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace, for I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee, for I have much people in this city. And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat, saying, This fellow persuadeth men to worship God contrary to the law. And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, reason would that I should bear with you, but if it be a question of words and names, and of your law, look ye to it yourselves, for I will be no judge of such matters. And he drave them from the judgment seat. Then all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things.
Discussion: Corinth pairs ordinary work with long ministry: Paul makes tents with Aquila and Priscilla, teaches for eighteen months, and is steadied by a night vision promising that the Lord has much people in this city. Gallio's refusal to judge a religious dispute then gives the mission legal room. Reflect: 1) How does working with your hands shape your witness? 2) What does the Lord's promise, I have much people in this city, mean before you can see them? 3) When does a ruler's indifference become God's protection?
Significance: Corinth becomes a major church through steady work, a long stay, and a vision's courage: the gospel takes root among Jews and Gentiles, Crispus's household believes, and Gallio's judgment seat becomes an unexpected shelter for the mission.
KeyPeople: Paul; Aquila; Priscilla; Silas; Timothy; Crispus; Gallio; Sosthenes
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Apollos Taught at Ephesus

Retelling: A certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus. This man was instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John. And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue, whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly. And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him, who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace, for he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publicly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
Discussion: Apollos is gifted, eloquent, and incomplete, and Aquila and Priscilla correct him privately rather than shaming him publicly. Their quiet teaching turns a partial preacher into a powerful defender of the faith in Achaia. Reflect: 1) How do you correct a gifted person without crushing them? 2) What does it mean to know the Scriptures mightily and still need the way expounded more perfectly? 3) Why does private correction produce public fruit?
Significance: Apollos shows that zeal needs completion: a learned preacher who knows only John's baptism is gently taught the fuller way, and then mightily convinces the Jews from the Scriptures that Jesus is Christ.
RelatedEvents: Paul at Corinth; The Disciples at Ephesus

Retelling: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper coasts, came to Ephesus, and finding certain disciples, he said unto them, Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed? And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost. And he said unto them, Unto what then were ye baptized? And they said, Unto John's baptism. Then said Paul, John verily baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying unto the people, that they should believe on him which should come after him, that is, on Christ Jesus. When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them, and they spake with tongues, and prophesied. And all the men were about twelve.
Discussion: Twelve disciples at Ephesus know John's baptism but not the Holy Ghost, and Paul does not rebuke them for what they lack but leads them from repentance to faith in Jesus, baptism in his name, and the Spirit's coming. Partial knowledge is met with fuller teaching, not contempt. Reflect: 1) How do you test whether someone's faith is complete without questioning their sincerity? 2) What is the difference between John's baptism of repentance and baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus? 3) Why does Luke record this small group so carefully?
Significance: The twelve at Ephesus mark the boundary between John's preparatory ministry and the church's full life in the Spirit, and their completion opens Paul's long Ephesian ministry.
RelatedEvents: Apollos Taught at Ephesus; Paul Teaches in the School of Tyrannus

Story: Paul Teaches in the School of Tyrannus
Retelling: Paul went into the synagogue at Ephesus, and spake boldly for the space of three months, disputing and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God. But when divers were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil of that way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, and disputed daily in the school of one Tyrannus. And this continued by the space of two years, so that all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks.
Discussion: After three months in the synagogue, Paul moves to a rented lecture hall and teaches daily for two years, until a whole province hears the word. The Ephesian ministry is not a campaign but a school: steady, daily, public reasoning. Reflect: 1) When is it right to leave a hostile room and find another? 2) What does two years of daily teaching do that a single visit cannot? 3) How does a local school reach a whole province?
Significance: The school of Tyrannus is the mission's longest classroom: from one hall in Ephesus, the word spreads through all Asia, and the churches of the province trace their hearing to these two years.
RelatedEvents: The Disciples at Ephesus; The Sons of Sceva at Ephesus

Story: The Sons of Sceva at Ephesus
Retelling: God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul, so that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them. Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth. And there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew, and chief of the priests, which did so. And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are ye? And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. And this was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus, and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. And many that believed came, and confessed, and shewed their deeds. Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men, and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver. So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed.
Discussion: The sons of Sceva try to use Jesus' name as a formula, and the spirit's answer exposes them: Jesus is known, Paul is known, but they are not. The result is fear, confession, and a public bonfire of magic books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. Reflect: 1) What is the difference between invoking Jesus' name and knowing Jesus? 2) Why does true conversion at Ephesus cost people their books and their trade? 3) How does the word grow mightily through fear and repentance, not only through miracles?
Significance: Ephesus learns that the name of Jesus is not a spell to be borrowed: borrowed authority fails, genuine faith confesses and burns its past, and the word prevails over the city's magic trade.
Themes: Spiritual Conflict; Repentance; Jesus' Name; Power
RelatedEvents: Paul Teaches in the School of Tyrannus; The Riot at Ephesus

Retelling: After these things, Paul purposed in the spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, After I have been there, I must also see Rome. So he sent into Macedonia two of them that ministered unto him, Timotheus and Erastus, but he himself stayed in Asia for a season. And the same time there arose no small stir about that way. For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen, whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth. Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands, so that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought, but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth. And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians. And the whole city was filled with confusion, and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre. And when Paul would have entered in unto the people, the disciples suffered him not. And certain of the chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre. Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was confused, and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together. And they drew Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. And Alexander beckoned with the hand, and would have made his defence unto the people. But when they knew that he was a Jew, all with one voice about the space of two hours cried out, Great is Diana of the Ephesians. And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter? Seeing then that these things cannot be spoken against, ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly. For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess. Wherefore if Demetrius, and the craftsmen which are with him, have a matter against any man, the law is open, and there are deputies: let them implead one another. But if ye enquire any thing concerning other matters, it shall be determined in a lawful assembly. For we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse. And when he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
Discussion: The riot begins with money, not theology: Demetrius fears for his craft, and a city shouts for two hours in the theatre for a goddess most of the crowd cannot explain. The town clerk, not the apostles, restores order by pointing to lawful courts. Reflect: 1) How often is opposition to the gospel really about wealth and livelihood? 2) What does it mean that Paul's companions, not Paul, are seized, and his friends keep him out? 3) Why does a pagan official's appeal to law protect the church here?
Significance: The Ephesian riot shows the gospel striking at an idol economy: when preaching turns people from gods made with hands, craftsmen, crowds, and civic pride combine, yet the assembly disperses without a verdict against the mission, and Paul's purpose to go to Jerusalem and Rome stands.
KeyPeople: Paul; Timothy; Erastus; Demetrius, the Silversmith; Gaius of Macedonia; Aristarchus; Alexander of Ephesus
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Eutychus Raised at Troas

Retelling: Upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow, and continued his speech until midnight. And there were many lights in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together. And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep, and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead. And Paul went down, and fell on him, and embracing him said, Trouble not yourselves, for his life is in him. When he therefore was come up again, and had broken bread, and eaten, and talked a long while, even till break of day, so he departed. And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted.
Discussion: A long sermon, a warm room, a window seat, and a fall from the third storey: Luke tells it plainly, without scolding Eutychus or Paul. The raising is quiet, Paul embraces the young man, and the church breaks bread and talks till dawn. Reflect: 1) Why does Luke include a story that could embarrass both preacher and hearer? 2) What does Paul's embrace, rather than a display, say about how miracles serve a church? 3) How does a community turn a frightening night into comfort?
Significance: Eutychus's fall and raising is the mission's most human miracle: a young man lost to sleep and restored to life, and a church that leaves its midnight gathering comforted rather than afraid.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders

Story: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
Retelling: From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus, and called the elders of the church. And when they were come to him, he said unto them, Ye know, from the first day that I came into Asia, after what manner I have been with you at all seasons, serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell me by the lying in wait of the Jews, and how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publicly, and from house to house, testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ. And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit unto Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there, save that the Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions abide me. But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God. And now, behold, I know that ye all, among whom I have gone preaching the kingdom of God, shall see my face no more. Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men, for I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God. Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood. For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them. Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears. And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified. I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel. Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me. I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive. And when he had thus spoken, he kneeled down, and prayed with them all. And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul's neck, and kissed him, sorrowing most of all for the words which he spake, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him unto the ship.
Discussion: Paul's farewell is a ministry in miniature: humility, tears, public and house-to-house teaching, a course to finish, a warning about wolves from outside and perverse teachers from inside, and a commendation to God and the word of grace. He asks for nothing but leaves them a saying of Jesus found nowhere in the Gospels: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Reflect: 1) What would it mean to declare the whole counsel of God, not only the popular parts? 2) How do elders feed a flock that wolves will enter? 3) Why does Paul commend them to God and the word, rather than to a successor?
Significance: The Miletus farewell is Paul's testament to the Ephesian elders: a life poured out in teaching and tears, a warning to watch over the blood-bought flock, and a parting prayer that leaves the church in God's hands rather than in Paul's.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Agabus Foretells Paul's Bonds

Retelling: Paul's company came unto Caesarea, and entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven, and abode with him. And the same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy. And as they tarried there many days, there came down from Judaea a certain prophet, named Agabus. And when he was come unto them, he took Paul's girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. Then when they heard these things, both they of that place, and others, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? For I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. And when he would not be persuaded, they ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done.
Discussion: Agabus acts the prophecy with Paul's own girdle, binding his hands and feet, and everyone hears it as a reason not to go. Paul hears it differently: as a warning to be faced, not a prohibition to be obeyed, and he is ready to die at Jerusalem for the name of Jesus. Reflect: 1) How do you tell a prophetic warning from a prophetic command? 2) Why do Paul's friends weep, and why does he call their weeping heart-breaking? 3) When does submitting to the Lord's will mean walking into the danger you were warned about?
Significance: Agabus's acted prophecy gives Paul his clearest warning and his clearest resolve: Jerusalem will bind him and hand him to the Gentiles, and he will go anyway, ready for bonds and for death, because the will of the Lord is to be done.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders; Paul Purifies Himself at the Temple

Story: Paul Purifies Himself at the Temple
Retelling: When Paul was come to Jerusalem, the brethren received him gladly. And the day following Paul went in with his company unto James, and all the elders were present. And when he had saluted them, he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified the Lord, and said unto him, Thou seest, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe, and they are all zealous of the law, and they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs. What is it therefore? The multitude must needs come together, for they will hear that thou art come. Do therefore this that we say to thee: we have four men which have a vow on them. Them take, and purify thyself with them, and be at charges with them, that they may shave their heads, and all may know that those things, whereof they were informed concerning thee, are nothing, but that thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law. As touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled, and from fornication. Then Paul took the men, and the next day purifying himself with them entered into the temple, to signify the accomplishment of the days of purification, until that an offering should be offered for every one of them.
Discussion: Paul, who fought for Gentile freedom, purifies himself with four men under a vow to show Jewish believers he keeps the law himself. The elders hold both truths at once: Gentiles need not keep the law, and Paul has not abandoned it. It is a costly act of peace-making, and it ends in arrest. Reflect: 1) How do you honour another group's conscience without surrendering the gospel? 2) Why does a true report, that Paul teaches Gentiles freedom, become a false rumour that he teaches Jews to forsake Moses? 3) What do you do when a peace-making gesture fails?
Significance: Paul's purification is his last attempt to keep Jewish and Gentile believers together in Jerusalem: he submits to a vow to prove the rumours false, while the elders reaffirm Gentile freedom, and the temple visit that follows leads to his seizure.
Themes: Unity; Peacemaking; Law and Freedom; Misunderstanding
KeyPeople: Paul; James, Brother of Jesus; Luke
RelatedEvents: Agabus Foretells Paul's Bonds; Paul Seized in the Temple

Retelling: When the seven days were almost ended, the Jews which were of Asia, when they saw Paul in the temple, stirred up all the people, and laid hands on him, crying out, Men of Israel, help: this is the man, that teacheth all men every where against the people, and the law, and this place, and further brought Greeks also into the temple, and hath polluted this holy place. For they had seen before with him in the city Trophimus an Ephesian, whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple. And all the city was moved, and the people ran together, and they took Paul, and drew him out of the temple, and forthwith the doors were shut. And as they went about to kill him, tidings came unto the chief captain of the band, that all Jerusalem was in an uproar. Who immediately took soldiers and centurions, and ran down unto them, and when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, they left beating of Paul. Then the chief captain came near, and took him, and commanded him to be bound with two chains, and demanded who he was, and what he had done. And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude, and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle. And when he came upon the stairs, so it was, that he was borne of the soldiers for the violence of the people. For the multitude of the people followed after, crying, Away with him.
Discussion: A supposition becomes a charge: because Trophimus had been seen with Paul in the city, the crowd assumes he was brought into the temple, and a purification visit ends in a lynching stopped only by Roman soldiers. Paul is bound with two chains, exactly as Agabus foretold. Reflect: 1) How does a rumour harden into a mob's certainty? 2) What does it mean that Roman chains, not Jewish justice, first save Paul's life? 3) How do you respond when a false charge is shouted louder than any defence?
Significance: Paul's seizure ends the free missionary journeys and begins his long captivity: dragged from the temple, bound with two chains, and carried up the stairs above a crying crowd, he enters the custody that will carry him to Caesarea and to Rome.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; Paul Addresses the Jerusalem Crowd

Retelling: Standing on the stairs, Paul asked the chief captain for leave to speak to the people, and beckoning with the hand, he addressed them in the Hebrew tongue: Men, brethren, and fathers, hear ye my defence which I make now unto you. When they heard that he spake in the Hebrew tongue, they kept the more silence. He told them he was a Jew, born in Tarsus, brought up in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, zealous toward God as they all were that day, and that he had persecuted this way unto the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women, as the high priest and all the estate of the elders could bear witness, and had received letters to Damascus to bring those in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. He told of the journey at midday, when suddenly there shone from heaven a great light round about him, and he fell to the ground and heard a voice saying, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? And he answered, Who art thou, Lord? And the voice said, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest. Those with him saw the light and were afraid, but heard not the voice. He asked, What shall I do, Lord? And the Lord said, Arise, and go into Damascus, and there it shall be told thee of all things which are appointed for thee to do. Being blinded by the glory of that light, he was led by the hand into Damascus. There Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there, came and said, Brother Saul, receive thy sight, and the same hour he looked up upon him. Ananias said, The God of our fathers hath chosen thee, that thou shouldest know his will, and see that Just One, and shouldest hear the voice of his mouth, for thou shalt be his witness unto all men of what thou hast seen and heard. And now why tarriest thou? Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord. Paul told how, when he had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple in a trance, he saw Jesus saying, Make haste, and get thee quickly out of Jerusalem, for they will not receive thy testimony concerning me. He answered that they knew he had imprisoned and beaten believers, and had consented to Stephen's death and kept the raiment of them that slew him. And Jesus said, Depart, for I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles.
Discussion: Paul's defence is his own story told in the crowd's own tongue: a Pharisee's training, a persecutor's zeal, a light at noon, Ananias's welcome, and a commission. The crowd listens in silence until one word, Gentiles, and then the shouting resumes. Reflect: 1) Why does Paul tell his conversion as a defence rather than arguing his case? 2) What does Ananias's role show about how God uses ordinary believers in great conversions? 3) Where does your own story meet the hearers' prejudice, and what word stops their listening?
Significance: The crowd speech turns Paul's arrest into a witness: his conversion, retold from the stairs in Hebrew, becomes the defence of the gospel itself, and the crowd's breaking point reveals that the Gentile mission is the true charge against him.
KeyPeople: Paul; Ananias of Damascus; Gamaliel, the Pharisee
RelatedEvents: The Conversion of Paul; Paul Claims Roman Citizenship

Retelling: The crowd gave Paul audience unto this word, and then lifted up their voices, and said, Away with such a fellow from the earth, for it is not fit that he should live. And as they cried out, and cast off their clothes, and threw dust into the air, the chief captain commanded him to be brought into the castle, and bade that he should be examined by scourging, that he might know wherefore they cried so against him. And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned? When the centurion heard that, he went and told the chief captain, saying, Take heed what thou doest, for this man is a Roman. Then the chief captain came, and said unto him, Tell me, art thou a Roman? He said, Yea. And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born. Then straightway they departed from him which should have examined him, and the chief captain also was afraid, after he knew that he was a Roman, and because he had bound him.
Discussion: One question stops a scourging: is it lawful to scourge a Roman uncondemned? Paul, free born where his captain bought his freedom at great price, uses a lawful right at the lawful moment, not to escape the gospel's cost but to secure a fair hearing. Reflect: 1) When is claiming a legal right faithfulness, and when is it evasion? 2) How does Paul's free-born citizenship change the terms of his captivity? 3) What lawful protections exist for believers today, and when should they be used?
Significance: Paul's citizenship claim turns a mob's prisoner into a Roman citizen awaiting trial: the scourging is stopped, the captain is afraid, and the path opens to a formal hearing before the Sanhedrin, then to Felix, Festus, Agrippa, and Caesar.
RelatedEvents: Paul Addresses the Jerusalem Crowd; Paul Before the Sanhedrin

Retelling: The next day, because the chief captain would have known the certainty wherefore Paul was accused of the Jews, he loosed him from his bands and commanded the chief priests and all their council to appear, and brought Paul down, and set him before them. And Paul, earnestly beholding the council, said, Men and brethren, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day. And the high priest Ananias commanded them that stood by him to smite him on the mouth. Then said Paul unto him, God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law? And they that stood by said, Revilest thou God's high priest? Then said Paul, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest, for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people. And when Paul perceived that the one part were Sadducees, and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, Men and brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee: of the hope and resurrection of the dead I am called in question. And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the multitude was divided. For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees confess both. And there arose a great cry, and the scribes that were of the Pharisees' part arose, and strove, saying, We find no evil in this man, but if a spirit or an angel hath spoken to him, let us not fight against God. And when there arose a great dissension, the chief captain, fearing lest Paul should have been pulled in pieces of them, commanded the soldiers to go down, and to take him by force from among them, and to bring him into the castle.
Discussion: Paul's hearing collapses into a theological riot: his appeal to conscience, his rebuke of an unlawful blow, and his cry that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection divide Pharisees from Sadducees, and the Pharisees' scribes find no evil in him. The gospel's central claim, resurrection, is what splits the council. Reflect: 1) How do you appeal to conscience without claiming perfection? 2) Why does the resurrection divide even those who share the Scriptures? 3) When does naming the real issue break a deadlock, and when does it inflame one?
Significance: Before the Sanhedrin, Paul's case becomes the resurrection's case: the council that meant to judge him divides over the hope of the dead, and Roman soldiers again carry him to safety, keeping the witness alive for Caesarea.
KeyPeople: Paul; Ananias, the High Priest; Claudius Lysias
RelatedEvents: Paul Claims Roman Citizenship; The Plot against Paul Foiled

Retelling: When it was day, certain of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. And they were more than forty which had made this conspiracy. And they came to the chief priests and elders, and said, We have bound ourselves under a great curse, that we will eat nothing until we have slain Paul. Now therefore ye with the council signify to the chief captain that he bring him down unto you to morrow, as though ye would enquire something more perfectly concerning him, and we, or ever he come near, are ready to kill him. And when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul. Then Paul called one of the centurions unto him, and said, Bring this young man unto the chief captain, for he hath a certain thing to tell him. So he took him, and brought him to the chief captain, and said, Paul the prisoner called me unto him, and prayed me to bring this young man unto thee, who hath something to say unto thee. Then the chief captain took him by the hand, and went with him aside privately, and asked him, What is that thou hast to tell me? And he said, The Jews have agreed to desire thee that thou wouldest bring down Paul to morrow into the council, as though they would enquire somewhat of him more perfectly. But do not thou yield unto them, for there lie in wait for him of them more than forty men, which have bound themselves with an oath, that they will neither eat nor drink till they have killed him, and now are they ready, looking for a promise from thee. So the chief captain then let the young man depart, and charged him, See thou tell no man that thou hast shewed these things to me. And he called unto him two centurions, saying, Make ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, and horsemen threescore and ten, and spearmen two hundred, at the third hour of the night, and provide them beasts, that they may set Paul on, and bring him safe unto Felix the governor. And he wrote a letter after this manner: Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting. This man was taken of the Jews, and should have been killed of them: then came I with an army, and rescued him, having understood that he was a Roman. And when I would have known the cause wherefore they accused him, I brought him forth into their council, perceiving that he was accused of questions of their law, but had nothing laid to his charge worthy of death or of bonds. And when it was told me how that the Jews laid wait for the man, I sent straightway to thee, and gave commandment to his accusers also to say before thee what they had against him. Farewell. Then the soldiers, as it was commanded them, took Paul, and brought him by night to Antipatris. On the morrow they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the castle, who, when they came to Caesarea, and delivered the epistle to the governor, presented Paul also before him. And when the governor had read the letter, he asked of what province he was. And when he understood that he was of Cilicia, he said, I will hear thee, said he, when thine accusers are also come. And he commanded him to be kept in Herod's judgment hall.
Discussion: More than forty men swear to fast until Paul is dead, and the plot is undone by an unnamed nephew who hears of it and tells Paul, who tells a centurion, who tells the captain. God protects Paul through an ordinary family warning and a Roman escort of nearly five hundred soldiers. Reflect: 1) How does God use small, unnamed people in great deliverances? 2) Why does Lysias's letter tell the story more favourably than the facts warrant, and what does that teach about official accounts? 3) What does it mean that Paul's safety comes by night, under guard, to a governor's judgment hall?
Significance: The foiled plot moves Paul from Jerusalem's danger to Caesarea's custody: a nephew's warning, a captain's escort, and a letter to Felix open the long legal road that will end in Rome, and the gospel travels under Roman guard.
RelatedEvents: Paul Before the Sanhedrin; Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa

Retelling: Paul writes that when Peter was come to Antioch, he withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. For before that certain came from James, Peter did eat with the Gentiles, but when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision. And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him, insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation. But when Paul saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, he said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?
Discussion: This is the only apostolic confrontation narrated in the Epistles: Peter's withdrawal from Gentile tables, out of fear, pressures Gentiles to live as Jews, and Paul rebukes him publicly because the truth of the gospel is at stake. The letter gives no record of Peter's reply. Reflect: 1) Why does table fellowship become a gospel issue rather than a manners issue? 2) How does fear make even leaders act against what they believe? 3) When is a public rebuke right, and what does it cost a friendship?
Significance: The Antioch confrontation guards the gospel's freedom: if Peter's fear had stood, Gentiles would have had to become Jews to belong, and Paul's public challenge keeps the table, and the church, open.
KeyPeople: Paul; Simon Peter; Barnabas; James, Brother of Jesus
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Retelling: Paul writes that when he could no longer forbear, he thought it good to be left at Athens alone, and sent Timotheus, his brother and minister of God and fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish the Thessalonians and to comfort them concerning their faith, that no man should be moved by their afflictions. But now when Timotheus came from Thessalonica unto Paul, he brought him good tidings of their faith and charity, and that they had good remembrance of Paul always, desiring greatly to see him, as Paul also desired to see them. Therefore, Paul writes, brethren, we were comforted over you in all our affliction and distress by your faith, for now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord. He asks what thanks they can render to God for all the joy wherewith they joy for their sakes before God, night and day praying exceedingly that they might see their face and perfect that which is lacking in their faith.
Discussion: This is a mission told by letter: a sending from Athens, a visit to a persecuted young church, and a return carrying good news that comforts the sender. Paul's anxiety and joy are both pastoral, not strategic. Reflect: 1) Why does Paul send Timothy rather than going himself? 2) What does it mean to be established and comforted concerning faith in affliction? 3) How does good news from a young church become comfort for its founder?
Significance: Timothy's visit holds the Thessalonian church together after Paul's sudden departure: the young church stands fast, and the report of its faith and love becomes the occasion for Paul's first letter to any church.
Themes: Encouragement; Faith under Affliction; Mission; Pastoral Care
RelatedEvents: Paul at Athens; Paul at Thessalonica

Retelling: Paul writes that when he was come into Macedonia, his flesh had no rest, but he was troubled on every side: without were fightings, within were fears. Nevertheless God, that comforteth those that are cast down, comforted him by the coming of Titus, and not by his coming only, but by the consolation wherewith he was comforted in the Corinthians, when he told Paul of their earnest desire, their mourning, and their fervent mind toward him, so that Paul rejoiced the more. Paul had made them sorry with a letter, and though he had repented of it at first, he now rejoiced, not that they were made sorry, but that they sorrowed to repentance, for godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of, but the sorrow of the world worketh death. He lists what their godly sorrow had wrought: carefulness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge. He writes that he did not write for the cause of him that had done the wrong, nor for his sake that suffered wrong, but that their care for Paul might appear unto them in the sight of God. Therefore they were comforted in their comfort, yea, and exceedingly the more joyed they for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by them all. For if Paul had boasted any thing to Titus of the Corinthians, he was not ashamed, but as he spake all things in truth, even so their boasting, which he made before Titus, was found a truth. And Titus's inward affection was more abundant toward them, whilst he remembered the obedience of them all, how with fear and trembling they received him. Paul closes, I rejoice therefore that I have confidence in you in all things.
Discussion: This is a reconciliation told by letter: a severe letter, a painful visit, and Titus returning with news of repentance that comforts a troubled apostle. Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, which leads to repentance, from the sorrow of the world, which leads to death. Reflect: 1) How do you tell godly sorrow from mere regret? 2) Why does Titus's refreshment matter as much as the Corinthians' repentance? 3) What does it take for a wounded relationship between a church and its founder to be restored?
Significance: Titus's news turns Paul's trouble in Macedonia into joy: the Corinthian church's repentance proves the severe letter's purpose, refreshes Titus, and restores Paul's confidence in a church he had feared losing.
RelatedEvents: Paul at Corinth

Retelling: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy his brother, write unto Philemon, their dearly beloved and fellowlabourer, and to Apphia, and Archippus their fellowsoldier, and to the church in Philemon's house. Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, and for the refreshing of the bowels of the saints by him. He writes that though he might be much bold in Christ to enjoin Philemon to do what is fitting, yet for love's sake he rather beseeches him, being such a one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. He beseeches Philemon for his son Onesimus, whom he hath begotten in his bonds, which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me. Onesimus Paul has sent again, and asks Philemon to receive him, that is, his own bowels, whom Paul would have retained with him, that in Philemon's stead he might have ministered unto him in the bonds of the gospel. But without Philemon's mind would Paul do nothing, that his benefit should not be as it were of necessity, but willingly. For perhaps, Paul writes, Onesimus therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever, not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord. If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account; I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it, albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides. Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord: refresh my bowels in the Lord. Having confidence in thy obedience, Paul writes, I wrote unto thee, knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say. He asks Philemon to prepare him also a lodging, for he trusts that through their prayers he shall be given unto them.
Discussion: The letter does not order Onesimus's fate; it asks. Paul sends back a man who was unprofitable and is now profitable, asks that he be received not as a servant but as a brother beloved, and offers to pay whatever is owed. The gospel remakes a household relationship without a single command about it. Reflect: 1) Why does Paul beseech rather than enjoin, when he could command? 2) What does it mean to receive someone for ever as a brother, not as a servant? 3) How does Paul's offer to pay model the way Christ bears what is owed?
Significance: Onesimus's return is the gospel applied to a household: a man who departed is sent back as a brother, a master is asked to receive him as Paul himself, and the church in Philemon's house is left to work out what brotherhood means in practice.
KeyPeople: Paul; Onesimus; Philemon; Timothy; Apphia; Archippus
RelatedEvents: Paul in Rome

Retelling: Paul writes that he supposed it necessary to send to the Philippians Epaphroditus, his brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but their messenger, and he that ministered to his wants. For Epaphroditus longed after them all, and was full of heaviness, because they had heard that he had been sick. For indeed he was sick nigh unto death, but God had mercy on him, and not on him only, but on Paul also, lest he should have sorrow upon sorrow. Paul therefore sent him the more carefully, that when the Philippians saw him again, they might rejoice, and that Paul might be the less sorrowful. Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness, Paul writes, and hold such in reputation, because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply the lack of service toward Paul on the Philippians' part.
Discussion: Epaphroditus is the church's messenger who nearly dies carrying its gift to a prisoner, and Paul's letter honours him precisely for risking his life in service. His recovery is called mercy, not a reward, and his return is a cause for gladness. Reflect: 1) How do you honour messengers and servants who bear the cost of ministry? 2) Why does Paul say God had mercy on him too, lest he have sorrow upon sorrow? 3) What does it mean to hold such in reputation?
Significance: Epaphroditus's sickness and recovery show the human cost of the gospel's supply lines: a Philippian messenger nearly dies serving a prisoner, God spares him, and Paul sends him home to be received with gladness and honour.
RelatedEvents: Paul in Rome

Retelling: Paul writes to Timothy from prison that at his first answer no man stood with him, but all men forsook him, and he prays that it may not be laid to their charge. Notwithstanding, he writes, the Lord stood with him, and strengthened him, that by him the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear, and he was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. And the Lord shall deliver him from every evil work, and will preserve him unto his heavenly kingdom, to whom be glory for ever and ever. This is Paul's own first-person report of a hearing at Rome, written when he expects his course to be finished, and it is the only account of this defence: Acts ends before it, and no other passage describes the hearing itself.
Discussion: This is not a court transcript but a prisoner's report: deserted by all, strengthened by the Lord, delivered out of the mouth of the lion, and still confident of preservation unto the heavenly kingdom. The letter's context is Paul's expectation of death, which makes the confidence more striking, not less. Reflect: 1) What does it mean to be stood with by the Lord when all men forsake you? 2) How does Paul pray for those who deserted him rather than blaming them? 3) What is the difference between deliverance from death and deliverance unto the heavenly kingdom?
Significance: Paul's first defence, known only from this letter, closes his public witness: deserted at his hearing, strengthened to preach fully to the Gentiles, delivered once from the lion's mouth, and confident of a final deliverance into the heavenly kingdom.
KeyPeople: Paul; Timothy; Luke; Demas; Alexander the Coppersmith
RelatedEvents: Paul in Rome; Paul Before Felix, Festus, and Agrippa

Retelling: The elder writes unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom he loves in the truth, rejoicing greatly because brethren came and testified of the truth that is in him, even as he walketh in the truth, and because of his hospitality toward the brethren and strangers, whom he has brought forward on their journey after a godly sort. John writes that he wrote unto the church, but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. Wherefore, if John comes, he will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against them with malicious words, and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church. Beloved, John writes, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God, but he that doeth evil hath not seen God. Demetrius hath good report of all men, and of the truth itself, yea, and John and his companions also bear record, and Gaius knows that their record is true.
Discussion: Three men stand in one short letter: Gaius, who receives travelling brethren; Diotrephes, who loves preeminence, refuses the elder, talks maliciously, and casts out those who would receive; and Demetrius, who has a good report from all. The occasion is a church's hospitality, and the issue is who rules it. Reflect: 1) How does love of preeminence show itself in a church today? 2) Why is receiving travelling brethren a test of truth, not just of manners? 3) What does it mean to follow good rather than evil when the evil is done by a church leader?
Significance: Diotrephes's refusal is the Epistles' clearest picture of a leader who puts himself above the church: hospitality refused, dissenters cast out, and the elder answered with a commendation of Gaius and Demetrius instead.
KeyPeople: John the Apostle; Gaius (3 John); Diotrephes; Demetrius (3 John)

Story: John's Vision of the Risen Christ on Patmos
Retelling: This is a vision John saw, not an event that happened on earth: John, who also am their brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. He was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and heard behind him a great voice, as of a trumpet, saying, I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, and, What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia: unto Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea. And he turned to see the voice that spake with him, and being turned, he saw seven golden candlesticks, and in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle. His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow, and his eyes were as a flame of fire, and his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace, and his voice as the sound of many waters. And he had in his right hand seven stars, and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword, and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength. And when John saw him, he fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon him, saying unto him, Fear not; I am the first and the last: I am he that liveth, and was dead, and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen, and have the keys of hell and of death. Write the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter. The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
Discussion: Everything in Revelation hangs on this framing: John is exiled on Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and what follows is what he saw and was told to write. The risen Christ is described in symbols, white hair, fiery eyes, brass feet, a sword from his mouth, and he speaks as the first and the last who was dead and is alive for evermore. Read every later vision in this book as vision, not as earthly history. Reflect: 1) Why does the book begin with a command to write rather than with an event? 2) What does it mean for an exiled prisoner to see Christ holding the churches' stars? 3) How does Fear not, from the one who holds the keys of death, steady a persecuted church?
Significance: The Patmos vision commissions the whole book: an exiled apostle sees the risen Christ among the seven churches and is told to write what he has seen, what is, and what shall be hereafter, and every vision that follows is given under that command.
Themes: Vision; Risen Christ; Commission; Comfort in Exile
RelatedEvents: The Letter to the Church in Ephesus

Story: The Letter to the Church in Ephesus
Retelling: In a vision, John was told to write unto the angel of the church of Ephesus: These things saith he that holdeth the seven stars in his right hand, who walketh in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks. I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience, and how thou canst not bear them which are evil, and thou hast tried them which say they are apostles, and are not, and hast found them liars, and hast borne, and hast patience, and for my name's sake hast laboured, and hast not fainted. Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love. Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works, or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent. But this thou hast, that thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches. To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.
Discussion: This is a vision-message, not a historical visit: Christ walks among the candlesticks and knows Ephesus's works, patience, and testing of false apostles, yet charges it with leaving its first love. Orthodoxy without love is the rebuke, and the remedy is to remember, repent, and do the first works. Reflect: 1) How can a church be right about false teachers and still lose its first love? 2) What are the first works in your own life? 3) What does it mean for a church's candlestick to be removed?
Significance: The Ephesian letter warns every orthodox church that labour and patience cannot replace love: remember, repent, and return to the first works, or the light itself is at stake, and the overcomer is promised the tree of life.
RelatedEvents: John's Vision of the Risen Christ on Patmos

Story: The Letter to the Church in Smyrna
Retelling: In a vision, John was told to write unto the angel of the church in Smyrna: These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive. I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, but thou art rich, and I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried, and ye shall have tribulation ten days. Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches. He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.
Discussion: This is a vision-message, and it is the only letter with no rebuke: Smyrna is poor yet rich, facing prison and tribulation, and is told to fear none of it and to be faithful unto death. The crown of life is promised not for success but for faithfulness through suffering. Reflect: 1) How can a poor church be rich? 2) What does faithful unto death mean when death is a real prospect? 3) Why does Christ introduce himself here as the one who was dead and is alive?
Significance: The Smyrna letter is the book's word to a suffering church: poverty is not failure, prison is a trial with a limit, and faithfulness unto death receives a crown of life that the second death cannot touch.
Themes: Suffering; Faithfulness; Poverty and Riches; Martyrdom
RelatedEvents: John's Vision of the Risen Christ on Patmos

Story: The Letter to the Church in Pergamum
Retelling: In a vision, John was told to write unto the angel of the church in Pergamos: These things saith he which hath the sharp sword with two edges. I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is, and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
